title: Atlanta Falcons uniforms: A complete history
summary: Throughout their history, the Atlanta Falcons have undergone several uniform changes, from their original black jerseys and iconic red helmets in 1966 to the more modern designs of recent years. Some looks have become beloved classics, while others have sparked plenty of debate among fans. Whether it’s the classic red helmets, the black throwback jerseys, […]
full_text: Throughout their history, the Atlanta Falcons have undergone several uniform changes, from their original black jerseys and iconic red helmets in 1966 to the more modern designs of recent years. Some looks have become beloved classics, while others have sparked plenty of debate among fans. Whether it’s the classic red helmets, the black throwback jerseys, or the uniforms worn during some of the franchise’s most memorable seasons, each era has brought something unique to Atlanta’s identity. With that in mind, let’s take a look back at the complete history of the Falcons’ uniforms, how they’ve evolved over the years, and some of the memorable players and moments associated with each look. 1966-1970 The 1966 season marked the Atlanta Falcons’ inaugural year in the National Football League, and the team debuted with one of the more unique uniform combinations in the league. The original look featured black jerseys with white numbers outlined in red, white pants, and the now-iconic red helmets featuring the original Falcons logo. The away uniforms featured white jerseys with black numbers, while both combinations included distinctive red and black striping. It’s a classic look that remains a favorite among Falcons fans to this day. One particularly interesting detail was the addition of two thin gold stripes on the helmets. As the story goes, the Falcons’ original uniforms looked a little too similar to those worn by the University of Georgia, which didn’t exactly sit well with their rivals at Georgia Tech. To keep everyone happy, the Falcons incorporated gold into the helmet striping as a nod to Georgia Tech, while maintaining the red and black associated with Georgia. The gold stripes remained through the 1969 season before being removed in 1970. The uniforms also underwent a few minor adjustments in 1968, including the removal of the Falcons logo from the jersey sleeves in favor of additional striping. Otherwise, the original design remained largely unchanged throughout the franchise’s first five seasons. Some of the most recognizable players to wear these uniforms included legendary linebacker Tommy Nobis, the Falcons’ first-ever draft pick, and Hall of Fame defensive end Claude Humphrey. Although Atlanta struggled to find success on the field during its early years, these uniforms established the franchise’s identity. Decades later, the Falcons would bring back this classic combination as a throwback in 2009, proving that sometimes the original look is still one of the best. 1971-1977 The 1971 season brought the first major change to the Falcons’ uniforms, as the team ditched its original black home jerseys in favor of red. The new look featured red jerseys with white numbers outlined in black, along with updated sleeve striping and red socks. The Falcons kept their iconic red helmets and white pants, creating a simple yet classic look that would help define the franchise throughout the 1970s. Although the switch from black to red was significant, the overall design remained relatively unchanged during this era. In fact, red would remain the Falcons’ primary home jersey color all the way through the 1989 season, making it one of the longest-lasting traditions in franchise history. Notable players who wore these uniforms included quarterback Steve Bartkowski, wide receiver Alfred Jenkins, and defensive end Claude Humphrey. While the Falcons didn’t experience much postseason success during this period, these uniforms helped establish the red-and-black identity that fans still associate with the franchise today. 1978-1989 In 1978, the Falcons introduced another significant change to their uniforms, replacing their traditional white pants with silver ones. Personally, I’ve always liked the addition of silver, which became a staple of the Falcons’ color scheme through the 2002 season. The jerseys also received some updates, including more detailed collar and sleeve striping, the return of the Falcons logo to the sleeves, and a switch from black to red numbers on the white road jerseys. Another notable change came in 1984, when the Falcons switched from white facemasks to black, a look that would remain part of the team’s identity for decades to come. This era is perhaps best remembered by longtime Falcons fans for the team’s success during the 1980 season. Led by quarterback Steve Bartkowski, Atlanta finished 12–4, capturing its first division title and setting a franchise record for wins at the time. Other notable Falcons who wore these uniforms included running back Gerald Riggs and wide receiver Alfred Jenkins. Although the team experienced its share of ups and downs throughout the 1980s, the combination of red jerseys, silver pants, and red helmets remains one of the more classic looks in Falcons history. 1990-1996 As the Falcons entered the 1990s, they decided it was time for a bold new look. The team brought back black jerseys as its primary home uniforms, but this time with a major twist: black helmets. For the first time in franchise history, Atlanta ditched its iconic red helmets in favor of an all-black look, signaling a new era for the franchise. Red was almost entirely removed from the uniforms, appearing only as subtle accents around the numbers and along the stripes on the silver pants. The away uniforms also received a makeover, featuring black numbers and black socks to complement the new helmets. It was a simple, intimidating design that quickly became one of the most recognizable looks in Falcons history. Of course, this era is also closely associated with one of the most electrifying players to ever wear a Falcons uniform: Deion “Prime Time” Sanders. Between Sanders’ unforgettable highlights and the team’s embrace of a new identity, these uniforms became synonymous with the Falcons of the early 1990s. Although the design would undergo some minor changes in the years that followed, the introduction of the black helmet helped establish a look that would remain a defining part of the franchise’s identity for decades to come. 1997-2002 In 1997, the Falcons made some subtle improvements to their uniforms, bringing back a little more red to a look that had become predominantly black and white. While the home uniforms remained largely unchanged, the away jerseys once again featured red numbers, along with the return of red socks. It wasn’t a revolutionary redesign by any means, but the added red helped bring back some of the franchise’s original identity. This era also featured some of the greatest moments in Falcons history up to that point. Most notably, the legendary 1998 “Dirty Birds” team, led by head coach Dan Reeves and running back Jamal Anderson, shocked the NFL by finishing 14–2 and advancing to the franchise’s first-ever Super Bowl appearance. Although Atlanta ultimately fell to the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XXXIII, that season remains one of the most memorable in team history. The Falcons also made history during the 2002 playoffs, becoming the first visiting team to defeat the Green Bay Packers in a postseason game at Lambeau Field. Led by a young Michael Vick, Atlanta pulled off a stunning 27–7 victory, ending Green Bay’s previously perfect home playoff record. Between the unforgettable Dirty Birds and Vick’s emergence as one of the NFL’s most exciting young quarterbacks, it’s safe to say these uniforms hold a special place in the hearts of many Falcons fans. 2003-2008 Ahead of the 2003 season, the Falcons underwent one of the most revolutionary changes in franchise history, completely redesigning their uniforms and, for the first time since their inception in 1966, introducing a new primary logo. The updated logo featured a sleeker, more aggressive-looking falcon, incorporating red and silver accents while resembling the letter “F.” The uniforms themselves also received a modern makeover, featuring a new number font, bold striping, and several different combinations. For the first time in franchise history, the Falcons…

title: Falcons vs. Ravens: What will Week 5’s win or loss mean for Atlanta
summary: The season has done a full 180 in the best possible way for the Falcons. Just two weeks ago the doomsday scenarios were being looked at in a magnifying way following two early losses with Cooper Rush under center. Since then, Michael Penix Jr. has returned, the Falcons’ offense has taken off with the arrow […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 24: Linebacker Patrick Queen #6 of the Baltimore Ravens breaks up a pass intended for tight end MyCole Pruitt #85 of the Atlanta Falcons in the second half at M&T Bank Stadium on December 24, 2022 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Rob Carr/Getty Images) | Getty Images The season has done a full 180 in the best possible way for the Falcons. Just two weeks ago the doomsday scenarios were being looked at in a magnifying way following two early losses with Cooper Rush under center. Since then, Michael Penix Jr. has returned, the Falcons’ offense has taken off with the arrow now firmly pointing up. Nothing has given this fanbase as much joy in a very long time as spoiling the New Orleans Saints’ 20th year anniversary of their dome re-opening, and doing it in such an emphatic way on national television. The next test is another one in prime time, this time broadcast into living rooms across the country via NBC on Sunday Night Football. The opponents are the Baltimore Ravens, one of the serial contenders in the AFC. The Falcons caught a break in that they will not have to face Baltimore’s two time MVP winning quarterback Lamar Jackson, but this remains a formidable team nonetheless. Here is the scenario the Falcons face if they beat the Baltimore Ravens in Week 5, as well as if they lose. If the Falcons win They will have completely won back over the majority of the fanbase, including the many folks who are still highly (and very fairly) skeptical waiting in anticipation for the rug to get pulled out from under them. Three straight prime time triumphs will also showcase to the country just how good this team can be and will generate some national respect for the first time in a while. With the Carolina Panthers on a bye week, Atlanta will move into sole possession of first place in the NFC South and this division will all of a sudden not only be a very real goal but also an expectation at this point. The Falcons would win just their third ever game against the Ravens, and their first one since a Thursday Night Football showdown between Matt Ryan and Joe Flacco in 2010. This is the franchise against whom Atlanta has the joint-fewest victories against along the Steelers, who kept that win total at two earlier this season. While it’s still a hilariously low sample size, it will technically be correct to say that Kevin Stefanski will become just the sixth ever Falcons head coach with a record above .500, alongside Mike Smith, Dan Quinn, Leeman Bennett, Jim Mora and Wade Phillips (who has an all time 3-2 record as the head man in Atlanta). If the Falcons lose The wind will promptly be taken out of the sails and the momentum completely halted following back to back dominant wins against NFC opponents. Losing to an AFC team isn’t the end of the world, but for a Falcons team that’s still trying to dig themselves out of the hole they created with Cooper Rush, it’ll still be a blow. For as embarrassed as the Saints were this past week, if they beat Minnesota then they will finish the week tied with the Falcons in second place while the idle Panthers move into sole possession of first place with a 2-2 record. The schedule is tightening up now and there really aren’t too many breaks in it. Games against the Bears, 49ers, Bengals and Chiefs await before the bye week and to go into that stretch below .500, having just lost to a Ravens team missing Lamar, it will feel like one of those missed opportunities that comes back to bite at the end of a season.

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 5: Huntley steps up in spot-start at quarterback
summary: Offense Tyler Huntley played all 76 offensive snaps at quarterback in-place of Lamar Jackson. In the backfield behind him, Derrick Henry’s 42 snaps edged out Justice Hill (35 snaps). Henry was given 24 rushing attempts and Hill had six touches for a season-high 78 scrimmage yards. Hill played a lot late in the game as […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 11: Starting quarterback Tyler Huntley (5) of the Baltimore Ravens with a big smile after winning the Sunday evening NFL game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Baltimore Ravens on October 11, 2026 at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Offense QB: Tyler Huntley 76 RB: Derrick Henry 42, Justice Hill 35 WR: Zay Flowers 62, Rashod Bateman 61, Devontez Walker 45, Chris Moore 7 TE: Mark Andrews 55, Matthew Hibner 30, Josh Cuevas 19, Nick Vannett 19 OL: Emery Jones Jr. 76, John Simpson 76, Ronnie Stanley 76, Roger Rosengarten 74, Carson Vinson 6, Chuma Edoga 1 Tyler Huntley played all 76 offensive snaps at quarterback in-place of Lamar Jackson. In the backfield behind him, Derrick Henry’s 42 snaps edged out Justice Hill (35 snaps). Henry was given 24 rushing attempts and Hill had six touches for a season-high 78 scrimmage yards. Hill played a lot late in the game as the Ravens were in hurry-up offense mode. Every Ravens’ starting offensive lineman nearly went the distance. Roger Rosengarten left the game for two plays after suffering a knee injury early in the game but fortunately returned quickly afterwards. Carson Vinson played two snaps at right tackle in relief of Rosengarten and four snaps as an additional blocker. Chuma Edoga was also used as an extra lineman on one play. Emery Jones Jr. played all 76 snaps in his first career start at right guard. Zay Flowers, who was questionable to play with a foot injury, took 62 offensive snaps with a team-high eight catches. Rashod Bateman nearly matched him with 61 snaps, leading the team in receiving yards (62). It was the biggest snap share of the season for Devontez Walker as the No. 3 wideout (45 snaps). He caught the late touchdown pass in the fourth quarter that resulted in a tied game after a successful two-point conversion. At tight end, Mark Andrews easily led the group with 55 snaps. Andrews caught four passes for 28 yards but had several notable miscues (dropped balls, fumble). Matthew Hibner exited the game early with a hand injury but returned in the second half to finish with 30 snaps. Josh Cuevas had a season-high 26 receiving yards in his 19 snaps. Nick Vannett played his first action of the year and took 19 snaps as well with Durham Smythe now out. Defense DL: Nnamdi Madubuike 53, Travis Jones 38, Calais Campbell 32, Broderick Washington Jr. 15, John Jenkins 10 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 48, Mike Green 37, Zion Young 26, Ethan Burke 17 ILB: Roquan Smith 64, Trenton Simpson 36, Teddye Buchanan 19 CB: Nate Wiggins 64, Marlon Humphrey 64, Chandler Rivers 19, Chidobe Awuzie 2 S: Malaki Starks 62, Kyle Hamilton 60, Jaylinn Hawkins 38 For the third straight game, Nnamdi Madubuike led the defensive line group in snaps played (53). Travis Jones exited the game late after getting shaken up and finished with 38 snaps. On the edge, Tavius Robinson (48 snaps) and Mike Green (367 snaps) led the way with Trey Hendrickson sidelined again. Ethan Burke received a good amount of playing time again as well as the fourth edge rusher. Teddye Buchanan saw his snap count increase slightly for a third consecutive game at linebacker since returning from injury. Buchanan is cleary still playing third banana behind Roquan Smith (64 snaps) and Trenton Simpson (36 snaps), though. Simpson stuffed the sheet again with a tackle for loss, sack and quarterback hit along with seven total tackles. Cornerbacks Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey, who was questionable to play with a calf injury, did not leave the field (64 snaps each). There was a big drop-off to the next corner, Chandler Rivers, whose playing time took a dip from the last few games. Rivers played 19 snaps and veteran Chidobe Awuzie was only on the field for two defensive plays. Kyle Hamilton exited the game briefly with an injury but returned after four plays, in time to make the game-winning interception in overtime. Malaki Starks played all but two snaps on defense (62) and had a team-high 10 tackles with two tackles for loss. Notably, No. 3 safety Jaylinn Hawkins’ snap share took a decrease, as he played just 38 snaps.

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 5: Clutch performances lead to comeback road win
summary: The Baltimore Ravens earned a comeback win on the road in Week 5, defeating the Atlanta Falcons by a touchdown difference (30-23). The Ravens used a game-tying touchdown drive to force overtime and then took the lead with another score, erasing a prior eight-point deficit to come from behind. Here are report card grades for […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against the Atlanta Falcons in overtime of a game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens earned a comeback win on the road in Week 5, defeating the Atlanta Falcons by a touchdown difference (30-23). The Ravens used a game-tying touchdown drive to force overtime and then took the lead with another score, erasing a prior eight-point deficit to come from behind. Here are report card grades for each position group from the exhilarating victory. Quarterback: B+ Tyler Huntley came alive late and delivered a clutch final two drives for the Ravens. Over the final game-tying drive of the fourth quarter and overtime touchdown drive, Huntley completed 12-of-12 passes with multiple timely first-down throws. He capped both drives off with a touchdown via a back-shoulder throw and tough quarterback sneak. Huntley’s performance up to that point was not necessarily spectacular, but the way he came through when needed most. In relief of Lamar Jackson, the backup finished the game with a line of 24-of-32 completed passes for 201 yards and two touchdowns, along with 20 rushing yards and another rushing score. Most importantly, Huntley avoided committing any turnovers. Running Back: A- The Ravens ran for over 200 yards and averaged an efficient 5.9 yards per carry, led by Derrick Henry and Justice Hill. Henry was limited to a longest run of only 11 yards on the night but grinded out 102 yards in total and ran hard in the fourth quarter and overtime. He also an impressive 18-yard receiving score after a catch-and-run screen reception. Justice Hill exploded for 73 rushing yards on just four carries, ripping off a huge 47-yard run where he was lined up in the fullback spot. Wide Receiver: B + The Ravens’ downfield passing attack was limited for most of the game, but their wide receivers made big plays in the fourth quarter and overtime. Huntley connected with Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman and Devontez Walker for timely receptions that moved the chains. Walker reeled in the game-tying touchdown on a back-shoulder catch in the end zone. Flowers finished with a team-high eight catches and 66 scrimmage yards while Bateman had five catches for 62 receiving yards. The starting wide receiver duo combined for eight receptions over the final two drives of the game. Tight End: D+ It was a forgettable performance for Mark Andrews, who had a few costly miscues. He dropped a wide-open pass at the goal line in the first quarter, then fumbled on the second drive of the game and it was returned by the Falcons for a touchdown. Andrews was unable to reel in a two-point conversion catch in the third quarter that would have tied the game. He did catch a couple first down grabs late in the game to help move the chains. Josh Cuevas had a season-high two catches for 26 yards and Matthew Hibner was not targeted after exiting with a hand injury early in the contest – although he did return later in the second half. Offensive Line: B- The Ravens surrendered four sacks and eight quarterback hits on the night. Huntley was not able to get comfortable in the pocket in the first half and was flushed out into a scramble drill on several occasions. However, the Ravens’ offensive line settled down in pass protection more as the game went along. They also did a good job getting push in the run game, springing Hill free for long breakaway run and Henry for multiple positive-yardage gains. Vega Ioane struggled with some low snaps but was strong as a blocker at center again. As a unit, the offensive line did a much better job with penalties as well. Defensive Line: B Bijan Robinson finished the game with 86 rushing yards on 17 carries (5.1 yards per carry), but the Ravens were able to control him at the line of scrimmage for most the night. A good chunk of Robinson’s damage came on two long runs. Calais Campbell, Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones all made plays up front. Madubuike and Jones each had a quarterback hit on Michael Penix, while Campbell recorded a tackle for loss. Edge Rusher: A- Mike Green’s strong run of play continued in Atlanta with another impactful showing. Green had a sack, quarterback hit and two tackles for loss. He set the edge well and made strong stops against the run. Tavius Robinson similarly had a high-level performance. Robinson stuffed the stat sheet, recording six tackles along with a sack, quarterback hit, pass defense and tackle for loss. The Ravens were disciplined on the edge for most of the game against the Falcons’ rushing attack and crashed inside well to close gaps. Ethan Burke played a good amount of snaps again with Hendrickson sidelined and had three tackles. Linebacker: B + Trenton Simpson’s career-best campaign marched along on Sunday night as he posted seven tackles with a sack, tackle for loss and quarterback hit. Simpson was party to a couple passes allowed in zone coverage but otherwise had another impactful all-around game. Roquan Smith had eight tackles, which ranked second among all Baltimore defenders. Smith and Simpson are pairing well together as a tandem. Teddye Buchanan added two tackles of his own as the third banana of the group. Cornerback: B- The Ravens had some difficulties covering star wide receiver Drake London, who racked up 118 yards on seven catches. He did most of his damage against zone coverage, though, but did get behind Nate Wiggins for a long reception. Jahan Dotson also beat the Ravens’ deep for a 36-yard catch. Wiggins had a tackle for loss and Marlon Humphrey recorded a clutch quarterback hit, pressuring Penix on a play action pass to force an incompletion. Chandler Rivers had a costly missed tackle on a short third-down throw in the flat. Safety: A- Malaki Starks had a strong performance against the Falcons, racking up a team-high 10 tackles with two tackles for loss. Starks had some timely wrap-ups in the open field and was very impactful versus the run, providing a lurking presence against Robinson. Kyle Hamilton’s game-sealing interception in overtime was textbook deception and high IQ, as he read the eyes of the quarterback perfectly. Hamilton had six tackles with a pass defense and missed a few plays after suffering an injury before returning. He remains the most indispensable player on the Ravens’ defense. Special Teams: B+ Tyler Loop was a big factor in the Ravens’ win, as he accounted for all of the team’s points in the first half. Loop made two 51-yard field goals and another chip shot from 21 yards out. LaJohntay Wester’s lone punt return opportunity turned into a nice 11-yard gain. Rasheen Ali had a big tackle in the return game.

full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Head coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens reacts with Tyler Huntley #5 following the 30-23 victory in overtime against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens stole a 30-23 overtime win from the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday night. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s top takeaways from the thrilling victory: Jesse Minter and his staff deserve credit for confident finish Jesse Minter landed on a favorite mantra shortly after arriving in Baltimore: “Be at your best when the best is needed.” His team heeded his words on Sunday night, overcoming self-inflicted errors throughout the first three quarters for a masterful fourth-quarter comeback and overtime win. There were big moments when the Ravens fell short, but in the biggest ones, calm coaching and smooth execution prevailed. Minter and his staff were prepared for seemingly every scenario. Case in point: asking Tyler Huntley to drive 70-plus yards down the field for a game-tying touchdown was probably not on Baltimore’s pre-game wish list. But Declan Doyle pulled all the right levers, including targeting Falcons depth cornerback Mike Ford as soon as he entered the game for a touchdown. Doyle followed that up with a brilliant two-point conversion call, using Zay Flowers as eye candy to break Derrick Henry into open space out on a wildcat sweep. Opting to take the ball in overtime to keep a gassed Falcons defense on the field for a long, punishing drive was another smart decision that paid off with a Huntley touchdown seven minutes and 14 plays later. – Nikhil Mehta It’s time for a changing of the guard at tight end After looking fairly good through the first four weeks of the season, Mark Andrews’ performance in Week 5 was a reminder of his limitations at this stage of his career. While he did have a couple of timely first-down catches in the fourth quarter and overtime, it was a disaster class showing from Andrews up to that point. The veteran dropped a would-be touchdown on the opening drive of the game, failed to reel in a two-point conversion catch that would have tied the score, and lost a fumble that was then returned for a touchdown. He also failed to reel in a couple other passes that were knocked out of his hands by a defender. Andrews can still have value to the offense, but the Ravens need to begin featuring their rookie tight ends more and lessen his role. Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas have both shown some pass-catching juice in their limited opportunities thus far. They both bring more to the table athletically than Andrews does right now, and Andrews’ hands unfortunately continue to prove themselves as unreliable in big spots. – Frank Pla tko The Ravens badly needed a real center First-round rookie Vega Ioane deserves praise for stepping in as the Ravens’ emergency center over the past few weeks, but his inconsistent snapping would have cost the team eventually. Huntley did an excellent job of handling Ioane’s snaps on Sunday night, but last week’s acquisition of Cam Jurgens will hopefully bring some stability via a true center. Ioane will also be able to move back to his natural position, where he can continue a strong start to his NFL career without the burden of running the operation at the line of scrimmage. – Nikhil Mehta Baltimore is turning over a new leaf in close games After the win, Kyle Hamilton and Zay Flowers both acknowledged that the Ravens have a history of losing these tight matchups. But Jesse Minter’s “be at your best when the best is needed mantra” may have taken root in the locker room. His team did not play their best football for the first three quarters, but the defense kept them in the game and the offense mounted two impressive scoring drives to close it out. That would have been impressive with Lamar Jackson and Trey Hendrickson on the field; without them, it’s a tremendous accomplishment. – Nikhil Mehta
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens-Falcons game balls: Tyler Huntley commands offense to OT win
summary: The Baltimore Ravens stunned the Atlanta Falcons in a 30-23 overtime win on Sunday night. Here are the Ravens most responsible for the victory: QB Tyler ‘Snoop Huntley Say it with me: SNOOOOOOOOOOP. Every Huntley dropback was a heart attack until late in the fourth quarter, when he confidently drove the offense 71 yards in […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens reacts during the first quarter against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens stunned the Atlanta Falcons in a 30-23 overtime win on Sunday night. Here are the Ravens most responsible for the victory: QB Tyler ‘Snoop Huntley Say it with me: SNOOOOOOOOOOP . Every Huntley dropback was a heart attack until late in the fourth quarter, when he confidently drove the offense 71 yards in under two minutes for a game-tying touchdown and two-point conversion. In overtime, he understood the assignment: take care of the ball, stay ahead of the sticks, and chew away as much of the 10 minutes as possible. Any time the Ravens can take home a victory without Lamar Jackson, Snoop adds another game ball to his cabinet. – Nikhil Mehta S Kyle Hamilton Georgia-raised safety Kyle Hamilton was a hometown villain on Sunday night. With 500 friends and family in Mercedez-Benz Stadium, he was inches away from a tide-turning play throughout the contest and finally delivered in the biggest moment possible. Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa tried to look Hamilton off on his game-ending interception, but the All-Pro defender wasn’t fooled and slammed the door shut on an overtime win. This should be the first play on Hamilton’s Defensive Player of the Year highlight tape. – Nikhil Mehta RB Derrick Henry On National Running Back Day, Henry outrushed Bijan Robinson and proved the NFL’s ballcarrier crown still belongs to The King. His 4.2 yards per carry were not anything to write home about, but he protected the ball and consistently picked up chunk gains on early downs to keep Baltimore’s offense ahead of the sticks. Henry then bullied a gassed Falcons defense into submission in overtime with a series of punishing runs that set up the game-winning score. They say Father Time is undefeated, but there’s a reason he keeps ducking Henry. His ability to get the edge at 32 years old and 250 pounds is unparalleled, and the Ravens needed it on Sunday night. – Nikhil Mehta Wide receiver room When the Ravens needed it most, these guys showed up. Zay Flowers was a clear focal point as always with eight catches for 53 yards. But it was Bateman who lead the group this week with 62 yards on five catches. Both were vital to the final two drives that tied the game and then won it in overtime. Then Tez Walker caught a beautiful back shoulder fade ball to give the top trio an excellent day when they needed to step up without their main quarterback. The passing offense runs through those three guys right now. – Zach Canter K Tyler Loop The redemption arc season the Ravens’ second-year kicker continued in Atlanta, where Loop was a perfect 3-for-3 on field goal attempts and made an extra point. Each of Loop’s field goal makes came in the first half, where he accounted for all nine of the team’s points. Loop connected on two 51-yard attempts and nailed a 21-yard chip shot. His field goals kept the Ravens within striking distance. If he missed even one of the three first-half attempts, the Ravens go into halftime trailing by over a touchdown instead of just four points and ultimately the game could have gone differently. Loop is still perfect on 50+ yard kicks for the season. – Frank Platko

title: Ravens Roundtable: Reactions to a thrilling comeback victory in Week 5
summary: After trailing for most of their Sunday night matchup with the Atlanta Falcons, the Ravens secured a come-from-behind victory thanks to some late-game heroics on both sides of the ball. Here are the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reactions to a thrilling 30-23 Ravens’ win in Week 5. Wow. I barely gave the Ravens a fighting chance […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against the Atlanta Falcons in the first quarter of a game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images After trailing for most of their Sunday night matchup with the Atlanta Falcons, the Ravens secured a come-from-behind victory thanks to some late-game heroics on both sides of the ball. Here are the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reactions to a thrilling 30-23 Ravens’ win in Week 5. Wow. I barely gave the Ravens a fighting chance in this game. I saw a path with limiting the Falcons to field goals and not turning the ball, but I figured eventually, Bijan Robinson and Atlanta’s new high powered offense would get them. Instead, the defense stood up, only allowed one touchdown all game, kept Robinson under 100 yards, and sealed the game with an interception. Despite rocky play and failing to seize moments multiple times by Huntley and the offense in the middle of the game, they showed up when it mattered. Their last two drives to tie the game and get the overtime score were masterful. Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, and Tez Walker took over when they needed it. Now the Ravens will get Lamar Jackson, Trey Hendrickson, and Ja’Kobi Lane back soon while the defense continues to get better. — Zach Canter Somehow, someway, the Ravens walked into Atlanta and took down a red-hot Falcons team without Lamar Jackson. Things looked shaky at certain points in this one, but Baltimore stuck to Derrick Henry while Tyler Huntley delivered when it mattered most. The defense had issues getting stops on third down, but was otherwise strong against a previously humming Atlanta offense, and when a play was needed to win the game, Kyle Hamilton stepped up with the interception in overtime. Baltimore moves to the top of the AFC North now with a chance of Jackson returning next week for their first divisional game against the Browns. You cannot overstate just how impressive and important this win is for this team. Jesse Minter and Declan Doyle deserve a ton of credit. — Dustin Cox With the odds stacked against them, and their star QB out, the Ravens gutted out an incredible win against the red-hot Atlanta Falcons. The Ravens looked like the better team for most of the night but, a few costly mistakes put them in a hole late in the fourth quarter. Fortunately, Tyler Huntley was able to lead the Ravens down the field for the tie, 2pt conversion, and win in overtime. Huntley was largely ineffective tonight but showed up when it mattered. Defensively the Ravens were largely impressive, only allowing 17 points. Some of the 3rd down mistakes and missed tackle issues reared their head, but they stepped up when they needed to. With Jackson still healing from his injury, the Ravens are now at 4-1 a-top the AFC North. More importantly, we’ve seen some resilience from these Ravens over the last few games that just wasn’t there in prior years. — Stephen Bopst This was a huge confidence-building win for the Ravens. For most of the game, they appeared destined to come up short largely due to some poor execution in timely moments. However, with their backs against the wall, Tyler Huntley and the starting offense delivered in a huge way. Huntley’s composure over the final two drives and the contributions from an array of playmakers was impressive. For a backup quarterback in a big spot on the road, Huntley’s performance late was nothing short of clutch. Jesse Minter’s defense locked in late as well and Kyle Hamilton’s game-sealing interception was a fitting cherry on top. Minter and the coaching staff put together a sound gameplan that, if not some notable offensive miscues (dropped balls, fumble returned for a touchdown), may have resulted in a more convincing victory. — Frank Platko

title: The benefit of Buffalo Bills needing to lean on youth against Rams in Week 5
summary: I like to avoid low-hanging fruits, and the large, ripe, and colorful low-hanging fruit for this gameday column would be to wax poetic about the Buffalo Bills dealing with adversity for the first time this season after their loss to the Patriots in Week 4. I’m going in a different direction. Injuries are a frustrating, […]
full_text: I like to avoid low-hanging fruits, and the large, ripe, and colorful low-hanging fruit for this gameday column would be to wax poetic about the Buffalo Bills dealing with adversity for the first time this season after their loss to the Patriots in Week 4. I’m going in a different direction. Injuries are a frustrating, ubiquitous element of football, particularly in the NFL. Sometimes, they force a team’s hand in the necessary direction. There’ll be no Josh Palmer tonight against the Rams. He injured his shoulder late in practice this week. Bills starting veteran slot cornerback Dee Alford got hurt against New England. He missed practice on Thursday and Friday before getting in a limited session on Saturday. He’s questionable. Rookie Skyler Bell would replace Palmer. Brady said so himself. Rookie Jalon Kilgore may very well fill in for Alford in the nickel spot. It’s very likely neither has every intricacy of Brady’s offense or Leonhard’s defense ingrained into their minds yet. But it’s not as if Palmer or the rest of the Bills secondary, those who’ve forced Bell and Kilgore into healthy scratch status the first month of the season, have followed their respective duties within the offensive and defensive schemes to regularly be at the right place at the right time in the first four games. What Bell and Kilgore can bring — speed and explosiveness. Bell ran 4.40 with a 41-inch vertical and 133-inch broad jump. That 40-yard dash time placed in the 85th percentile among all combine WRs since 1999. The jumps were in the 95th percentile. At the UConn Pro Day, Bell managed a blisteringly fast 6.65 second time in the three-cone drill that measures agility. At nearly 6’2” and 210 pounds, Kilgore ran 4.40 in the 40-yard dash (94th percentile) with a 37-inch vertical and 130-inch broad jump (92nd percentile). Sure, the Rams are not an American Athletic Conference foe that’d be familiar to Bell. They’re drastically more collectively challenging than any SEC opponent Kilgore faced during his time at South Carolina. But their raw talent should be viewed as a welcomed addition to a team that’s suddenly trying to find itself on offense and has yet to piece together a full game of sound defense this season. Even T.J. Sanders, the club’s second-round pick a year ago — an excellently explosive athlete in his own right — should make his 2026 debut with Ed Oliver out. Now, Oliver is a proven disruptive force on the interior. But playing next to Deone Walker should provide Sanders ample one-on-one opportunities to showcase all of his natural gifts at defensive tackle. And how did I get this far into this column without mentioning my ultimate draft crush, linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr? I loved what I saw from him on film last week . He’s another youthful, high-caliber athlete at his position. His 40-yard dash, vertical, and broad jump all placed in the 84th percentile or higher at linebacker. In an ideal world, a coordinator has nothing but experienced veterans working in perfect unison within the system thanks to a their strong grasp of what each individual play is set out to accomplish. The NFL is hardly an ideal world. Scheme knowledge is vital. Communication is key. Those skills usually come with experience. But sometimes a team is forced to roll with inexperience. The upside in the Bills collection of youngsters — they’re all tremendous athletes. And for as much as scheme matters, oftentimes in this game the best athletes are those who make the biggest plays, even if they aren’t an extension of the coach on the field. With Bell, Kilgore, Sanders, and Elarms-Orr (potentially) moving into more prominent roles, don’t be surprised if the Bills look faster and more explosive in tonight’s game.

title: Buffalo Bills fans beginning to doubt team’s chances in 2026
summary: The Buffalo Bills’ Week 4 loss to the New England Patriots feels like ages ago, and it’s left a very sour taste in the collective mouths of Bills Mafia. The extra time off ahead of Week 5 has allowed doubt to creep in from all corners of the football world. To put the wrongs of […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills’ Week 4 loss to the New England Patriots feels like ages ago, and it’s left a very sour taste in the collective mouths of Bills Mafia. The extra time off ahead of Week 5 has allowed doubt to creep in from all corners of the football world. To put the wrongs of last week behind them, Buffalo must rebound by taking down a potent Los Angeles Rams team in primetime under the lights of Monday Night Football . No pressure, right? It comes with the territory when a team wins as consistently as the Bills have since quarterback Josh Allen rose to stardom. So how are Bills fans feeling in the aftermath of the team’s first loss of the season — also its first loss in the new Highmark Stadium? Confidence is at a season low, and among the lowest figures we’ve seen since starting this endeavor some seasons back. Fans down on Bills heading into Week 5 Just 27% of Rumblings voters are confident the team is headed in the right direction. Yikes! Quarterback Josh Allen picked a really bad game to struggle, and the defense had zero answers for quarterback Drake Maye and company. More to the point, it’s uncertain when or how Buffalo’s defense will improve under the direction of defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. We’ve heard that this season will be a bit of a bridge as the team continues its transition from a base 4-3 to a base 3-4 scheme. Right now fans and analysts are curious whether the biggest problem is a matter of system or personnel. If the current players given long-term contracts don’t mesh well with the new defense, that could have adverse affects on the team’s salary cap in the near and distant future. You’ll often hear some variety of: “With Josh Allen, no Super Bowl window is ever closed.” That’s true and remains the team’s goal. However, it might have been a bit generous expecting the same level of success sustained during prior head coach Sean McDermott’s tenure. Buffalo should fight its way to a playoff berth, but it’s going to be a bumpy ride. This is a new era at One Bills Drive, and Joe Brady is not Sean McDermott. It’s going to take time for things to properly gel, and the front office believes Brady is the right person to get the team over the hump in the playoffs. Last Sunday’s loss to the Patriots smelled a lot like the one McDermott’s team lost at home last season. Like that situation, the Bills may find themselves chasing the Patriots for a while into the back half of the regular season. Winning division games is key to chasing a first-round bye. So far in 2026, the Bills are 0-1 in that column, with five more to go against the AFC East. Bills Mafia not confident Buffalo wins vs. Rams Week 5 Rumblings voters are also a bit skeptical about the Bills winning their Week 5 matchup with the Rams. The results of our poll showed just 40% of respondents saying that Buffalo will win and improve to 4-1 following their Monday Night Football game. Okay, the Rams are a good team and remain one of the popular picks to represent the NFC in Super Bowl LXI. The game will be played in their home stadium, after all. They have the current NFL MVP in quarterback Matthew Stafford, a talented group of wide receivers in Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, a stellar rushing attack led by Kyren Williams, and a pair of future Pro Football Hall of Fame defenders in Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald. But the Rams are beatable. Their defense hasn’t scared often in the first month. Garrett is currently sidelined after having knee surgery following his Week 1 Rams debut in Australia. Donald looks old, and their special teams are a work in progress. Buffalo could go into SoFi Stadium and steal a win in primetime. Like the last matchup between these teams, it could turn into an offensive shootout. Both teams run heavy 13 personnel, so it could also turn into a ground & pound event. Who knows? Will the 40% of confident Bills fans prove correct when the dust settles on Week 5? Never count out Josh Allen! Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? title: 5 Buffalo Bills to watch at the Los Angeles Rams
summary: The Buffalo Bills fly out west this week for a big-time battle against the Los Angeles Rams. While the Bills might have the better record on the season, the oddsmakers have less confidence in Buffalo than they do Los Angeles. Buffalo is anywhere from a 2.5-to-3-point underdog this week, so if we take into account […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 4: Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills looks to tackle during the NFL game against the New England Patriots at Highmark Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills fly out west this week for a big-time battle against the Los Angeles Rams. While the Bills might have the better record on the season, the oddsmakers have less confidence in Buffalo than they do Los Angeles. Buffalo is anywhere from a 2.5-to-3-point underdog this week, so if we take into account the three points Vegas usually gives home teams, it’s essentially a pick ‘em. However, after losing 29-26 to the New England Patriots at home last week, the mood around the Bills has shifted a little. Quarterback Josh Allen looked hesitant to run, and he threw a bad interception to end the game. The Bills’ defense couldn’t stop a nose bleed, let alone an opposing offense, as they allowed New England to secure season-high totals in points (29), first downs (26), total yards (405), passing yards (262), and rushing yards (143). The Bills are going to need a much more consistent offensive effort combined with a significantly better defensive effort if they want to fly back to the Eastern time zone with a win. One player who obviously needs to step up is Josh Allen, so I’m intentionally leaving him off this week. We know he needs to play well, but here are five of his teammates who need to have a big day in order for the Bills to pull out a big win in the City of Angels. _____________________________________________________________________________ TE Dalton Kincaid There has been a lot of discourse about Kincaid’s blocking ability—or lack thereof—making it difficult for head coach and offensive play-caller Joe Brady to keep Kincaid on the field. That may be true, as Kincaid often serves as an indicator for defense about the play Buffalo is set to run: If it’s a run play, they almost never run directly to Kincaid’s side, and if it’s a pass play, opponents can treat him like a wide receiver rather than as a tight end. Regardless of whether his blocking struggles (he’s definitely improved in that area, although nobody is going to confuse him with teammate Jackson Hawes, let alone Dawson Knox), Kincaid needs to be a big part of the passing game. He can’t see just one target in the first 58 minutes of the game. He can’t make his first reception on the team’s final drive. Kincaid has to be a consistent target, especially if DJ Moore is out or limited by his injured shoulder. Brady has to find ways to use his best playmakers, and Kincaid is inarguably one of his best. Look for the Bills to try to find ways to put the ball in his hands early. G Alec Anderson This next statement could really go for the whole interior line, but I’m going to focus on the new guy in the starting lineup. Aaron Donald is likely to play this week. He may have just come out of retirement, but he still has plenty of juice left. Donald is one of the best defensive tackles ever to play the game, so the Bills need to have a plan to limit him. Anderson’s play has been spotty this season. I’ve found him to be good in double-team situations where he can help, but he’s left a lot to be desired as an anchor or in one-on-one blocks. Buffalo’s offensive line has regressed this season, and while Anderson isn’t the only issue (his counterpart on the left side has had a poor year in pass protection, as well), he’s one of them. Monday night would be a good time for him to have an “invisible” performance. If we aren’t talking about the offensive line, then we know they did their jobs. Let’s hope we don’t have to say much about No. 70 this week. OLB Greg Rousseau On defense, the key to Buffalo’s game plan has to be pressuring quarterback Matthew Stafford. If Buffalo can influence the veteran by speeding him up and putting him on the ground, it’s going to help their struggling secondary about as much as any shift in scheme could help. Whereas Drake Maye beat the Bills with his legs last week, buying time in the pocket to make strong off-platform throws and scrambling for 54 yards on eight rushes, Stafford is more stationary at age 38. He can still slide and avoid in the pocket, but he’s not going to take off and scramble much. Rousseau has six sacks already this season, as he’s taken a huge leap forward in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme. He needs to impact the game, and he can do it in multiple ways: strip sacks, QB knockdowns, pass bat-downs, and other plays that disrupt the timing and flow of the Los Angeles offense will lead to good things for the Bills. ILB Terrel Bernard Buffalo’s “green-dot” on defense is a polarizing player at this point. Fans and media members see a player who isn’t playing as well as he has in the past, but coaches continue to praise his play and talk about how well he’s doing his job on the field. Bernard has 29 tackles, second on the team. He has one pass deflection, one tackle for loss, and one fumble recovery. According to Pro Football Reference , he’s also missed five tackles and allowed 11 completions for 112 yards on 16 total targets. I’m far from an expert, but I see a player who has lost a step. I also see a player who is trying to process a new defense, which could be contributing to the slower-than-expected reactions to plays I think he would have made two years ago. It’s also possible that injuries have sapped Bernard of his best trait as a player: quickness. Whatever the case, a game where he reacts quickly and decisively to what’s in front of him would be nice, especially against a talented, efficient Rams squad. The Bills need him to be better, regardless of what the coaching staff says publicly. S Cole Bishop Where is he going to line up this week? With the team down its top three slot corners—Dee Alford has an ankle injury, Jordan Hancock is on injured reserve with a hamstring injury, and Te’Cory Couch hurt his hamstring in his debut from the practice squad—defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard had to be creative last week. He had Damar Hamlin in the slot, which didn’t work, and he also had Bishop move inside in some nickel situations. Bishop was beaten badly by Hunter Henry on the last meaningful play from scrimmage of the game, as he sold out on the run fake with New England facing a third-and-ten. Bishop has the athleticism to move around the back of the defensive formation, but he hasn’t yet shown the awareness to do more than one task at once. Depending on what Leonhard wants to do, or has to do thanks to injuries, we might see Bishop in some different places this week. It would be a good time for him to make a play on the ball, as well, though he might end up in the slot matching up against someone like Puka Nacua. Bishop has 25 tackles this season without a pass breakup to his line. Dee Alford is listed as questionable thanks to his ankle injury, so we’ll see if he’s ready to go tomorrow night. Whether he is or not, Bishop making a play would certainly help Buffalo’s chances on Monday.

title: Buffalo Bills game-day drink: Gam Gam’s Secret ready for primetime in Week 5
summary: How the heck long have I been doing this anyway? It doesn’t matter; the mad-kitchen scientist is back for another season of recipes to make your Buffalo Bills game days even more memorable. For those of you new to this, it’s pretty simple. We love the Bills. We love food. Every week, you’ll get a […]
full_text: How the heck long have I been doing this anyway? It doesn’t matter; the mad-kitchen scientist is back for another season of recipes to make your Buffalo Bills game days even more memorable. For those of you new to this, it’s pretty simple. We love the Bills. We love food. Every week, you’ll get a themed recipe based on the Bills and their opponent. This week you’re getting a fun one, but you’re going to want to plan ahead for Monday. Sharing this early on Sunday will hopefully allow you to budget time in the day to stop at your favorite liquor store that hopefully sells corn whiskey (I can recommend Mellow Corn ), or you could substitute with your preferred bourbon. Gam Gam’s Secret Recently I made a reference to the movie Beerfest , which is an all-time great. Then the Rams game was coming up, and there’s a SPECTACULAR reference to rams (the animal), which led me to the idea to make a drink for this week’s game. We’re calling it “Gam Gam’s Secret” but if you know the movie, you know the real name of this cocktail. Based off of the Brown Derby drink with a little agricultural and spicy twist to it, Gam Gam’s Secret will help you for any international beer drinking competition. Because if you can drink this, **** you can drink almost anything. This recipe is for Rumblers who are 21 and over. Please drink responsibly. Gam Gam’s Secret Makes: About 8 drinks Active time: 10 min Total time: 3 hours Ingredients 1 serrano pepper, seeded, chopped 1 shot (1.5 oz) + 16 oz corn whiskey, divided (see directions) 1/2 cup water 1/2 cup honey 8 oz grapefruit juice (1 oz per drink) Essentials: Measuring cups; shaker, ice, and garnish (if you like); it’s a drink, I think you can handle it Soak chopped serrano in measuring cup filled with one shot of corn whiskey 2-3 hours. Make honey syrup : Add 1/2 cup warm water and 1/2 cup honey to separate measuring cup; stir until honey is thoroughly mixed in. Combine 2 oz corn whiskey, 1 oz grapefruit juice, and 1 oz prepared honey syrup into shaker with ice. Shake until chilled, 10-15 seconds; pour into serving glass. Garnish as desired, and enjoy responsibly. The recipe should yield about 1 cup of prepared honey syrup, which is enough for eight drinks. Wingin’ It tips I don’t have many tips on this one. I’m a big fan of chilling everything and skipping the shaker, but I know that can be controversial with bartending. Feel free to also play around with the ratio of things, if you want it sweeter go ahead and increase the syrup amount. Also, I should note that corn whiskey might not be easy to find. I had recently tried some at a Polish festival and was impressed. I also figured the clear color would help steer this away from a brown liquid. Alas, without a ton of driving, I wasn’t getting my hands on the clear stuff, but my sister picked up a bottle of Mellow Corn , which was perfect for the flavor profile I wanted — and it’s yellow, which also works if you know the Beerfest reference. I originally wasn’t sure if I’d get my hands on corn whiskey, so I tried it with bourbon as well (which is what’s in a Brown Derby). I will say that I preferred the corn whiskey in this, and it’s more “Western New York-y”. That said, the bourbon was also quite good. full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after defeating the Detroit Lions 32-26 at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers entered their Week 5 bye exhilarated and exhausted. A thrilling and convincing win over the Detroit Lions on Sunday Night Football in Week 4 put the team atop the NFC South. Injuries have mounted for the Panthers, but an early bye has the team set to return players who were injured both during and before the season. How did the rest of the NFC South fare this week? Week 5 NFC South results Tampa Bay Buccaneers 24, Dallas Cowboys 16 The 1-4 Bucs notched their first win of the season against the Cowboys on Thursday Night Football thanks to the efforts of undrafted free agent quarterback Jalon Daniels. Daniels was playing in relief of an injured Baker Mayfield and may have, albeit briefly, saved head coach Todd Bowles’ job. Put one way, chaos is afoot in Tampa. Put another, grab your popcorn and let’s watch this dumpster burn. Minnesota Vikings 23, New Orleans Saints 13 The now 1-4 New Orleans Saints have come along way since being crowned the 2026 NFC South champs by most of the national media in the offseason. Tyler Shough, expected to be the division MVP if that were a thing, completed 16 of 25 passes for 96 yards and two interceptions. They will still be a tough out for the Panthers, because that’s how the NFC South works, but they seem less like the ascendant team who lucked into a talented quarterback and more like Uncle Rico and his imaginary friends trying to throw a ball over that mountain. Baltimore Ravens 30, Atlanta Falcons 23 (OT) The 2-3 Falcons are the closest competition the Panthers have in the South. Michael Penix has been a revelation at quarterback compared to Cooper Rush and their defense has been taking major strides forward in recent weeks, sort of They took the momentum of a two-week winning streak against the Packers and the Saints and snapped it against a Ravens team without Lamar Jackson. Their defense, despite giving up 30 points to Tyler Huntley & co., played alright. This loss largely comes down to their offense. Penix’s crew didn’t score until late in the second quarter and then couldn’t finish a drive in the fourth. Settling for two field goals despite holding the ball for 12:58 in the fourth quarter doomed the Falcons as much as Penix’s game sealing interception in overtime. NFC South Standings Carolina Panthers (2-2) Atlanta Falcons (2-3) Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) New Orleans Saints (1-4)

title: Bears vs. Packers: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and Jordan Love’s Explosives
summary: All that offensive ball control dominance the Chicago Bears have had so far this season didn’t help them against Jordan Love and the explosive Green Bay Packers offense yesterday. In Chicago’s 31-7 loss, Love was 25 of 31 (80.6%) for 367 yards, with 2 touchdowns and a passer rating of 137.5. His 367 passing yards […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates a touchdown pass against the Chicago Bears during the fourth quarter at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images All that offensive ball control dominance the Chicago Bears have had so far this season didn’t help them against Jordan Love and the explosive Green Bay Packers offense yesterday. In Chicago’s 31-7 loss, Love was 25 of 31 (80.6%) for 367 yards, with 2 touchdowns and a passer rating of 137.5. His 367 passing yards are the most ever against the Bears at Lambeau Field, and it wasn’t a bunch of YAC (yards after catch), as Love was finding open receivers downfield. On passes over 20+ air yards, Love was 6 of 8 for 258 yards, which is the second-most deep passing yards in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). His five passes of 30+ air yards are tied for the most in a single game since ESPN started tracking that stat 20 years ago. Chicago’s defense had no answer for Love, who just kept looking deep. The Bears sacked Love twice, but his 2.54-second time to throw was his longest this season. What stings so much is that the Packers used Chicago’s defense to get their offense back on track. Before yesterday’s game, the Packers’ offense struggled to find consistency, but the Bears offered no resistance. Green Bay had more yards (428 to 246), more first downs (18 to 17), a better time of possession (30:24 to 29:36), and was better on third downs (33.3% to 28.6%) and fourth downs (1-1 to 2-5). The Bears ran more plays (68 to 59) and had fewer penalties (3 for 20 yards to 4 for 25), but the turnover margin (5 for Chicago, 0 for Green Bay) was impossible to overcome. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing-time breakdown and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE Tyson Bagent, who was making just his sixth career start, performed like we should have expected a backup quarterback to perform on the road. He’d never been in an environment as loud and hostile as Lambeau Field, and his inexperience showed all day. He wasn’t decisive. He wasn’t confident. He was late in his progressions. He seemed to be aiming the ball instead of letting it rip, and with below-average arm strength, he can’t afford to take anything off his passes. Case Keenum came in and wasn’t much better, but it was too little, too late, and the Packers were in full pass-rush mode at that point. The Bears are now 2-1 in games started by their backup quarterbacks, and most NFL teams would be happy with that. DEFENSE In case you missed it, the Bears lost three defenders to injury during the game: linebacker TJ Edwards (hamstring), cornerback Tyrique Stevenson (hamstring), and defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo (quad). Chicago’s secondary either busted coverages or simply couldn’t keep up with Green Bay’s Christian Watson (6 receptions, 143 yards, 2 TDs), Marcus Golden (6 for 123), or Tucker Kraft (5 for 64). SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos was wide left on a 43-yard field goal and hit his only extra point try. Tory Taylor had 4 punts with a 53.0 average (46.3 net) with 1 punt inside the twenty. Zavion Thomas returned 6 kickoffs for a 32.0 average, with a long of 61. Kalif Raymond had a 9-yard punt return. To check out the complete Bears vs. Packers box score, I find ESPN’s site is easy to navigate. All statistics and snap counts, as well as the accompanying pictures, are taken directly from the NFL’s Game Statistic and Information System.

title: Bears falter on both sides of ball in blowout loss to Packers
summary: The Chicago Bears have had a rough history with the Green Bay Packers throughout the last decade or so, and that bad luck continued on Sunday. Their 31-7 loss to Green Bay dropped them to a 3-2 record for the 2026 season, and it saw them dominated on both sides of the ball. Though the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Tyson Bagent #17 of the Chicago Bears passes against the Green Bay Packers during the fourth quarter at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have had a rough history with the Green Bay Packers throughout the last decade or so, and that bad luck continued on Sunday. Their 31-7 loss to Green Bay dropped them to a 3-2 record for the 2026 season, and it saw them dominated on both sides of the ball. Though the absence of Caleb Williams at quarterback significantly impacted the Bears’ ability to generate explosive plays on offense, the defense gave up plenty of those through the air at Lambeau Field. Green Bay’s dynamic passing attack helped its offense get out to an insurmountable lead in the second half, and bad play from both Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum made it impossible for the Bears to catch up. If you watched the game, you know it wasn’t pretty, and you likely don’t want to think too much about it. For those of you who do, however, and for the ones who didn’t get to watch the game, here are some of my key takeaways from the Bears’ loss so you don’t have to. It’s time to be realistic about Tyson Bagent There’s no other way around it; Bagent was bad on Sunday. He finished the game 12-for-21 (57.1%) with just 87 passing yards, no touchdowns, and two interceptions. He made several throws into tight coverage or outright double-team situations, making baffling decisions that one wouldn’t expect from a quarterback who has been touted for his intelligence. Eventually, the Bears chose to put Keenum into the game, though his results weren’t much better. Let’s be realistic about Bagent. He’s not one of the best 32 quarterbacks in the NFL. He is not a starting-caliber player. In four years in the NFL, he has three passing touchdowns and nine interceptions. The Bears would not be better off with him than they are with Caleb Williams. The hyperbole around Bagent, a tremendous success story from the Division II level as an undrafted free agent, has built his hype into something much greater than he actually is. He’s not a terrible football player, and even after this performance, I’d argue he’s still a solid backup quarterback (there are a lot of really bad NFL quarterbacks out there), but Sunday showed what he really is. Deep coverage struggles vs. Packers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden each surpassed 120 receiving yards on Sunday against the Bears. Tucker Kraft had a 48-yard gain in the game. Jordan Love finished the matchup with 367 passing yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions, a 137.5 passer rating, and an initial PFN QB Impact grade of 84.6, which ranks second in the NFL in Week 5, as of this writing. Simply put, Chicago struggled to stop the Packers’ vertical passing game this week. Xavier Woods had some instances where he looked out of position as the deep safety help. Dillon Thieneman appeared to have a play or two of poor processing and positioning, as well. Tyrique Stevenson, Malik Muhammad, and Jaylon Johnson all seemed to have lapses in coverage over the course of the afternoon, pending further All-22 review. The Bears’ secondary simply isn’t fast enough right now. They don’t have the raw speed at cornerback to make up for the lapses in judgment along the perimeter that Stevenson and Johnson make, and Coby Bryant’s presence at safety is sorely missed. It’s not the end of the world The Bears went 2-1 in the three games that Caleb Williams missed due to injury. In the grand scheme of things, it could’ve been a lot worse. Sure, they were utterly outclassed on both sides of the ball against the Packers. Their lapses in coverage will need to be addressed in the remaining 12 games of the season. But a calling card of this Bears team has been their offense, which has looked dynamic when Williams is throwing the ball more often than not. In most cases, having a backup in at quarterback significantly limits how much an NFL offense can operate to its full potential, both from an execution and a play-calling perspective. There’s a chance that Williams returns for the Bears’ game against the Falcons next week. With how Atlanta has looked in recent weeks, the Bears will need all the help they can get. But they’re still 3-2, and there’s plenty of football left to be played. Sunday’s result is nothing to panic over.

title: Green Bay Packers rout the Bagent-led Chicago Bears in Lambeau
summary: Lambeau Field has rarely been kind to the Chicago Bears in recent seasons, but Sunday’s 31-7 dismantling felt especially deflating for a team that entered the afternoon with a chance to seize control of the NFC North. Even more so in the wake of the loss of Iron Mike Ditka. Without Caleb Williams under center […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears and Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers embrace after the Packers defeated the Bears at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Lambeau Field has rarely been kind to the Chicago Bears in recent seasons, but Sunday’s 31-7 dismantling felt especially deflating for a team that entered the afternoon with a chance to seize control of the NFC North. Even more so in the wake of the loss of Iron Mike Ditka. Without Caleb Williams under center or Kyle Monangai in the backfield, Chicago’s offense never found a rhythm against a Packers defense that forced three interceptions from Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum, while Jordan Love and Christian Watson repeatedly exploited coverage breakdowns on explosive plays that turned a one-score halftime deficit into a rout. D’Andre Swift’s late second-quarter touchdown offered a brief flicker of competitiveness, yet the second half belonged entirely to Green Bay, whose efficient passing attack and opportunistic red-zone execution exposed the limitations of an injury-thinned Bears roster in a rivalry game that had looked winnable just weeks ago. 1st Quarter Thoughts Tyson Bagent looked bad from the start (spoiler alert – it only gets worse). Bagent fell down on third down – and if there was ever a play that symbolized an entire game – Bagent falling down on his own to kill a Bears drive is certainly it. Then the Packers drove the ball 91 yards in 10 plays with what was frankly a beautiful script from Matt LaFleur. The flea-flicker TE screen to Kraft was a signal of what was to come – creativity and explosives from the Packers offense. The drive was capped by a play-action deep ball (that too will be a theme) where the deep coverage never made it over to Watson. This game was bad from play one. While the Bears ran on the Packers with Swift seemingly at will, the passing game was completely disconnected, mostly because of Bagent’s poor play. 2nd Quarter Thoughts In the Keys to the Game this week I asked…nay, I warned…nay, I begged Tyson Bagent to just not throw late over the middle and give up stupid interceptions – like he has done time and time again when he has been on the field. Tyson did not listen to me. He threw into double coverage, and Xavier McKinney (the guy I was most worried about in this game) picked the deflected pass. Given a short field – Love and LaFleur made short work of us, as Marshawn Lloyd scored a rushing TD to make it 14-0, the Pack. The Bears then decided to be the Bears – Chicago put together a long, methodical, Ben Johnson-inspired, 16-play, 78-yard drive for the touchdown. Swift was everywhere on the field. However, the Bears continue to show a frustrating lack of ability to punch the ball within the red zone. While Swift got the TD on 4th down, it required a Packers penalty to give them a fresh series with goal-to-go. Hey – at least we have Austin Booker to celebrate! Two sacks to end the Packers’ drive and the half. Halftime Thoughts That sucked. But shockingly, we’re only down seven (Gooch from the future: more shock to come). 3rd Quarter Thoughts Packers again come out with creative play design, with Love hitting Tucker Craft on a beauty long pass where Craft ran his route against all of the action on the play – frankly, it reminded me of Ben Johnson. Then LaFleur and Love go into “screw it, go deep” mode, and it works time and time again. One TD is nullified on a correct offensive pass interference play. But on the ensuing 3rd and 22 they chuck it deep again and Watson brings it down for the TD. I have no idea why Allen backed out of pressure in that situation. On the bright side, Smack missed the extra point. Here is a thought: why is Roschon Johnson on this team? I mean, I hear he is a nice guy. But he is a power running back with not noticeable power who doesn’t run…well. I’m seeing that Office meme: “What, exactly, would you say you do here?” The Bears drive and briefly give me hope again, but Santos misses a field goal. I’d be mad at him, but of the two field goal kickers in the game, Santos screwed up the least. That said Smack added another field goal. 4th Quarter Thoughts I have discovered a hidden cost to writing the post-game article for WCG. I am obligated to watch the whole game instead of turning it off in disgust. After Bagent throws another interception, basically icing the game for the Packers, the Bears finally put Keenum in. But it is way too late. The Pack score again making it 7.31 with Love again chucking it deep, this time to Golden. After Thomas nearly houses one on the kickoff, Keenum leads us to goal-to-goal. But on 4th down there is another free rusher from the outside, and Case has to get rid of it – throwing a pick (he had to throw the ball). LaFlaeur had Love go for a two-point conversion. He then had Love take a big hit on a massive chuck it down the field pass (which Love completed). Sure, Smack missed another field goal. But if that wasn’t a “screw you, Ben” I don’t know what one would be. Blah, blah blah…more stuff happens. So I’m trying a new whiskey today (well, new for me) called 2Xo the Sneakerhead Blend. It’s a Kentucky Straight Bourbon, and it is quite nice. Final Thoughts Bears lose. Pack Win. The boss was right about “Pain” being the correct prediction, via Clubber Lang. He just had who the pain was for wrong. Look, most teams lose when they start their backup; the Bears got a way with starting a backup in three games and went 2-1. The Bears were without their thumper running back, That Guy, and they lost three defensive starters in the game (Motivated Dayo, Old Man Edwards, and Stephenson). We were on the road against an embarrassed team whose coach was on the hot seat and who clearly had a chip on their shoulder. That said, BJ didn’t call a good game for the most part; starting Bagent over Case seems hard to justify, especially since he was pretty bad last week, and our record against the North under BJ isn’t exactly above water. So…well, we hopefully will get Caleb and Kyle back, and next week will be different. Meanwhile, time to pour another drink. Gooch out.
