title: NFC East chaos keeps Cowboys in the thick of things
summary: Things are not going well for the Dallas Cowboys. They are coming off a hugely disappointing game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where they allowed an undrafted quarterback to beat them despite the Bucs being 8.5-point underdogs. The defense was awful once again, and the offense decided they wanted to be awful too. It was […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images Things are not going well for the Dallas Cowboys. They are coming off a hugely disappointing game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where they allowed an undrafted quarterback to beat them despite the Bucs being 8.5-point underdogs. The defense was awful once again, and the offense decided they wanted to be awful too. It was embarrassing, and honestly, most of us felt like the season was slipping away. Well, leave it to their NFC East divsion mates to give them new hope. It started with an early game in London, where the Philadelphia Eagles completely blew it at the end. After jumping ahead with a field goal with only eight seconds left in the game, Nick Sirianni made one of the most boneheaded coaching decisions we’ve seen in a while, and that says a lot. He opted to kick the ball in the field of play, allowing Jacksonville Jaguars returner Ameer Abdullah a chance to return it, and return it, he did. Abdullah returned the ball into Eagles territory, allowing big-leg kicker Cam Little to kick the game-winner. The Jags didn’t have any timeouts left, so they didn’t have any time to run a play unless they were able to get out of bounds, which would’ve been heavily guarded. The game was essentially over, but because of Sirianni’s coaching blunder, it wasn’t, and the Eagles lost. The three points the Eagles got with eight seconds left were the only three points the Eagles have scored in the second half over the past three games combined. It’s no surprise that Philly is falling and falling fast. Whether from retirement or trade, they lost some key parts of their offensive line this past week and were without a couple of their best offensive weapons due to injury. Their future is very cloudy right now. So, what about the New York Giants or the Washington Commanders? The Giants entered the week 3-1, but they already had lost their starting quarterback, Jaxson Dart, for the season. The Giants are off to a good start, but can Jameis Winston carry them the rest of the way? The Commanders were 1-3, and they just got Jayden Daniels back. Healthy or not, they have issues. So, who do we root for? Which of these teams are a serious threat to win the NFC East? They squared off today, so one of them had to win, right? Not so fast. Both teams certainly had a chance to win. In fact, they each should have won. The Giants drove the ball deep into Washington territory late in overtime, but then Cam Skattebo fumbled the ball, giving the Commanders new life. Just protect the ball and kick the game-winning field goal. Nope. Opportunity squandered. But don’t worry, Giants fans. The Commanders can do you one better. Washington proceeded to move the ball down the field in what looked like a game-winning drive, but then something weird happened. Daniels curiously scrambled around and was brought down as time was winding down, but the Commanders showed no sense of urgency. The Commanders didn’t have any timeouts! It was as if they had no idea of the situation they were in. Instead of just kicking a chip-shot game-winning field goal, time expired, and nobody won. With no team winning this week and no one showing themselves as alphas, the division is wide open. If the Cowboys can somehow find a way to get their act together, they have a great opportunity to win the division. Nobody else seems to want it. The ineptitude of the division allows the Cowboys to work through their obvious early-season growing pains. They’ll need to get better for any of this to mean anything, but at least their division foes are giving them a chance.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys might have to move on from another bad contract
summary: It is hard to believe how quickly the mighty can fall in the NFL, but the Dallas Cowboys are currently watching a former defensive playmaker become a major liability. It really does not seem like all that long ago when DaRon Bland was the apple of every fan’s eye. This fifth-round pick from Fresno burst […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It is hard to believe how quickly the mighty can fall in the NFL, but the Dallas Cowboys are currently watching a former defensive playmaker become a major liability. It really does not seem like all that long ago when DaRon Bland was the apple of every fan’s eye. This fifth-round pick from Fresno burst onto the scene with an incredible 14 interceptions over his first two seasons in the league. During his second year, he put together one of the most historically impressive cornerback stretches in modern football, returning interceptions for touchdowns at a ridiculously high frequency. It resulted in an All-Pro 2023 campaign where he set the NFL single-season record with five pick-sixes. Bland showcased top diagnostic skills and exceptional closing burst whenever quarterbacks dared to test him. This knack for creating game-changing turnovers made him a fan favorite and earned him a long-term deal. Sadly, all that changed abruptly. The last two seasons have been hindered by recurring foot injuries that made him unavailable, or highly ineffective when he actually was on the field. First, a stress fracture in his left foot that required a surgical screw sidelined him for most of 2024. Then things got even worse last year when he hurt his right foot early in the season, only to re-injure that same stubborn fifth metatarsal bone in his left foot. This chronic instability has stolen a massive amount of reps over the past two seasons, but he was fully healthy entering this year with heightened expectations. Unfortunately, the Bland we are seeing now is someone we do not recognize. Even during his All-Pro season, he would occasionally get his hand caught in the cookie jar and give up a big play, but what is happening now is hard to explain. That elite ball-hawker has completely vanished. These days, we are lucky if he finishes a play without falling down. Without his patented route-jumping interceptions to mask his deficiencies, Bland’s flaws in coverage have been heavily targeted by opposing play-callers. He is constantly taking the cautious approach, generously laying back and making it very easy for receivers to find a well-vacated space. You would think this cushion would prevent big plays, but that is not happening either. Instead, he constantly bites on any double-move and routinely finds himself chasing after his own mistakes. He is not reading the play well, and when he does, his brain does not seem to be communicating with his feet. It is painful to say, but he just looks incredibly clumsy. Even when he finally had the opportunity to redeem himself after perfectly jumping a route late in the game against Tampa Bay, the ball just bounced right off his hands. It was as if his lone superpower had officially been extinguished, leaving behind a regular, well, bland cornerback. The Cowboys must now consider if they have other cornerback options on the roster who can hold down the outside, even if it means relegating Bland to a backup role. While it is disappointing to see things play out like this, the team is set up nicely for a smooth transition. They just traded for a proven, reliable coverage corner in Joey Porter Jr. and got him for cheap because he is in the final year of his rookie contract. Retaining Porter long-term will be expensive, but if management chooses to move on from Bland, they can easily reallocate those funds. Cutting ties with Bland after the 2026 season means they will have to eat $21.5 million in dead money from his signing bonus and recent contract restructuring. However, it frees them from the remaining $55.7 million left on the four-year, $90 million deal he signed just last year. The front office previously watched Trevon Diggs fall to injury and pivoted to Bland in response. Now, they may have to pull off that exact same magic trick once again. At least this time around, they have a replacement who might lack a flashy takeaway résumé, but also does not come with those catastrophic coverage breakdowns. Football is a business where past production buys very little patience. If Bland cannot find his footing, the front office cannot afford to continue to invest and get diminishing returns. Swapping a broken ball-hawk for a lockdown technician like Porter could be exactly what this defense needs to stabilize the boundary. Turning the page is never easy, but at least the Cowboys have taken measures to make the next chapter of this story a little more appealing.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Comparing Cowboys Brian Schottenheimer to other new 2025-26 HCs
summary: Following the Dallas Cowboys Week 3 loss in Brazil against the Baltimore Ravens, we said it was going to be a long week for head coach Brian Schottenheimer after his team snatched defeat from the jaws of victory in that international game. It was a long week indeed, but at least the Cowboys weren’t actually […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Following the Dallas Cowboys Week 3 loss in Brazil against the Baltimore Ravens, we said it was going to be a long week for head coach Brian Schottenheimer after his team snatched defeat from the jaws of victory in that international game. It was a long week indeed, but at least the Cowboys weren’t actually favorites to beat the Ravens, plus they followed it up with a bounce back win at the Houston Texans where Schotty cooked up a second half comeback led by his offense. Thursday night at home against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers changed all of this, sending the Cowboys and their head man into an even longer week, in more ways than just literally as the Cowboys will have 12 days in between this loss and their next game at the Green Bay Packers. The extra time will just be even more of an opportunity to question the leadership of this team, coaching and players. Unlike the Ravens game, the Cowboys were favorites, by a lot, to beat the Buccaneers, and instead lost to an undrafted rookie quarterback and had no answers for the Todd Bowles defense. Cowboys fans got the familiar speech from Jerry Jones last season when Schottenheimer was hired that he’s willing to live with inexperience with coaches in order to see them learn from mistakes and develop. Here at the start of year two (a start with a very “it’s getting late early” vibe to it) under Schottenheimer though, there’s been much more talk about the team willing to do what it takes to win. Instead, they’re seeing Schotty still look inexperienced, under-prepared, and unmotivating. The new and inexperienced play-calling coach is supposed to be defensive coordinator Christian Parker, and the Cowboys are certainly paying a cost on that side of the ball through his learning process as well. Throw in special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen not having the third phase of the game playing well either, and it’s far too much to overcome when the Cowboys are bad in all three phases at different times throughout every single game. Even with all this doom and gloom, the Cowboys can’t just pack up shop and call it quits on a 2026 season where they sit at 2-3. The NFC East is still there for the taking, only two teams league-wide are still undefeated with four wins, and the Cowboys have some significant injuries that aren’t season-ending. One way to look at the bigger picture of where this Cowboys team is at right now though is to look at their progression under Schottenheimer compared to the other new head coaches from the 2025 cycle he was a part of, as well as this year’s class. The new head coaches in the league last year beside Schottenheimer were Ben Johnson with the Chicago Bears, Mike Vrabel with the New England Patriots, Aaron Glenn with the New York Jets, Liam Coen with the Jacksonville Jaguars, Pete Carroll with the Las Vegas Raiders, and Kellen Moore with the New Orleans Saints. Johnson, Glenn, Coen, and Moore all carried the tag of being first-time head coaches in this cycle, while Vrabel and Carroll had, of course, been head coaches before, se we’ll leave both of them out of the comparison. All but Carroll are still in place with the same teams. Ben Johnson Johnson is possibly the best game-planning head coach on offense in the league right now, thinking of diabolical ways to toy with defenses the second he arrived in Chicago from the Detroit Lions. Lions fans would even be the first to tell anyone that would listen that losing Johnson as offensive coordinator was going to sink their team’s status as a true contender, even though they kept Dan Campbell as head coach. It’s funny how no other team ever even considered this of Schottenheimer who was offensive coordinator for the 12-5 Cowboys in 2023 under Mike McCarthy, and again OC in 2024. One win in Johnson’s head coaching debut season came against that dreadful Matt Eberflus defense, as the Bears beat the Cowboys in week three. That win was actually Johnson’s first after an 0-2 start, and it started a stretch where the Bears would win nine of ten through November. The Bears won the NFC North and beat their division rival the Packers in the Wild Card round, before losing by three to the LA Rams in the Divisional game. The Bears currently sit at 3-1 with a 59-point performance in week one, and 20-point win on primetime over the Philadelphia Eagles with Case Keenum starting for Caleb Williams. Kellen Moore Enough on that since it was always a pipe dream the Cowboys would hire Ben Johnson, so let’s stay in the NFC and look at the head coach that Schottenheimer replaced as offensive coordinator in Dallas when he got hired in 2023. Kellen Moore’s first head coaching gig with the Saints saw him go 6-11. After an 0-4 start that fell to 1-8 by week nine, the Saints won four straight in December to give them something to feel good about going into the offseason. The carryover effect saw the Saints lose by one in overtime in week one after Moore went aggressive to play for the win on a two-point conversion, then respond to beat the Ravens on the road in week two. At this exact moment the Saints are in a tough spot having lost two straight after that win to the Las Vegas Raiders and Atlanta Falcons, but the battery of Moore and QB Tyler Shough is still trending in the right direction and has that franchise excited about their young talent as a whole on both sides of the ball. Liam Coen Liam Coen, a longtime offensive coach that had quite the wait to get his first head coaching shot, got immediate results with a 13-4 record in year one. The Jaguars hadn’t won 13 games since 1999. No waiting around for Coen to learn on the job was necessary, apparently. They’re currently 3-1 with their only loss being of one-score variety at the Denver Broncos. Most recently, they held the Cincinnati Bengals to 17 points in their own stadium to get a 22-17 win, and the Jaguars look like real AFC contenders at the moment with Trevor Lawrence at QB. Aaron Glenn That leaves only Aaron Glenn with the Jets, the only other coach on this 2025 list that Schottenheimer coached against directly in his debut season as well. The Cowboys rolled to victory against a Jets team that was hapless under Glenn last year, but already have shown a few more signs of life in year two of his program. It’s always baby steps when talking about the Jets and positivity, but they opened the season with a win and then had real chances to take games against the Packers and Lions the next two weeks to be 3-0 instead of now 1-3, also losing to the Bears in week four. If this means that Schottenheimer is only clearly better than Glenn as the Jets head coach, it’s fair to say that’s not exactly what the Cowboys hired him for. This picture of the Cowboys falling behind in a crucial way yet again doesn’t get much prettier when looking at the 2026 head coaches that are new this season either. 2026 new head coaches They are Joe Brady with the Bills, Jesse Minter with the Ravens, Mike LaFleur with the Arizona Cardinals, Klint Kubiak with the Raiders, Todd Monken with the Cleveland Browns, Jeff Hafley with the Miami Dolphins, and John Harbaugh with the New York Giants. Only Harbaugh goes in the “previous head coaching experience” bucket here. We started this post talking about Minter’s win against the Cowboys already, and who could forget former Ravens coach John Harbaugh beating the Cowboys in week one with the Giants too. The Raiders were 3-0 before a close loss to their rival Kansas City Chiefs last Sunday under Kubiak. Brady has Josh Allen playing at his usual MVP level for the Bills, and Monken is also getting the best QB play the Browns have had in some time out of Deshaun Watson. The energy around the Browns is entirely different under Monken right now, and you don’t hear an endless stream of buzzwords to hide behind out a team not even expected to have a winning standard for some time. The Cowboys always find a way to prove this wrong,…
author: Sean Martin

title: What the stats really say about the Cowboys playoff chances
summary: We know that 26% of teams that started 2-3 from 2020 through 2025 eventually made the playoffs. But does 2-3 accurately describe the 2026 Cowboys? As it currently stands, there is no chance this team makes the playoffs. Instead, the lowly Giants currently look to be the NFC East favorite right now – not because […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 8: Head coach Brian Schottenheimer of the Dallas Cowboys leaves the field following the team's loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium on October 8, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images We know that 26% of teams that started 2-3 from 2020 through 2025 eventually made the playoffs. But does 2-3 accurately describe the 2026 Cowboys? As it currently stands, there is no chance this team makes the playoffs. Instead, the lowly Giants currently look to be the NFC East favorite right now – not because they have a better roster, far from it, but simply because they are better coached. But how bad are the 2-3 Cowboys really? In statistics, the relationship between two variables is called a correlation, and the strength of that correlation is measured by the “correlation coefficient”. This coefficient (r²) is expressed as a number between 0 and 1. The closer the r² number is to 1, the stronger the relationship between the two variables. The closer it is to zero, the weaker the relationship. In 2025, the metrics most strongly correlated with wins in the NFL were Points differential (r² = 0.845) EPA/Play differential (r² = 0.76) Passer Rating differential (r² = 0.68) Conveniently for us, all three can be used to calculate projected wins. Points differential : Last week , the Pythagorean win projection (essentially a souped up version of points differential), adjusted for the games already played, showed the Cowboys as a 9.2-wins team. Five games into the season, the Cowboys have now scored 138 points and allowed 136. The Pythagorean projected wins for that stat line: 8.6 wins, and adjusted for the games already played: 8.1 wins. EPA/Play differential : One of the interesting things about both EPA/Play and Passer Rating Differential is that they can both be plugged into a very simple formula to predict win totals in the NFL. The EPA/Play formula (Projected Wins = EPA Differential * 25 + 8.5) based on a 0.158 offensive EPA/Play and a .182 defensive EPA/Play projects the Cowboys for 7.9 wins . Passer Rating Differential (PRD): The PRD formula (Projected Wins = PRD * 0.17 + 8.5) based on a 98.2 offensive passer rating and a 109.6 defensive passer rating projects the Cowboys for 6.6 win s. Prediction markets : A different sort of math, but similar results nonetheless. Kalshi has the Cowboys with 8.7 wins . Predictionmarketspicks.com has the Cowboys with 7.9 wins . The historical numbers give the Cowboys a 26% playoff rate from this position. That’s a useful baseline, but it tells us nothing specific about this team. The three statistical models put Dallas somewhere between 6.6 and 8.1 wins. The prediction markets are in roughly the same neighborhood. That’s not a playoff profile. And if anything, those numbers may be flattering the Cowboys. Seven or eight wins looks like a reasonable statistical baseline. But depending on your eye test, even that might be optimistic. Let us know if you think there is any chance they can turn this around, or are they going to miss the playoffs again?
author: One Cool Customer

title: The Cowboys coaching decision no one is talking about
summary: The Dallas Cowboys lost on Thursday night. It remains incredibly frustrating. If I asked you for the most contentious decision that the coaching staff made in the process, you would likely bring up the decision that Brian Schottenheimer made to go for two when down by eight in the fourth quarter. This particular author supported […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 8: Brandon Aubrey #17 of the Dallas Cowboys warms up against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers prior to an NFL football game at AT&T Stadium on October 8, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys lost on Thursday night. It remains incredibly frustrating. If I asked you for the most contentious decision that the coaching staff made in the process, you would likely bring up the decision that Brian Schottenheimer made to go for two when down by eight in the fourth quarter. This particular author supported that for what it’s worth, just about the only thing I endorsed from Schottenheimer throughout the loss. While that decision has inspired a lot of responses there is another Cowboys coaching decision that merits discussion. This one came much earlier in the game. Almost halfway through the second quarter, Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb failed to connect on a 3rd and 10. It was 4th and 10, obviously, and the Cowboys chose to punt. The thing is the Cowboys were on the Tampa Bay 47-yard line. They turned down a 64-yard field goal attempt, something that Brandon Aubrey is regarded to be very good at. Aubrey hasn’t exactly been super reliable on these as of late, though. He had a 59-yard attempt blocked by the Baltimore Ravens, and a week later he had a 62-yard attempt blocked by the Houston Texans. Schottenheimer also chose to have Aubrey attempt a 65-yarder against Houston on the possession after the block and he missed it outright. In the week after the game, Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans talked about how they were partly able to block the kick they did because of something they saw on film from Dallas’ game against Baltimore. DeMeco Ryans details how the Texans saw the Ravens blocked kick vs the Cowboys and moved Will Anderson Jr. inside like they did when he blocked a FG in 2023 vs JAX pic.twitter.com/Dbdyc3wm7E — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) October 7, 2026 You never want to see this kind of thing. It looks bad on the Cowboys, it looks bad on Schottenheimer, and it specifically looks bad on special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen. Did those two blocks occupy some rent in the Cowboys’ minds on the decision to not let Aubrey attempt the 64-yarder against Tampa? It is hard to say not. The Fort Worth Star-Telegram’s Nick Harris pulled the last time that Dallas punted from across the 50-yard line and it was midway through last year, but the last time they punted from inside of the 47-yard line specifically was late in the 2024 season. It is worth noting that by that time in that season Dak Prescott was out for the year already so the calculus was a bit different. Last time: Week 7 2025 vs. WAS (punted from the WAS 49) Last time it was punted from the 47-and-in: Week 13 2024 vs. NYG (punted from the NYG 47 and the NYG 45) — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) October 9, 2026 To be clear, it is impossible to say with full certainty that the Cowboys punted because of a lack of faith in any one person or side of the ball. But it is certainly a legitimate theory. That particular decision was hardly costly. The Buccaneers went on the punt themselves so there was no blood drawn. But what if Aubrey had attempted the 64-yard attempt? What if he had made it? Then the Cowboys could have gone for two when they did in an effort to make the game (at that time) a three-point contest. And if they had gotten it, they didn’t get it as we all know, then they would have only needed a field goal to tie at the end of regulation. That is a lot of ifs and hypotheticals, but they rest on the decision that Dallas made to not have Brandon Aubrey attempt the field goal. What do you think? Was it a lack of faith? Or something random?

Hats off to the entire unit! – Tim Lynch Justin Herbert over the last four drives: 0-for-4, two stripsacks, one sack, one interception, one fourth-down sneak stuffed — Bill Barnwell (@billbarnwell) October 11, 2026 Bo Nix I’m going to give a gameball to Bo Nix. title: Broncos Will Lutz cause for concern?
summary: While most of Broncos Country has been wringing their hands over the offensive play of the 2026 Denver Broncos, there has been another area of growing concern in Denver. What is up with Will Lutz? Lutz joined the Broncos as one of the handful of Saints players that followed coach Sean Payton over from the […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Wil Lutz #3 of the Denver Broncos looks during the game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images While most of Broncos Country has been wringing their hands over the offensive play of the 2026 Denver Broncos, there has been another area of growing concern in Denver. What is up with Will Lutz? Lutz joined the Broncos as one of the handful of Saints players that followed coach Sean Payton over from the New Orleans Saints in 2023. While in New Orleans, he was 195 of 169 field goals attempted clocking in at 84.6%. His time in Denver has been an improvement, making 97 of his 111 attempts for an 87.4% success rate. However, this season he has not continued on that trajectory, making 8 of 11, for a much diminished 72.7% make rate. Against the Rams, Lutz missed a 43-yarder in the 1st quarter. His 58-yard attempt against the 49ers in the 4th quarter was no good. Then, on Sunday against the Chargers, his 42-yard attempt could not find the uprights. While it’s still relatively early in the season, things are not trending well for a franchise that has high expectations for kickers. Denver has had a wealth of clutch kickers over the years. While in Denver, ring of fame kicker Jason Elam averaged 80.6% of his kicks. Matt Prater hit 82.9% of his kicks. Brandon McManus was solid for 81.4% of his kicks. While those numbers are less than the 87% Lutz mustered last season, these guys were also known for crushing the big kick when it mattered most. Jason Elam tied the NFL record at the time with a kick 0f 63-yards and McManus set the record at the time of 64-yards. Matt Prater didn’t set a record for kicking in Denver, but turned in a killer 61-yard field goal in 2021. Will Lutz’s career longest field goal was 60-yards back in 2022 and with Denver, hasn’t hit one longer than 57-yards. Simply put, if you don’t have the leg to make those big time kicks, you need to at least be consistent. If these first 5 games are any indication, concern over Will Lutz leg is becoming more and more justified. Is it a momentary blip on an otherwise solid career or is it a sign of yet another unforeseen challenge these Denver Broncos will have to overcome this season? More importantly, if it does continue at this rate, will Sean Payton have the wherewithal to make appropriate adjustments? Broncos Country will have to wait and see.

title: Winners and Losers from the Denver Broncos’ 23-17 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers
summary: The Broncos are back to winning ugly! Ugly is the best way to describe this game. The Chargers played like a 0-4 team that has been decimated by injuries, while the Broncos continued to struggle on offense and had lapses on defense. However, despite the ugliness, the Broncos and quarterback Bo Nix led yet another […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - OCTOBER 11: Denver Broncos defensive tackle D.J. Jones (93) celebrates after getting the sack on Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert (10) during the game between the Los Angeles Chargers and the Denver Broncos on October 11, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. (Photo by David Dennis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Broncos are back to winning ugly! Ugly is the best way to describe this game. The Chargers played like a 0-4 team that has been decimated by injuries, while the Broncos continued to struggle on offense and had lapses on defense. However, despite the ugliness, the Broncos and quarterback Bo Nix led yet another 4th quarter comeback and came away with the win with the help of their defense. This team makes winners and losers difficult because they are a complete rollercoaster through 4 quarters, but we’ll figure it out. With all that said, here are your winners and losers from the Denver Broncos 23-17 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. LOSER – QB Bo Nix/Broncos offense Nix is once again having a slow start to his season. We saw this last season, when Nix looked just off, lacked confidence, and he and the entire offense tended to struggle. In the past, he has snapped out of it as the season went on and has played well late, but right now, he just looks off again. Sean Payton was back calling plays, but it didn’t really help too much. Nix looked a bit shook, took some sacks/hits he doesn’t typically take, and the offense once again looked disjointed. Now, it’s not just a Bo Nix thing. The offense struggled throughout. The offensive line was giving up pressure quickly, the run game was non-existent, and they struggled to move the ball and put points on the board. With that said, they did score 13 points in the 4th quarter, including a Nix touchdown pass to Courtland Sutton. Nix finished the game going 16 of 27 for 123 yards and 1 touchdown. He also fumbled the ball during a scramble, which led to a Chargers touchdown on the very next play. It wasn’t pretty, and it needs to improve, but they made plays when they needed to and came away with the win. At the end of the day, that is all that matters. WINNER – Broncos defense/pass rush Outside of one run play and a couple of third downs, the Broncos defense played very well against this struggling and banged up Chargers offense. They held Justin Herbert to just 121 passing yards, sacked him 5 times, had 3 turnovers, and came up big in the 4th quarter when it mattered the most. The Broncos’ defense kept them in this game and, at the end of the day, won them this game. STRIP SACK BY ZACH ALLEN BRONCOS BALL!!! pic.twitter.com/vnaf4Jxbia — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 It should be noted how far from 100% this Chargers offense is. They were down all but one of their starting offensive lineman, down multiple wide receivers, and were already struggling to begin with. Even though the Broncos were down their top two corners, they should have dominated this game, and they did for the most part. They had three blemishes throughout. Giving up a first down on 3rd and 15, allowing Herbert to run for 20+ on 3rd down, and forgetting how to tackle on a Vidal run that led to a go-ahead touchdown. Outside of that, they played well and squashed any hope of a comeback by the Chargers late in the game. They are going to need this type of effort from this defense moving forward. WINNER – EDGE Nik Bonitto Broncos star pass rusher Nik Bonitto has had a slow start to his season, but he was a big part of their defense today. He made multiple plays in the backfield and had 2 sacks of Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert. BONITTO SACK x2 💪💪 pic.twitter.com/CYONjsXk8k — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 The Broncos will need Bonitto to get things going and go on a roll moving forward. This defense is known for its sacks and needs to get back to having multi-sack games more often. WINNER – EDGE Que Robinson Robinson had what ended up being the biggest momentum shift in the game. It was 4th and 1 with 10:35 left in the 4th quarter; the ball was near mid-field, and the Broncos were trailing the Chargers 17-10. Jim Harbaugh decided to go for it and trust his big and athletic quarterback, Justin Herbert, to sneak it for the first down easily. He does it often. Not this time. Broncos’ second-year edge rusher Que Robinson stonewalled him and pushed him backwards. Turnover on downs. QUE ROBINSON STOPS JUSTIN HERBERT ON 4TH DOWN pic.twitter.com/fqaxPoFDpl — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 The Broncos would get the ball at midfield, drive down the field, and tie the game up with a touchdown pass to Courtland Sutton. From this point on, the Broncos would go on a 13-0 run, and we can pinpoint the exact spot where the game swung in the Broncos’ favor. WINNER – WR Courtland Sutton and RB JK Dobbins The box score may not look great, but both veteran players have had a slow start to their season and had huge impacts on this game. JK Dobbins looked off for most of the game, despite scoring his first touchdown of the season early in the game. He once again looked to lack the explosiveness he had last season throughout most of the game, but he came alive late. He had some big runs in the 4th quarter and finished with 18 carries for 68 yards (3.8 YPC) and 1 touchdown. Again, not great, but saw some life late from the veteran back, and hopefully, we can build on that moving forward, As for Sutton, he was mostly invisible for most of the game and finished the game with just 2 catches for 18 yards. However, his touchdown tied the game late, and like Dobbins, he showed some life. We need more of that from both, and hopefully, he can build on this momentum moving forward. LOSER – WR Jaylen Waddle This sucks. He’s showing his frustration on the field, and once again, his production is lacking. Just 2 catches for 19 yards on 5 targets. He would have had a big play over the middle of the field late in the game, but he ended up dropping the ball. The production and impact we all, and probably the Broncos, thought we would get from Waddle isn’t happening. He has dropped a handful of balls now, Nix is having his struggles, the OL isn’t giving Nix much time consistently, and the play-calling is in flux. They need to get Waddle going if they want to get things going on the offense. LOSER – Broncos offensive line I am not an offensive line expert. I will always state this, but this “top-ranked unit” is certainly not passing the eye test for me. Multiple times in this game, pressure got to Nix almost immediately, and the running lanes for most of the game seemed non-existent. Now, could some of this be on Nix and the Broncos’ running backs? Yes, and probably is. Still, this unit has not been playing up to its reputation thus far, at least according to my eye test. WINNER – CBs Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine Listen, I know the Chargers lacked a passing offense due to injuries all over their offense, but the Broncos were also down their CB1 and CB2 in Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss. Former first-round pick Jahdae Barron and reserve Kris Abrams-Draine were your starters tonight, and the Broncos’ defense did not miss a beat. Again, the Chargers had their many issues, but if you can escape a game down Surtain II and Moss and get away with it unscathed, that’s a win in my book. Barron played well in this one. He had multiple nice tackles and did not give up much at all in the passing game. Abrams-Draine had an INT called back by DPI but also played well and was not a weak link of the Broncos’ defense. Other notable Winners and Losers S Brandon Jones – WINNER: Had an INT late in the game and was making plays all over the field. He has been one of the Broncos’ top defenders all season. PR Marvin Mims Jr. – WINNER: Mims, who has had a tough start to the year, flexed his return skills and had a 26-yard punt return to set the offense up in good…

title: 7 Things we learned from Broncos comeback win vs Chargers
summary: Another week, another comeback win for the Denver Broncos. And another game where, through the first three quarters, Bo Nix and the Broncos looked completely incompetent. Yet, as has become the norm with Nix and this team, they just find a way to win. The 23-17 victory over the hapless Los Angeles Chargers is the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers fumbles the ball after a tackle by D.J. Jones #93 of the Denver Broncos during the fourth quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Another week, another comeback win for the Denver Broncos. And another game where, through the first three quarters, Bo Nix and the Broncos looked completely incompetent. Yet, as has become the norm with Nix and this team, they just find a way to win. The 23-17 victory over the hapless Los Angeles Chargers is the latest chapter in this story. Denver improves to 3-2 on the young season and keeps Justin Herbert and the Chargers winless at 0-5. Here’s what we learned from Sunday’s win for the Broncos. Denver is a fourth-quarter team If it wasn’t obvious over the last season and five games, Denver is never out of any game. That’s a helluva thing for a team to possess. No matter what the Broncos encounter, no matter how bad they play, they have a shot. It’s what this team is – good and bad. Thankfully, Denver survived on Sunday. It really is amazing how the Broncos just look like a completely different team in the final quarter. The same is true for Nix. Defense showed up when needed After the Kimani Vidal 42-yard touchdown at the end of the third quarter, it didn’t look great for the defense or the Broncos. Denver’s defense had more whiffs than a kid who picked up a baseball bat for the first time and tried to hit a ball off a tee. But after the play, something clicked in the Broncos defense. They finally realized LA was playing four rookies on the offensive line and had no receivers. But from that point on, Denver completely ransacked Herbert and the Chargers offense. Four of the Broncos’ five sacks came in the fourth quarter, and they forced three turnovers. Casa Bonitto is open for business Nik Bonitto showed up and showed out on Sunday. The Denver edge rusher led the team with two sacks. Bonitto also finished with four tackles (three solo), three tackles for loss, and two quarterback hits. Helluva game for Bonitto. But it wasn’t just Bonitto, especially in the fourth quarter. Zach Allen had a huge strip-sack of Herbert, and the pass rush got home. For the game, the Broncos defense had five sacks, 12 tackles for loss, and six quarterback hits. Nix and the offense have to get better earlier Nix and the offense finally got going in the fourth quarter, but this can’t continue. There must be some semblance of consistency from the quarterback and this unit earlier in the game. On Sunday, it was downright atrocious in the first three quarters. It starts with running the ball better. It’s no coincidence that Nix and the Denver offense started to play better when the running game was effective. Whatever the Broncos do in the fourth quarter would be nice to see earlier in games. But how many times has that been said since last season? Running game comes alive in fourth quarter As just noted, it’s no coincidence Denver’s offense found life in the fourth quarter when the running game got going. It was led by J.K. Dobbins, who finally looked like the running back from a season ago. Now just find a way to do this earlier in the game, please and thank you. Dobbins led the Broncos in rushing with 68 yards on 13 carries and a touchdown. Evan Engram and Courtland Sutton live Engram led Denver with four receptions for 55 yards, and Sutton caught a massive 13-yard touchdown. Getting both of these guys involved is a positive sign for the Broncos. For the offense to take the next step or two, both Engram and Sutton will play a big role. Special teams showed up There was a punt by Jeremy Crawshaw that was a freaking beauty in the third quarter. It was then that the Broncos punter blasted a 58-yard punt and pinned the Chargers at their 3-yard line. If that wasn’t enough, Crawshaw had five punts, three inside the LA 20-yard line for an average of 45.6 per punt. Marvin Mims Jr. had a fantastic punt return after an LA penalty forced a rekick due to a penalty. It made up for an earlier questionable fair-catch decision by Mims.

title: Instant reaction: Fourth quarter heroics help Broncos defeat Chargers 23-17
summary: The Denver Broncos battled the winless Los Angeles Chargers this afternoon. It was a back-and-forth matchup throughout all ninety minutes. After four quarters of play, the Broncos were victorious defeating their AFC West rival 23-17. Here are some instant reactions from today’s game. The Broncos’ issues on offense go far beyond the play-caller The big […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Inglewood, California, USA; Denver Broncos linebacker Dondrea Tillman (92) looks to recover a fumble against the Los Angeles Chargers during the second half at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gary A. Vasquez-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Denver Broncos battled the winless Los Angeles Chargers this afternoon. It was a back-and-forth matchup throughout all ninety minutes. After four quarters of play, the Broncos were victorious defeating their AFC West rival 23-17. Here are some instant reactions from today’s game. Got it done. #DENvsLAC pic.twitter.com/UJLkzjyXMB — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) October 11, 2026 The Broncos’ issues on offense go far beyond the play-caller The big headline this week was Head Coach Sean Payton’s announcement that he would be taking over play calling duties. The Davis Webb experiment only lasted four games. However, whether or not such a switch was merited will be debated for a while. Some think it was, while others certainly believe Webb didn’t get a fair shake. Even with the switch, Denver’s offense failed to take off against Los Angeles. Sure, they got a few touchdowns on short fields gifted to them by the defense. However, I’d say the Broncos’ issues go much deeper than who is dialing up the plays. Let’s be honest—it’s just bad offense—with a ton of blame to go around. For most of the game, the offensive line couldn’t get push in short yardage situations when attempting to run. They did better late in the game with everything on the line. With respect to pass protection, I felt they gave up quite a bit of pressure for most of the game. The highly touted unit has been very underwhelming to date. In my opinion, that position group could use multiple premium investments in next year’s draft. Bo Nix and the passing attack were inconsistent again. There were very few explosive plays down the field. Moreover, they were dreadful on third down conversion attempts. It took until the fourth quarter to get their first chain-moving play of the second half. Outside of a few plays, Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle were missing in action. The lack of impact from those two is one of the biggest disappointments of the season. Where was RJ Harvey? He had ten catches last week and was barely involved on offense this afternoon. Why not try and get the ball in his hands as a receiver out of the backfield? Sure, the Broncos found a way to win. But the overall effort from the offense throughout the game was extremely inconsistent. They host the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football in just a few days. Is that enough time to fix what we saw today? I’m not so sure about that. Defense dials up the heat on Justin Herbert in fourth quarter With a bunch of injuries, the Chargers were forced to start four rookies on their offensive line. Given such, this was a prime game for the Broncos’ defensive front seven to get back on track. After limiting the Chargers to just three points through two quarters, the defense had a really bad third quarter performance. Los Angeles was able to dial up a 93-yard scoring drive to start third quarter that evened up the game 10-10. Several drives later after a Nix fumble, Kimani Vidal was able to capitalize with a 42-yard touchdown scamper that gave them a seven-point lead heading into the final quarter of play. At that point in time, it seemed like the defense was set to crumble and the Broncos were on their way to a sure-fire loss. But in the fourth quarter, with the game on the line, the defense finally dialed up the heat on Justin Herbert. They were able to get a big fourth down stop and force several turnovers due to their pass rushing prowess. Seeing them struggle to rattle him for most of the game was tough to watch, yet it was worth the wait to see them go off in the fourth quarter. A tip of the cap to Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players for rising to the occasion. Had it not been for their ferocious fourth quarter effort, the Broncos would have not won this game.

title: Broncos defense goes crazy in fourth quarter to lead team to victory over Chargers
summary: The Denver Broncos were looking like a team on the cusp of stumbling on the road against the winless Los Angeles Chargers down 17-10 in the fourth quarter. Then the defense went crazy and the offense did what it needed to do to capitalize on the big plays being generated by them. As much fun […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Eyioma Uwazurike #96 of the Denver Broncos celebrates after a tackle against the Los Angeles Chargers during the fourth quarter at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos were looking like a team on the cusp of stumbling on the road against the winless Los Angeles Chargers down 17-10 in the fourth quarter. Then the defense went crazy and the offense did what it needed to do to capitalize on the big plays being generated by them. As much fun as it was to enjoy another comeback win, this team has some serious issues it needs to correct and with a short week and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks coming to town it doesn’t get any easier. This stat below is not a long-term winning strategy… lol pic.twitter.com/KnjnNpNpbN — DNVR Broncos (@DNVR_Broncos) October 11, 2026 Broncos vs. Chargers final score Team 1st 2nd 3rd 4th Final Denver Broncos 7 3 0 13 23 Los Angeles Chargers 0 3 14 0 17 First Quarter Denver got their first first down on an opening drive all season, though they would end up punting on that drive anyway. The big play came on a third down catch and run by Chargers’ tight end Charlie Kolar who would have the ball knocked loose by safety Talanoa Hufanga to give Denver the ball on the plus side of the field. Two plays after the fumble, Bo Nix would find a wide open Evan Engram deep down the middle of the field for a 34-yard gain to the Chargers’ five yard line. NIX DEEP TO ENGRAM! pic.twitter.com/LCFIMv7Q9m — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 J.K. Dobbins would punch it in two plays later to put Denver up 7-0 early. That’s where it would remain with the two teams trading punts after that scoring drive. Broncos 7, Chargers 0. Full first quarter recap . Second Quarter Both teams traded good drives for field goals in the second quarter, with Denver’s drive being a 14-play, 60 yard clock-eating drive that ate up half the quarter. Even so, they struggled to close the deal. They had a chance to put up points before halftime too after a defensive pass interference call on Los Angeles on a deep pass to Jaylen Waddle. Though Courtland Sutton would then commit offensive pass interference on the next play to take them out of fringe field goal range. The quarter would end with very little offense outside of those two drives and a lot of good defense and bad penalties. Just your typical first half game play from these 2026 Broncos. Broncos 10, Chargers 3. Full second quarter recap . Third Quarter The third quarter was an absolute disaster for the Broncos. They gained five yards until the final seconds of the quarter and the defense could not generate any pass rush despite the Chargers’ offensive line being down to their second and third stringer at every position. Los Angeles would score on a long drive to start the half, then after a Bo Nix fumble, the defense would miss about five tackled to give Kiami Vidal a 42-yard touchdown for the lead. Kimani Vidal with the 42-yard TD run 🏃 @DENvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oWVJwoYm5a — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 All of the issues that plagued Denver last season that were washed over by the crazy comebacks are definitely showing again this year, but without the comebacks. Chargers 17, Broncos 10. Full third quarter recap . Fourth Quarter The two teams would trade three-and-outs, but then Marvin Mims Jr. showed why he is a few All-Pro selections as a special teamer with a 25-yard return to the Chargers’ 27-yard line. The Denver offense would do nothing and go nowhere with an offensive line that was as leaky as its been in years. Wil Lutz would hook the field goal attempt to leave the score unchanged. A critical decision was made on a fourth and short from their own 40-yard line by Los Angeles that the Broncos’ defense would stuff to give them another chance. QUE ROBINSON STOPS JUSTIN HERBERT ON 4TH DOWN pic.twitter.com/fqaxPoFDpl — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 On the first play, Nix finally hit Courtland Sutton for the first time in the game who fought his way for 13 yards and a first down. Nix would then keep it on a designed run for six and then hit Jaylen Waddle outside for a first down inside the red zone. A roughing the passer penalty would set them up with a first and goal. Two plays later Sutton came wide open on a slant for the game-tying touchdown. TOUCHDOWN COURTLAND SUTTON Broncos tie the game 💪 pic.twitter.com/mEI3dijXV1 — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 The momentum shift seemed to wake up the defense. They were all over the football, then on third down Zach Allen would take the stripe-sack to set Denver right back up at the Chargers’ 23 yard line. STRIP SACK BY ZACH ALLEN BRONCOS BALL!!! pic.twitter.com/vnaf4Jxbia — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 11, 2026 J.K. Dobbins took the first handoff up the middle for a big 14-yard gain to the nine yard line to setup a first and goal. Dobbins would gain minimally on the next play. Nix was faced with a third and goal from the seven. He would find Evan Engram open at the five where he would fight his way down to the one yard line. On fourth and goal, Sean Payton thought about going for it and then after burning a timeout changed his mind and took the points to put Denver up 20-17 with just over five minutes left in the game. The Chargers would go for it on fourth down again on their next drive where Brandon Jones got the interception to seal the comeback victory for Denver’s defense. Broncos 23, Chargers 17.

full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Rodney Shelley #24 of the Los Angeles Chargers is hit by Ja'quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos after a reception during the third quarter at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images Justin Herbert and the Los Angeles Chargers would get the ball to start the second half. It looked like it would be a quick three-and-out after a holding call forced a 3rd and 15, but Alex Singleton was beat in coverage, missed a tackle and gave up the first down. This would spark them on offense and they would keep making plays to get first downs. The first true resistance came just inside field goal range on a third and seven where Herbert would just take a design quarterback run 24-yard down to the Denver seven yard line for a first and goal and would convert it into a touchdown two plays later to tie the game up. The drive would eat up nearly 10 minutes of the quarter. Broncos 10, Chargers 10. After a predictable three-and-out by the Broncos, the Chargers would get the ball right back to face a Denver defense that has shown zero pass rush all game long. A 58-yard punt by Jeremy Crawshaw was the lone highlight that pinned the Chargers down at their own three yard line for their next drive. Denver would flip that advantage by forcing a punt and getting the ball back to the Broncos offense at their own 40 yard line. title: Broncos vs. Chargers second quarter recap
summary: The Los Angeles Chargers punted to start the second quarter where the Denver Broncos would take over at their own nine yard line. They would — predictably — go three-and-out after the run game does nothing as has been the case on most drives this season. A poor punt from Jeremy Crawshaw would set Justin […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Evan Engram #1 of the Denver Broncos runs after a catch against Cam Hart #20 of the Los Angeles Chargers during the first quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers punted to start the second quarter where the Denver Broncos would take over at their own nine yard line. They would — predictably — go three-and-out after the run game does nothing as has been the case on most drives this season. A poor punt from Jeremy Crawshaw would set Justin Herbert and the Chargers up with good field position on their next drive. They were able to turn that good field position into a decent drive. The Broncos defense woke up with a tackle for loss and back-to-back pressures to force the 42-yard field goal from Cameron Dicker. Broncos 7, Chargers 3. On Denver’s next drive, they found a bit of legs in their run game behind J.K. Dobbins. Though by little, I mean he had one decent run then two runs for three yards to bring up fourth and inches. Bo Nix plunged forward for what was called a first down, but challenged. The review didn’t really show anything conclusive and they lost the challenge. Denver would keep the ball near midfield with a fresh set of downs on that drive. An end-around to Jaylen Waddle would pick up eight yards into Chargers’ territory. A good run by RJ Harvey for another first down and a quick pass to Troy Franklin outside for another would bring Denver to the 30. A defensive pass interference call on Waddle would set Denver up in the red zone two plays later. Things would stall there, but the Wil Lutz field goal put them back up by a touchdown. Broncos 10, Chargers 3. After forcing a three-and-out, the Broncos were able to get the ball back with less than 90 seconds left in the half. From their own 19 yard line and one timeout left, Nix and the Broncos had a chance to put points up before halftime. On the very first play, Nix went deep to Jaylen Waddle. The throw was very underthrown, but the defender was all over Waddle to draw the defensive pass interference call to put Denver immediately in fringe field goal territory. Courtland Sutton then got called for offensive pass interference followed by a sack on Nix to bring up a third and forever and that is how the half would end.

title: Detroit Lions Week 5 snap counts: Keith Abney adds range to Secondary
summary: The Detroit Lions got back to their winning ways in Arizona, handily defeating the Cardinals 45-21. The Lions got off to a slow start, falling behind 7-0 in the first quarter, but they responded with 24 consecutive points in the second quarter, along with five consecutive three-and-outs forced by the defense. The Lions scored another […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Keith Abney II #6 of the Detroit Lions intercepts a pass during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions got back to their winning ways in Arizona, handily defeating the Cardinals 45-21. The Lions got off to a slow start, falling behind 7-0 in the first quarter, but they responded with 24 consecutive points in the second quarter, along with five consecutive three-and-outs forced by the defense. The Lions scored another touchdown on their first offensive possession of the second half, and it was pretty much a wrap from there. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 63 (95%) Josh Dobbs: 3 (5%) Goff was once again terrific. His efficiency was impressive, registering a 125.8 passer rating (he averages 111.3 for the season, third-best in the NFL), and his 271 passing yards vault him to the top of the NFL passing yards list (save for the results of Monday Night Football). Here’s coach Dan Campbell on Goff’s performance: “Goff is just Goff. He’s as good as they come. I’ve just been so impressed with the way he’s played these five games here. I thought he’s just gotten better every year, and here we are five in, and he’s even better than last year. He’s the real deal.” Dobbs got in the game for the final drive, after the Lions pulled their starters, but he didn’t attempt a pass and simply handed the ball off to Sione Vaki three times to run the clock. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 46 (70%) Sione Vaki: 23 (35%) — 21 special teams snaps (66%) Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 21 (66%) With the Cardinals’ run defense checking in fourth in DVOA, most analysts didn’t anticipate the Lions working hard to establish their rushing attack. While it wasn’t perfect early, the offensive line leaned on the Cardinals’ front, and Gibbs gashed them for chunk yards, amassing 151 rushing yards on 25 carries, while Vaki added another 11, and Goff earned a yard on a goal-line QB sneak for a score. Gibbs also caught five receptions for 56 receiving yards, and probably could have had more had the Lions not started scaling his touches back late in the game. Both Gibbs and Vaki were also very solid in their pass-protection roles as well. Long developing plays like this do not work unless you have great blocking. The OL does a great job and just watch Vaki. pic.twitter.com/yJvglhYdwr — Talking Grit: Detroit Lions Podcast (@talkinggritpod) October 12, 2026 Wide receiver Jameson Williams: 59 (89%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: 57 (86%) Isaac TeSlaa: 26 (39%) Tay Martin: 3 (5%) — 21 (66%) Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 4 (12%) — INJURED St. Brown fumbled twice in this game (the Lions recovered both), once on offense and once on his first punt return after taking over for an injured Kennedy, but Goff never lost his trust in the All-Pro, who led the team with 11 targets and six receptions. Williams caught only two of his four targets, but both went for long touchdowns and helped open things up for the rest of the offense. Martin was once again stellar on special teams. He recovered St. Brown’s fumble and downed a Jack Fox punt inside the five-yard line. The unfortunate news from this group came via injury, as Kennedy looks like he’ll miss some time, according to Campbell: “It doesn’t look good. As far as anything short-term, we’ll know a lot more tomorrow. I think it could be a sprain somewhere in there – a pretty good sprain. Neither one of them (Kennedy and LB Devin White) are going to be around here for a while so I hate that. Both players have done a really good job for us. “‘TK’ I really thought he really hit it. We challenged him on hitting some of these returns. His first was outstanding, and I thought his second one – he caught it, put his foot in the ground, and he took it to heart. I hate it for him that (it) happened. I don’t think it’s long-term — I think it is something where we’ll miss him for a little bit. We will see.” Tight end Sam LaPorta: 59 (89%) Brock Wright: 44 (67%) — 11 (34%) Tyler Conklin: 8 (12%) Jackson Meeks: DNP ( INACTIVE ) When the Lions were stuck in an offensive rut in the first quarter, LaPorta pulled them out, converting a tough fourth-down on the Lions’ first scoring drive and then scoring a touchdown on the next drive to help them gain momentum. Among the reserves, Wright saw his snaps increase as the Lions deployed more 12-personnel sets, while Conklin got the nod over Meeks, allowing the Lions to use more 13-personnel. Offensive line LG Christian Mahogany: 66 (100%) — 7 (21%) RT Blake Miller: 66 (100%) — 7 (22%) LT Penei Sewell: 63 (95%) C Juice Scruggs: 63 (95%) — 7 (22%) RG Tate Ratledge: 63 (95%) — 7 (22%) LT/6th OL: Larry Borom: 8 (12%) — 7 (22%) C Seth McLaughlin: 3 (5%) RG Miles Frazier: 3 (5%) LG Ben Bartch: DNP ( INJURED ) The Lions offensive line made a pass-blocking mistake on each of the Lions’ first two drives, causing them to stall, but they cleaned it up quickly and dominated the rest of the game. In the run game, they routinely moved bodies around, opening holes for Gibbs. Here’s more from Campbell: “We have a young (team). Our right tackle is young, our right guard is young, our left guard is young. So when your O-line has some youth in it, they have to continue to grow and you have to be able to trust if we get certain looks, or we get a curveball, (or) it’s 4th down. There’s a lot that goes into it, and I really feel like they’re growing. They did a heck of a job today.” On the final drive, the Lions rested Sewell, Scruggs, and Ratledge, letting Borom, McLaughlin, and Frazier fill in at left tackle, center, and right guard, respectively. Borom also saw the field in Jumbo packages as a sixth offensive lineman five times. Here comes the massive wave that’s coming at you, and it felt that way a little bit, so that’s good.” Williams and Gill-Howard provide a solid complementary 1-2 punch opposite McNeill, while Onwuzurike could be in danger of losing reps to Wingo if he keeps making mistakes. title: Lions report card, grades: Secondary takes huge strides vs. Cardinals
summary: The Detroit Lions got back on track on Sunday afternoon with their most complete win of the season over the Arizona Cardinals. Here are my grades for each position in their convincing victory. Quarterback: A Jared Goff wasn’t electric against the Cardinals, but he also played pretty close to mistake-free football. He finished the game […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Roger McCreary #21 of the Detroit Lions breaks up a pass intended for Reggie Virgil #82 of the Arizona Cardinals during the second quarter of an NFL football game at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions got back on track on Sunday afternoon with their most complete win of the season over the Arizona Cardinals. Here are my grades for each position in their convincing victory. Quarterback: A Jared Goff wasn’t electric against the Cardinals, but he also played pretty close to mistake-free football. He finished the game with 271 yards, a season-high 9.0 yards per attempt, three passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown. He still has yet to turn the ball over this season, and has produced 13 total touchdowns. Hard to disagree with Dan Campbell here: “Goff is just Goff. He’s as good as they come. I’ve just been so impressed with the way he’s played these five games here. I thought he’s just gotten better every year, and here we are five in, and he’s even better than last year. He’s the real deal.” Running backs: A Jahmyr Gibbs was phenomenal again on Sunday. NextGenStats credited him with 10 missed tackles forced against the Cardinals, and it honestly felt like more. No one was getting him down on the first attempt. His 93 yards after contract was second most of any running back in Week 5, and his +2.0 rushing yards over expected per rush was sixth-best of the week. Perhaps most impressively, Gibbs (and Sione Vaki) were excellent in pass protection, which helped the Lions hit on some big plays. Long developing plays like this do not work unless you have great blocking. The OL does a great job and just watch Vaki. pic.twitter.com/yJvglhYdwr — Talking Grit: Detroit Lions Podcast (@talkinggritpod) October 12, 2026 Tight ends: A+ When the Lions offense looked like they were stuck in a rut, it was Sam LaPorta who pulled them out with an impressive fourth-down catch that kept their first touchdown drive alive. Then, when Detroit was behind the sticks on a third-and-11 on the next drive, his individual effort to turn it into a fourth-and-1 was impressive. And, of course, on the very next play he did this. There goes Sam pic.twitter.com/jWOW1mJVFT — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 11, 2026 LaPorta finished the game by catching all five of his targets for 88 yards and a score. I thought this was also quietly one of Brock Wright’s best games as a blocker, and the PFF grades seems to back that up (79.5 pass blocking, 57.1 run blocking). Wide receivers: B- It’s odd to see that on such a dominant day on offense, the Lions’ receivers caught just eight collective passes for 116 yards and two touchdowns. Jameson Williams was obviously hugely impactful with his two touchdown catches (on two total catches), but it was a down game from Amon-Ra St. Brown. He had at least one drop, fumbled the ball twice, and just wasn’t that impactful until later in the game. That said, screen passes to St. Brown were highly effective because he’s such a smart, patient player who knows how to follow his blocks. Offensive line: B The Lions’ offensive line still has some problems clocking blitzes and adjusting properly—which gives me quite a bit of concern for the upcoming Vikings game—but they settled into this game very nicely. After allowing a sack on each of the first three drives of the game, Goff was spotless the rest of the way. The run game was a bit inconsistent, and I feel like Gibbs bailed them out quite a bit, but against a very good Cardinals run defense, they battled and wore them down. There was definitely more good than bad with the offensive line, but there is still clearly room for improvement, as well. Defensive line: B Oddly, this felt like a bit of a down game for the defensive front, despite Detroit tallying five sacks against Jacoby Brissett. Detroit produced their lowest pressure rate of the season (27.8%) and second-fewest amount of pressures overall (15). Considering they faced 53 passing plays, they need to be better than that. However, Detroit’s run defense was phenomenal on the day. They stuffed a career-high 27.8% of rushes in this game, and produced the best EPA/rush mark of the season (-0.24). Or, in more traditional stats, 56 rushing yards and 3.1 yards per carry are stellar numbers that are actually inflated by a very late Brissett scramble for 18 yards. Without that run, Arizona managed just 38 yards on 17 carries (2.2 YPC). Linebackers: B+ The linebackers deserve a lot of the credit for that improved run defense, including a much more familiar-looking Jack Campbell. The Lions’ All-Pro linebacker tallied 11 tackles, including four defensive stops. Most impressive, though, was this unit’s coverage against the Cardinals. It certainly wasn’t perfect, but when lined up in man-coverage against a pair of very talented Cardinals tight ends, Detroit held their own. Both Campbell and Malcolm Rodriguez were forcing Trey McBride and Elijah Higgins to make seriously contested catches, which was a relieving sight after how much Detroit has struggled against tight ends this year. Secondary: B Well, well, well. It seems the Lions’ cornerbacks can actually cover. Roger McCreary posted a franchise-best six pass breakups against the Cardinals on a whopping 18 targets. D.J. Reed may have even been better. Although he managed just one pass breakup, he also allowed just 30 yards in seven targets. Both players were absolute forces in the run game, as well. Reed produced three tackles for loss, and both players ranked in the top 15 in run defense grades for cornerbacks this week (Reed: 74.7, 14th; McCreary: 79.6, fifth). Keith Abney seemed to provide some stability at safety, even if he didn’t make too many plays (was only targeted three times). But there are still too many blown coverages by this unit. It was a step in the right direction, but Detroit’s defensive backs need to continue to improve if they want to compete against better offenses. Special teams: A Just a stellar day from Dave Fipp’s crew. Detroit’s punt return game averaged 17.3 yards per return, with three of their four plays going for at least 10 yards. Kick return was solid with a 27.3 average on four Jacob Saylors attempts. And the coverage teams were outstanding, as well. Throw in another perfect day from Jake Bates, a late pinning by Jack Fox, and it’s hard to complain about literally anything from this group outside of St. Brown’s fumble. Coaching: A- It sure sounds like Dan Campbell and company really lit into the Lions player this week at practice , and it was nice to see them respond to it on the field—albeit about a quarter late. The slow starts are certainly concerning, but hard to pinpoint on what exactly is going wrong. But Detroit made some very logical coaching decision throughout the week that made sense. The move to more man coverage was something that I was calling for given the front-four’s success at generating pressure on their own. The numbers could update in the morning, but TruMedia had the Lions in man coverage on 31 percent of their snaps against the Cardinals. That was the fifth-highest man rate among teams that played this week. The Lions were at 15.6 percent from Weeks 1-4. — Colton Pouncy (@colton_pouncy) October 12, 2026 They also deserve credit for putting Abney’s rangy athleticism at the safety position, and benching Christian Izien’s too-inconsistent play. Throw in some great passing design plays, and Dan Campbell’s invaluable aggression (three fourth-down touchdowns), and I thought this was a much-needed, well-coached game.

title: Detroit Lions vs. Arizona Cardinals post-game reaction: Is Detroit fixed?
summary: The Detroit Lions are heading into the bye week after an emphatic win over the Arizona Cardinals. It was a convincing win, not just because they ended up winning by 24 points, but because literally every phase of the game shined on Sunday. The offense scored on seven straight drives. The defense held Arizona scoreless […]
full_text: Arizona Cardinals receiver Michael Wilson (14) just misses catching a pass while being defended by Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4) at State Farm Stadium in Glendale on Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions are heading into the bye week after an emphatic win over the Arizona Cardinals. It was a convincing win, not just because they ended up winning by 24 points, but because literally every phase of the game shined on Sunday. The offense scored on seven straight drives. The defense held Arizona scoreless on seven straight drives—including five consecutive three-and-outs. The return and coverage teams were outstanding on special teams. So on this week’s PODcast, we celebrated a little. It’s been a while since we’ve seen a complete game from the Lions, and it’s nice to bask in that glory for a minute. It’s much better than the alternative of heading into the bye week 2-3, craving for some heads on a platter. Then we dig into the nitty gritty of the game. What changes did the Lions make to find some success on defense? How did the Lions’ cornerbacks—specifically Roger McCreary and D.J. Reed—suddenly look like top-tier coverage defenders? And what successes were offensive coordinator Drew Petzing able to find? We also look at the bigger picture of this team. While this was a good game, how will they look when they face a tougher Packers offense next game? What will Detroit do with the secondary when Brian Branch returns? And what the heck’s the deal with these slow starts on offense? We tackle it all on this week’s PODcast, which you can listen to on any podcasting platform you enjoy by searching “Pride of Detroit.” We’ve also made it easy for you by embedding this week’s episode below: You can always catch the video version of the PODcast—the live version with bonus content—over on our YouTube channel and Twitch pages .

title: Injury updates: Detroit Lions lose 2 players to potential significant injuries
summary: The Detroit Lions got off to a slow and tough start against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. Not only did they fall behind 7-0 in a hurry, but two Lions players also went to the locker room with injuries. While Detroit managed to rebound on the field in a big way, it wasn’t great news […]
full_text: Detroit Lions punt returner Tom Kennedy (85) celebrates a run against Arizona Cardinals during the first half at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions got off to a slow and tough start against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. Not only did they fall behind 7-0 in a hurry, but two Lions players also went to the locker room with injuries. While Detroit managed to rebound on the field in a big way, it wasn’t great news for the two injured players. First was linebacker Devin White. It wasn’t clear how White, who was active for the first time since Week 2, suffered his injury, but he was listed as questionable to return with a forearm. The FOX broadcast showed him taking a cart to the locker room. Unfortunately, coach Dan Campbell confirmed after the game that White suffered a broken forearm that will likely necessitate surgery. “I think Devin’s probably going to need surgery. It’s a broken forearm; it’s unfortunate. I hate it because he was doing some good things for us in this game,” Campbell said. In White’s absence, the Lions split LB3 snaps between Malcolm Rodriguez (23 snaps) and Trevor Nowaske (9). Shortly thereafter, Lions punt returner Tom Kennedy suffered a knee injury on a return in which his foot was caught in the ground and his body was bent awkwardly. Kennedy was initially able to walk to the sidelines and was treated in the blue tent. However, eventually, he was carted to the locker room. The Lions officially listed him as questionable to return with a knee injury before downgrading him to out in the second half. Campbell said they’ll know more about his condition on Monday after more tests, but the expectation is he will miss significant time, too. “It doesn’t look good, as far as anything short-term,” Campbell said. “We’ll know a lot more tomorrow. I think it could be a sprain somewhere in there – a pretty good sprain. Neither one of them are going to be around here for a while so I hate that.” He later added, regarding Kennedy, “I don’t think it’s long, long-term — I think it is something where we’ll miss him for a little bit. We will see.” On the subsequent punt, Amon-Ra St. Brown was the returner for Detroit, and fumbled the ball, but the Lions recovered. He’s unlikely to serve as Detroit’s full-time punt returner, so we’ll have to wait and see how Detroit responds. In kick return, it was cornerback Khalil Dorsey who took Kennedy’s spot.
