title: Vikings Overcome Red Zone Errors, Defense Dominates Again In Win Over Saints
summary: The Minnesota Vikings had what, for them, qualifies as an offensive explosion on Sunday afternoon at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, as they scored two touchdowns in the same game for the first time since Week 1. When you’re playing defense the way the Vikings have been, that’s just about all you need. Despite […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - OCTOBER 11: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings runs against the New Orleans Saints during the fourth quarter at Caesars Superdome on October 11, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings had what, for them, qualifies as an offensive explosion on Sunday afternoon at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, as they scored two touchdowns in the same game for the first time since Week 1. When you’re playing defense the way the Vikings have been, that’s just about all you need. Despite committing two turnovers in the red zone that led directly to all of the New Orleans Saints’ points, the Vikings did enough to keep themselves undefeated on the 2026 season, as the Vikings’ offense had its best game of the season and did enough to put together a 23-13 victory in New Orleans in Week 5. The Saints won the coin toss and elected to defer to the second half, giving the Vikings’ offense the football first in this one. Kyler Murray found T.J. Hockenson early on for a first-down completion that saw Hockenson get his head slammed into the ground awkwardly and end up going to the sidelines for a concussion evaluation. The Vikings’ offense continued moving down the field, including Murray finding Tai Felton for a 23-yard completion to get into Saints’ territory. A third-down completion to Justin Jefferson that would have put the Vikings into the red zone was negated by an illegal formation call, and the Vikings could not convert the ensuing third-down attempt, so on came Will Reichard. He connected from 40 yards out to give the Vikings an early 3-0 lead six minutes into the contest. The Saints’ offense saw their first possession turn into a very quick three-and-out, with Tyler Shough getting knocked to the ground twice. The Vikings took over and, once again, put together another nice drive, with Jefferson getting his first two official catches of the game to push the Vikings into New Orleans territory at the 30. A pair of carries by Aaron Jones moved the chains again and put the Vikings’ offense into the red zone for just the ninth time this season. The Vikings then found themselves facing a 3rd-and-1 from the New Orleans 10, and Jones took another handoff and fumbled the ball away. Chase Young picked up the loose ball for the Saints and returned it to the New Orleans 34-yard line, making it a turnover for the Vikings and yet another offensive possession that ended without a touchdown. The Saints’ offense picked up a first down as the first quarter ended, as Shough found Chris Olave at midfield. The Saints then converted on a couple of short fourth downs, one on a pass to Olave and another on a pass to Devaughn Vele. The New Orleans offense kept pushing and moved into the red zone and, eventually, into a goal-to-go situation behind a couple of runs from Kendre Miller. Miller then took the ball down to the 1-yard line, and eventually took the ball into the end zone from two yards out to give the Saints a 7-3 lead with eight and a half minutes left to go in the first half. The Vikings got the ball back, and three straight handoffs to Jones resulted in a three-and-out. New Orleans got the ball back at their own 21-yard line following the Brett Thorson punt. The Saints’ offense reciprocated with a three-and-out of their own, and Myles Price once again showed why he is quickly establishing himself as the best return specialist in the league. He fielded the punt from former Viking Ryan Wright and took it 43 yards, putting the ball on the New Orleans side of the field at the 47-yard line. As is their wont after a big play, the Vikings started the drive with a penalty, as Ryan Van Demark was called for holding, pushing the ball back to the Minnesota side of the field and making it 1st-and-20. The drive went nowhere after that, and Thorson had to punt it away once again. But the Saints went three-and-out at the two-minute warning, giving the Vikings the ball back with 1:56 left on the clock and one timeout left from their own 31-yard line. The Vikings managed to push the ball into Saints’ territory at the 39-yard line on a nice throw from Murray to Jefferson, but then Murray inexplicably took a sack to force the Vikings to burn their last timeout. Another pass to Jefferson got the ball a little closer to the end zone, and that meant another opportunity for Reichard, who put the ball through the uprights from 54 yards out to make it a 7-6 game going into halftime. The Vikings’ special teams made an impact on the second-half kickoff, as rookie Jake Golday punched the ball free from Saints return man Jayden Price, with Jeshaun Jones recovering the fumble for the Vikings to give them the ball right away. A trick play missed on first down, but then Murray corrected things by scrambling for 18 yards on 3rd-and-10 to avoid a three-and-out. Then, on another third-down play, the Vikings did something that they hadn’t done in over two full games. They scored a touchdown. On offense . Murray lofted one up in the back-left corner of the end zone for Jefferson in triple coverage , and Jefferson managed to come down with it for a 15-yard touchdown to put the Vikings back on top, 13-7. Speechless. @k1 @JJettas2 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/FOHP5Fh7oG — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) October 11, 2026 The Saints’ offense committed a second straight turnover on the next series, as a series of penalties pushed them back into a 2nd-and-26 situation, and Shough threw a pass right to Byron Murphy for an interception. Taking it right back. @byronmurphy 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/zownWfRtSy — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) October 11, 2026 Minnesota promptly moved back into the red zone and found themselves facing a 3rd-and-15 from the New Orleans 19-yard line. Murray flipped a short pass to Myles Price on the left side, and it looked like the Saints’ defense had taken him down, but the ball came loose and was picked up by Saints’ safety Jonas Sanker, who raced down the sideline for an 87-yard score, and just like that the score was tied at 13-13. And it remained tied because Daniel Carlson, the former Viking, pushed the extra point wide to the left. The Vikings got the ball back, and Murray found Jeshaun Jones for his first NFL reception, a 32-yarder that quickly put the Vikings back into New Orleans territory. Aaron Jones then took a handoff for 19 yards, and the Vikings were right back into the red zone. After they changed ends for the fourth quarter, Jones took a handoff from Murray and barreled over Julian Blackmon for an 8-yard score to put the Vikings back in the lead, 20-13. . @showtyme_33 😤😤😤 📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/ak0a4ouh5Q — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) October 11, 2026 The Saints’ offense, once again, went three-and-out, giving the Vikings’ offense another opportunity to add to their lead with around twelve minutes left in regulation. The Vikings’ offense was moving the bal until Kevin O’Connell, inexplicably, called a trick play that saw Jefferson try to throw a pass back to Murray that was nearly intercepted by a Saints’ defensive lineman but “only” wound up going down as an 11-yard loss. The Vikings did add more points, fortunately, thanks to another field goal by Reichard. He connected from 55 yards out to make it 23-13 with seven minutes left in regulation. New Orleans took their next possession into Minnesota territory and faced a 4th-and-7. Rather than have Carlson attempt a 62-yard field goal, they elected to go for it, but Shough’s pass to Juwan Johnson was stopped short of the line to gain for a turnover on downs. The Vikings wound up punting it away, but they got the ball back soon thereafter as the defense intercepted Shough again, with Byron Murphy getting his second of the day on a deep ball intended for Olave. Byron Murphy Jr. gets his SECOND interception of the day 😤 @MINvsNO on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/yFA3GYjaCP — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 The…

title: 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Raiders
summary: The New England Patriots went into their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday severely shorthanded and missing starters on both sides of the ball. It wasn’t a problem for them, though, as they cruised to a 45-17 win at Gillette Stadium. Let’s get into our lessons learned from the Patriots’ third win of […]
full_text: The New England Patriots went into their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday severely shorthanded and missing starters on both sides of the ball. It wasn’t a problem for them, though, as they cruised to a 45-17 win at Gillette Stadium. Let’s get into our lessons learned from the Patriots’ third win of the season. Drake Maye is back The Patriots’ starting quarterback started this season looking bad, but, similar to last year, it seems like the game against the Bills was the start of the turnaround for him. On Sunday against the Raiders, he was impressive, making some gorgeous throws, some excellent off-schedule plays, and, maybe most importantly, great decisions all day long. This is the Drake Maye that we’re used to seeing, if he can play like this moving forward, the Patriots are going to be in just about every game this season. Elijah Ponder is a problem The Patriots found a diamond in the rough when they signed outside linebacker Elijah Ponder as an undrafted free agent out of Cal Poly last year. He’s already up to 4.5 sacks this season, and almost gave his team a field goal on Sunday. when he strip-sacked Kirk Cousins at the end of the first half. He’s been a demon since midway through the season last year, and he’s been consistently getting even better as time went on. If he can continue to grow, the Patriots might have a guy who will be a force for years to come on this defense — and a viable long-term replacement for Harold Landry on the edge. Injury concerns continue As noted above, the Patriots came into Sunday’s game rather short-handed, and they lost some key contributors during the game as well. Will Campbell went down with a knee injury, and is reportedly expected to “miss some time” after suffering a sprain on the same knee he tore his MCL on last season. In addition, TreVeyon Henderson went down with an ankle injury, while Dre’Mont Jones and Cory Durden both were banged up. as well. It remains to be seen how bad these injuries are, but, with the depth already being tested, losing more guys could be a problem for the Patriots moving forward. Rhamondre Stevenson looks great The final stats may not look gaudy — 64 yards and a. touchdown on 13 carries — but Rhamondre Stevenson ran the ball well on Sunday. His wiggle is impressive, and he was able to continuously break the first tackle and pick up extra yards; he forced five missed tackles during Sunday’s game. The Patriots might need to add another back with Henderson going down, but Stevenson being so solid is a great thing for the Patriots. Being able to run the football is key, and having a back that is able to not only run, but also be effective out of the backfield, is huge for their offense. Caleb Lomu impresses The Patriots surprised some people earlier this year when they traded up in the first round to take offensive tackle Caleb Lomu. The Utah product has been a reserve behind Will Campbell and Morgan Moses all season, outside of coming in for Moses a few weeks ago against the Jaguars, before being called in after Campbell left with due to the aforementioned knee injury in the second quarter. When he went in, there were natural questions about his ability to hold up, but he played very well when he was in the game. Of course, with offensive line play, to really know how well they played, we have to watch the full film and take a closer look, but, on first watch, it was an impressive performance. That’s good too, because the Patriots are most likely going to have to rely on him to be their starter at left tackle for a bit. Short-handed receiver group gets the job done The Patriots were without A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins, but Drake Maye still had one of the best passing days of his career. DeMario Douglas had a great game, finishing with two touchdowns; Efton Chism continued to look like a more than capable contributor; Romeo Doubs didn’t finish a lot of his catches, but he did force a few defensive penalties; Kyle Williams even got in on the action, catching two deep passes, including a 34-yard touchdown. Tight ends Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon had solid games as well. So, even with a bunch of guys out, the Patriots were still able to have multiple threats in the passing game. When Brown and Hollins come back, that depth will be a great thing for the Patriots to lean on. Josh McDaniels is cooking For the second week in a row, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels put together a fantastic game plan that consistently put his players in a position to be successful. He had Drake Maye making plays that were comfortable for him, and you could tell that the team was feeling good about itself including on the Hunter Henry screen and the Efton Chism throw back to TreVeyon Henderson. If McDaniels continues to construct game plans and call them like he did against the Raiders, this offense is going to be in a good position moving forward. Reports of his demise were exaggerated. Penalties keep disrupting proceedings Patriots vs. Raiders featured 20 accepted penalties, and at least a handful of them were questionable at best. This has been a problem around the league, and unacceptable for a multi-billion dollar business. The Raiders game last week is one where it clearly wasn’t a catch, but they didn’t trigger the review quick enough. This week, the Seahawks lost, in part, because the ref marked the ball in the wrong spot when he couldn’t see where Cooper Kupp went out of bounds. I get that it’s a hard job, and that they make a lot of good judgment calls as well, but the refs across the league need to be better. Brock Bowers is incredible, and you just have to tip your hat The Raiders don’t have a ton of talent, but they have the best tight end in the league, and arguably a top-10 pass catcher in the league with Brock Bowers. If I were the Raiders, I would consider throwing to him every play. They didn’t quite do that on Sunday, but Kirk Cousins still targeted him 10 times, and he ended up with eight catches for 110 receiving yards, with a touchdown. He also fumbled once as well, but the verdict is still clear: he is a monster. The Patriots not having Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis made it a lot more difficult to cover him, but they were able to shut down most every other player on the team. Regardless of what the rest of the Raiders offense looks like, having a player of his caliber is a huge boost, especially with a rookie quarterback eventually taking over. A tough defense awaits Next up for the Patriots is another home game, this one against the New York Jets, who are coming off a 17-12 win over the Browns. The Jets terrorized the Browns offense all day, sacking Deshaun Watson eight times, forcing a total of five fumbles, and recovering two of them. The Patriots do have a much better offensive line than the Browns, but the Jets have heavily invested in their defense, including the No. 2 pick in this year’s draft, David Bailey, who had three sacks on Sunday. With Will Campbell likely out for this one, it bears watching if Caleb Lomu is going to make his first career start. Depending on what happens with the Bills on Monday night, the Patriots could be in first place in the division, and you’d hate to see them lose that with a home defeat to the Jets. It doesn’t look like they’re going to be a push over, however, so I’m looking forward to watching this one to see how the Patriots fare. One spot where they should have a clear advantage is coaching, which is important, especially with the amount of players that they have hurt right now.

title: Drake Maye has found his mojo again
summary: After a rough first three games of the 2026 season, in which Drake Maye turned the ball over seven times, the New England Patriots’ quarterback has now delivered back-to-back resurgent performances, resembling the MVP runner-up form he showcased last season. On Sunday, Maye and the Patriots handily defeated the Las Vegas Raiders, 45-17, returning home […]
full_text: After a rough first three games of the 2026 season, in which Drake Maye turned the ball over seven times, the New England Patriots’ quarterback has now delivered back-to-back resurgent performances, resembling the MVP runner-up form he showcased last season. On Sunday, Maye and the Patriots handily defeated the Las Vegas Raiders , 45-17, returning home to Foxboro following a two-game road trip. The third-year signal-caller finished just six yards shy of his career total in passing yards, throwing for 374 yards and four touchdowns while adding a fifth score using his legs. Setting the tone early, New England’s opening drive ended with Maye capitalizing on a Raiders’ busted coverage to find DeMario Douglas wide open for a 35-yard touchdown pass. With stout protection, Maye, standing poised in the pocket, delivered the deep attempt to cap off a five-play, 79-yard scoring drive, giving the Patriots an early 7-0 lead. “I’m going to come in at every game and week and attack it. I’m confident in myself, my abilities and the guys around me — and part of it is the first touchdown to [Douglas],” Maye said. “I had all day back there [in the pocket], and those are things I’m working on, when I have time, just to sit in there and find somebody open.” Through New England’s three initial matchups, the offense managed just two offensive touchdowns. On Sunday, it recorded five completions of 20 yards or more, following three against the Buffalo Bills last week. Maye’s rediscovered poise was a key factor in that downfield production, leading the Patriots to four scoring drives in under three minutes that totaled 24 points. “We need to hit [those plays] when we get the chance to, and we hit most of them today,” Maye said. “We still had some [plays] where we could have had even more explosives. I’m proud of the guys for executing when we got the chance. I thought everybody was making plays.” Opening the second half, Maye found another downfield target from 34 yards out, connecting with second-year receiver Kyle Williams down the left sideline, extending the Patriots’ lead to 28-7. “I felt like [Maye] was in control,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “We always talk about when we have clean pockets and his ability to transfer up into really good pockets [where] we’re going to gain yards. Being able to recognize man or zone [coverage], or where he wants to go with the football, and the timing of it.” Linebacker and defensive captain Robert Spillane credited the offense’s explosive plays for taking some stress off of the defense. In turn, New England’s defensive unit held Las Vegas to 17 points and forced the visiting offense into a third-quarter fumble. That dynamic was absent two weeks ago against the Jacksonville Jaguars. After two first-half turnovers, the Patriots, trailing 14-3, had a chance to make the deficit a one-score game with an Andy Borregales field goal; however, New England’s kicker missed, and after the offense failed to capitalize on the defense’s first-half efforts, the Jaguars scored three consecutive touchdowns in the second half. But the past two weeks have been different, as the Patriots have scored a combined 79 points over that duration. “It’s just fun to see Drake smiling big on the sidelines,” Spillane said. “That confidence is obviously back, and just watching him lead and push the ball down the field was fun.” While Maye reiterated his confidence in himself entering every game to make plays, as he said after the Jacksonville loss, his performance in Buffalo marked a turning point.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Patriots’ collective effort neutralizes Maxx Crosby, Raiders pass rush in Week 5 win
summary: The New England Patriots opened their Week 5 game against the Las Vegas Raiders with a bang, marching 79 yards in only five plays to take a 7-0 lead and set the tone for the rest of the afternoon. Drake Maye and his men capped the series with a 35-yard touchdown pass to DeMario Douglas, […]
full_text: The New England Patriots opened their Week 5 game against the Las Vegas Raiders with a bang, marching 79 yards in only five plays to take a 7-0 lead and set the tone for the rest of the afternoon. Drake Maye and his men capped the series with a 35-yard touchdown pass to DeMario Douglas, a play that also was exemplary for much of the game. Maye was able to operate from as clean a pocket as you will find on a third down: from snap to release, 4.5 seconds passed, allowing him to find Douglas wide open behind the Raiders secondary. “I’m back there, credit the offensive line, eating a ham sandwich. I’ve got all day back there,” said Maye. Maye could have had a lot of ham sandwiches on Sunday. The Patriots quarterback was pressured on a season-low 34% of his dropbacks in his team’s 45-17 victory , and sacked just once all day. That marked a drastic improvement from the last time Maye and company went up against the Raiders, on opening weekend 2025. The pressure rate that day was 40% and the young passer was taken down four times. Stalwart edge Maxx Crosby was a particular problem that day, registering seven disruptions and a sack. This time around, he was held to five pressures and failed to bring Maye down once — still solid production but a far cry from the game-wrecking potential he has shown throughout his career and back in 2025. That was the direct result of New England investing resources in slowing Crosby down and preventing him from having the same impact he had last season. “Hell of a football player ever since he’s touched this field, ever since he’s gotten to this league,” said right tackle Morgan Moses. “My hat goes off to him because you know it’s a battle. It’s going to be a 60-minute battle. Doesn’t matter what the score is, he’s going to rush the passer. That’s a guy that, obviously you have to detail throughout the week and understand where he’s going to be at. “Just a heck of a player,” added tight end Hunter Henry. “We have a ton of respect for him and all he’s done in this league, and this year. Know he can wreck a game pretty fast, so I’m over there a lot chipping and throwing some extra jabs to help out. The offensive line does a great job.” Morgan Moses in particular saw a lot of Crosby throughout the game, on whose side Crosby aligned for most of the game. “He’s on the right a lot against Morgan, and Morgan does a great job,” said Henry. “A guy that I love going to work with, is a lot of fun to compete with, has done it in this league for a long time, and have a ton of respect for. It was kind of a team effort to take care of that guy.” Moses, who was questionable with a foot injury heading into the contest, echoed his teammates thoughts: it was indeed a collective effort that helped neutralize Crosby and the rest of the Raiders’ pass rush. “It takes all 11. It’s not just one person. It takes the quarterback to get the ball out. It takes the receivers running the routes. It takes six or seven guys in protection to help out,” he said. “When we are connected and we do it together, this is what it looks like.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 6 winners and losers from Patriots win over Raiders
summary: The New England Patriots stayed in the win column on Sunday. Going up against a Las Vegas Raiders team that had previously lost just one of its first four games of the season and was ranked highly in various offensive and defensive categories, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel celebrated a convincing 45-17 victory […]
full_text: The New England Patriots stayed in the win column on Sunday. Going up against a Las Vegas Raiders team that had previously lost just one of its first four games of the season and was ranked highly in various offensive and defensive categories, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel celebrated a convincing 45-17 victory to improve to 3-2 on the season.. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Week 5 contest. Winners QB Drake Maye: MVP Drake Maye was back in Gillette Stadium on Sunday. The Patriots quarterback finished the game 26-of-34 for 374 yards and four touchdowns while adding a fifth score on the ground. His +0.76 EPA per drop-back ranked in the 100th percentile. The Raiders gave Maye and the Patriots’ pass catchers opportunities downfield, which is a puzzling game plan against the group. He capitalized, completing 8-of-11 passes over 10 air yards for 206 yards and three touchdowns. “Coach McDaniels was — it was beautiful,“ Maye said. “It was beautiful to be a part of today. He was clicking on all cylinders, making us look good, and we were executing.“ Kyle Williams and the WRs: The Patriots entered Sunday with just four wide receivers on the active roster with Mack Hollins and A.J. Brown on injured reserve. The group stepped up, led by Kyle Williams who hauled in a pair of deep passes from Maye en route to posting a career-high 91 yards and a touchdown. Drake Maye to Kyle Williams 😍 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/5o265S4HvW — New England Patriots (@Patriots) October 11, 2026 Behind Williams, fellow second-year receiver Efton Chism III filled the Hollins’ role nicely leading the team in targets (6) and catches (5) to post a career-high 57 yards. DeMario Douglas then found the end zone twice while Romeo Doubs made his mark by drawing a pair of defensive pass interference penalties. OT Caleb Lomu and the offensive line: With Will Campbell leaving the game with a knee injury, rookie first-round pick Caleb Lomu took his place at left tackle. Las Vegas immediately flipped Maxx Crosby to the rookie’s side but Lomu held up in his lone rep vs. the All-Pro. The rest of the game was much of the same as Lomu allowed just one hurry in live viewing and finished his defender to the ground on Maye’s rushing touchdown. As for the rest of the line, the unit was called for five penalties but Maye was under pressure on just 26% of his drop-backs. Las Vegas had six quarterback hits, but there were plenty of clean pockets throughout the day for Maye to operate in. “The first touchdown to Pop, I’m back there – credit the offensive line eating a ham sandwich, so I’ve got all day back there,” Maye said. ED Elijah Ponder and DT Milton Williams: The Patriots’ young edge rusher continued a strong start to the season, as Ponder recorded two sacks (one strip sack) and an additional quarterback hit and hurry. On one of Ponder’s sacks, the Raiders had all eyes on Milton Williams along the interior as the defensive lineman continues to get plenty of extra attention this season. Still, Williams produced his best game of the season with a team-high five pressures. Getting to Kirk Cousins was an emphasis on Sunday, and duo helped lead to a 48% pressure rate on the Raiders’ quarterback — which included a similar percent with a standard four-man rush. Losers Penalties: Speaking post game, Mike Vrabel noted his team still had plenty to improve and clean up. Among the issues to correct: penalties. The Patriots were flagged 12 times on Sunday for 116 yards, a “ridiculous” amount, according to Vrabel. Honorable mentions Rhamondre Stevenson ran well after dealing with a knee injury this week, finishing with 64 yards and a touchdown while adding 21 yards through the air. Career-highs for Eli Raridon with five catches for 57 yards. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see Raridon become more-and-more involved as the season goes on. Game ball for cornerback Kindle Vildor. With the Patriots down four cornerbacks, Vildor stepped up (43 snaps) and had a pass breakup and a forced fumble. Credit to the Patriots coaching staff on all sides of the football. They were down a handful of starters and lost more during the game, and didn’t miss a single beat. Everyone was prepared. Bonus shoutout to Brock Bowers. The Patriots tried all sorts of things to take him out of the game and he still finished with an 8/110/1 line. Beast.
author: Brian Hines

title: Will Campbell injury: Latest news about Patriots left tackle
summary: Update (10/11/26): Will Campbell expected to ‘miss some time’ after suffering knee injury vs. Raiders The blows keep coming for the New England Patriots offensive line. Starting left tackle Will Campbell, who exited Sunday’s win over the Las Vegas Raiders with a knee injury in the second quarter, is expected to “miss some time.” According […]
full_text: Update (10/11/26): Will Campbell expected to ‘miss some time’ after suffering knee injury vs. Raiders The blows keep coming for the New England Patriots offensive line. Starting left tackle Will Campbell, who exited Sunday’s win over the Las Vegas Raiders with a knee injury in the second quarter, is expected to “miss some time.” According to a report by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, the sophomore is believed to have suffered a knee sprain. He will undergo an MRI on Monday to confirm the initial diagnosis and determine the severity of the sprain. With Campbell out, first-round rookie Caleb Lomu is slated to remain as the starting left tackle. Lomu played a career-high 47 snaps in place of Campbell versus Las Vegas. Update (10/11/26): Patriots OT Will Campbell ruled out of Raiders game after suffering knee injury The Patriots have downgraded Will Campbell (knee) to out for the remainder of Sunday. Following the second quarter injury, Campbell did return from the locker room to the sideline. He put on his helmet and went though tests on the sideline before riding the stationary bike. Campbell then did not return to the sideline with the team following halftime and was eventually ruled out. Rookie Caleb Lomu worked in his place at left tackle. Original story (10/11/26): Patriots OT Will Campbell suffers knee injury vs. Raiders, questionable to return New England Patriots left tackle Will Campbell left Sunday’s game with a right knee injury. He is questionable to return. The injury occurred on a second quarter run play where Rhamondre Stevenson was brought down on Campbell’s right leg. He stayed on the turf acquiring medical attention before visiting the blue medical tent and quickly departing to the locker room. Last season, Campbell suffered a MCL sprain to the same right knee that landed him on injured reserve. He returned for the playoffs but struggled as he was not fully healthy. With Campbell in the locker room on Sunday, rookie Caleb Lomu filled in at left tackle. The Patriots traded up to select Lomu 28th overall in the draft this past April. Through four weeks, Lomu had played just 50 offensive snaps as the third offensive tackle and jumbo tight end.

title: Patriots’ short-handed receiver room delivers in win over Raiders
summary: The New England Patriots entered Sunday’s game with just four wide receiver on the game-day roster: Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III, and Kyle Williams. Being without two of their top pass catchers in A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins didn’t slow down New England’s offense. Instead, the remaining group delivered several career-best performances as […]
full_text: The New England Patriots entered Sunday’s game with just four wide receiver on the game-day roster: Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III, and Kyle Williams. Being without two of their top pass catchers in A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins didn’t slow down New England’s offense. Instead, the remaining group delivered several career-best performances as the Patriots put up 45 points in a blowout win over the Las Vegas Raiders. “They’re all ready to go,” head coach Mike Vrabel said of the group. “They all play different positions. That’s not easy, you know, to learn three different positions and being able to step in there and block and make plays. The ball found each and every one of them.” Doubs (62 snaps) and Chism (career-high 57 snaps) led the group in playing time Sunday. While Doubs made his biggest impact by drawing a pair of defensive pass interference penalties that helped set up touchdowns, Chism led the receivers with five receptions on six targets for a career-high 57 yards. The biggest plays, however, came from Douglas and Williams. Douglas opened and closed the scoring, getting wide open for a touchdown on both occasions. Williams, meanwhile, showcased the deep-ball ability he has flashed throughout his Patriots tenure. That included hauling in a 34-yard touchdown pass from Drake Maye before the two connected again in the third quarter on a deep post for 49 yards. Williams finished with a career-high 91 receiving yards, a needed performance aafter a slow start to the season. “Definitely a confidence booster,” Williams said. “Something I really needed to just bring the joy back for me. And it’s back now.” As the production spread across the room, so did the excitement. For Chism, that reflects the bond the group has built. “It’s just how much respect we have for everyone’s work ethic on a day-to-day basis,” Chism said. “We all love each other. We’re a tight group, and so I love seeing Kyle score, Rome score, Pop. It’s just awesome. And with Mack and A.J. out — everyone is just so close and tight. It’s an awesome room and I’m very blessed to be a part of it.” That chemistry is what Vrabel wants to see from his entire team. “They all care about each other,” Vrabel said. “They’re just as excited for the next guy if it was them, and I think that that’s truly what we want to build around here, you know? And I have to get it to be the entire team. I have to get the entire team to look at it like that.”
author: Brian Hines

title: ‘Next man up’ mentality crucial for Patriots cornerback group in win over Raiders
summary: When they released their final injury report of the week on Friday, the New England Patriots had six cornerbacks on their active roster. Five of those were listed, including four who had been ruled out for the Week 5 game against the Las Vegas Raiders. But even though they were without starters Christian Gonzalez and […]
full_text: When they released their final injury report of the week on Friday, the New England Patriots had six cornerbacks on their active roster. Five of those were listed, including four who had been ruled out for the Week 5 game against the Las Vegas Raiders. But even though they were without starters Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis as well as backups Channing Canada and Karon Prunty, the Patriots were able to keep the Raiders’ pass game largely in check. The three remaining cornerbacks — Marcus Jones, Charles Woods and recently-promoted Kindle Vildor — had a lot to do with this, as did another backup, big nickel safety Jaylen Reed. “Next man up mentality,” linebacker and defensive captain Robert Spillane called it after the Patriots’ 45-17 win . “Oftentimes in this league you’re an opportunity away from showing people that you deserve to be on the field. There are so many guys that stepped up huge for us, especially on the defensive side of the ball today.” Whereas Jones is a regular part of the Patriots’ three-cornerback groupings alongside Gonzalez and Davis, Woods and Vildor started the season as a fourth option and on the practice squad, respectively. On Sunday, however, they were asked to play prominent snaps against the seventh highest-scoring team in the NFL entering Week 5. The results were not perfect — Jones shadowing tight end Brock Bowers early was a mismatch the Raiders were happy to exploit — but the damage overall was kept in check. And not just that. Woods had a pair of pass breakups and a tackle for loss, while Vildor broke up a third-down pass intended for Bowers and later forced a fumble against the tight end. They also were able of holding their own in 1-on-1 situations when the Patriots ran blitz calls up front. “They showed up huge,” said Spillane. “When you blitz those corners are out there solo dolo a lot of the times, and they really stood up not only making the plays but helping us get off the field on numerous occasions, or getting the ball out, turnovers. Just really proud of all of those guys. At the end of the day, we knew they were going to step up. They prepared to be starters their whole careers.” “We try not to panic. We just try to get the next guy ready,” said head coach Mike Vrabel. “We ask everybody to be ready to prepare as a starter. It’s a credit to the football players. The guys on this team and the guys we’ve tried to bring in here, and they realize that when you get an opportunity and you do something with it, you’ll get more opportunities.” What Woods’ and Vildor’s opportunities in particular will look like once Gonzalez and Davis are back in action remains to be seen. At the very least, they have proven that they can be trusted. Not that that was any surprise. “We trust each other as a team. We trust whoever’s on the field to do their job,” said Spillane. “They’re one eleventh. We had a bunch of guys step up and really provide huge plays for us. Kindle getting that ball out on the turnover, solidifying that game — I just thought overall so many guys stepped in today and really did a good job for us.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Instant analysis from Patriots’ win over Raiders
summary: As members of the Super Bowl XXXVI team returned to Gillette Stadium, so did victory formation. The New England Patriots threw and ran through the Las Vegas Raiders for 536 total yards of offense and a 45-17 win on Sunday. Here’s a glance back on the 1 p.m. ET kickoff as head coach Mike Vrabel’s […]
full_text: As members of the Super Bowl XXXVI team returned to Gillette Stadium, so did victory formation. The New England Patriots threw and ran through the Las Vegas Raiders for 536 total yards of offense and a 45-17 win on Sunday. Here’s a glance back on the 1 p.m. ET kickoff as head coach Mike Vrabel’s side moves forward at 3-2. A repeat for AFC Offensive Player of the Week The reigning AFC Offensive Player of the Week put September’s turnovers further in the rearview. Drake Maye completed 26-of-34 passes for 374 yards in Sunday’s red throwbacks. The 24-year-old Patriots quarterback found four touchdowns through the air and a fifth on the ground after setting a season best in rushing last week. Taking the field in “12” personnel, New England’s opening drive stretched five plays, 55 yards and a penalty for defensive pass interference on the way to a 7-0 scoring strike to the end zone. The second series brought a pair of fourth-and-3 shotgun connections on the way to a 14-7 lead. Punter Mitch Wishnowsky was not called upon until the Patriots’ third drive stalled on the Raiders’ side of the field. Even so, a scamper of 26 yards by tenured tight end Hunter Henry helped make sure that wouldn’t reoccur by halftime. And as one Patriots captain looked back to another on the subsequent snap, an 11-yard touchdown was the result for a 21-7 advantage. Maye stood 11-of-15 passing for 160 yards with two touchdowns and a passer rating of 147.2 by intermission at Gillette Stadium. He managed to finish with a passer rating of 150.9. A certain former UNLV and Washington State speedster was hit down the left sideline coming out of the break for a 34-yard score on second-and-19. The QB kept the pedal down, delivering a pinpoint pass to rookie tight end Eli Raridon on a motioning wheel route for 31 yards before calling his own number to extend the lead to 35-10. Kneel-downs were dialed up once things stood at 45-17. Averaging 8.1 yards per play, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels’ Patriots attack closed the matchup with 29 first downs, going 6-of-12 on third down, 2-of-2 on fourth down and 4-of-5 in the red zone. Wide receiver room of four reels in three touchdowns After Mack Hollins sustained a non-contact calf injury during last weekend’s 29-26 AFC East upset against the Buffalo Bills, the wide receiver room went without its eldest statesman. The 33-year-old stood atop the team in targets, receptions and receiving yards before being sent to injured reserve on the eve of the 1 p.m. ET kickoff. But DeMario Douglas wasn’t forgotten about. At least not by his quarterback. The 5-foot-8, 185-pound slot was found in the end zone for his first touchdown of the fall on the Patriots’ opening drive. And in wide-open fashion behind an umbrella of Raiders. He went on catch four passes for 65 yards and his second touchdown of the game. It was a collective effort for a wideout depth chart of four. March signing Romeo Doubs drew 24 yards and then 27 yards worth of defensive pass interference on consecutive series versus cornerback Eric Stokes. Also getting the starting nod was Efton Chism III. A week after reeling in the game-winning TD with his right glove, the 2025 undrafted free agent out of Eastern Washington kept playing above the rim to the tune of five catches for 57 yards as well as a freelancing lateral for a third-and-11 conversion. And then there was Kyle Williams, who got in on the fun with his first sprint to the end zone since December of his rookie campaign and then broke off a 49-yarder on a raindrop deep to the middle of the field. The No. 69 overall pick from last year’s NFL draft entered the game with 44 receiving yards on the season and closed it out with a team-leading 91. Brown stays in at right guard, but Campbell departs from blindside Nearly two years had passed since Ben Brown joined the Patriots’ 53-man roster off the practice squad of the Raiders. Getting his second call at right guard after Greg Van Roten landed on injured reserve along with incumbent Mike Onwenu, the backup interior lineman was penalized for one false start and one hold on Sunday while 35-year-old right tackle Morgan Moses also twice drew flags for the same infractions. The musical chairs didn’t end there for the starting five. Left tackle Will Campbell, who limped off the field in the second quarter after having his right knee rolled up, was downgraded to out in the midst of Sunday. Rookie No. 28 overall pick Caleb Lomu went from reporting as an eligible tight end to lining up on the blindside next to left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker and center Jared Wilson. But one sack was in the cards for Las Vegas. Defensive linemen Jonah Laulu and Malcolm Koonce split it. A “ max-effort guy ” in five-time Pro Bowler and two-time All-Pro Maxx Crosby got his hands on a pair of quarterback hits. Stevenson visits end zone, tallies 85 scrimmage yards for lean backfield Rhamondre Stevenson turned 13 carries into 64 rushing yards and a plunge from the goal line for his second touchdown in a week’s span. Despite being questionable after hobbling off on the final drive in Orchard Park, the starting running back’s outing in Foxborough included decisive, knifing gains of 12 and 20 yards on the ground. It also included 21 receiving yards out of the backfield. TreVeyon Henderson rotated in for some trickery to move the chains, yet an ankle injury left the Ohio State product going from questionable to out midway through Sunday. The backfield depth chart was rounded out by Corey Kiner, a trade pickup at the 53-man roster deadline, who lost a fumble on his first handoff and returned to record 59 scrimmage yards on seven touches. With fullback Reggie Gilliam moved to injured reserve with ankle and knee issues, the Patriots’ committee followed undrafted tight end Tanner Arkin on occasion. Down four corners, Cousins turns to Bowers as No. 1 wideout The 172nd start of Kirk Cousins’ NFL career was on deck. The Raiders quarterback completed 19-of-28 passes for 243 yards with one touchdown and no interceptions before it ended on the sideline. That was against a secondary missing All-Pro Christian Gonzalez due to a shoulder injury, fellow outside starter Carlton Davis III due to a neck injury, as well as rookies Karon Prunty and Channing Canada due to hamstring injuries. With that CVS receipt printed out, Marcus Jones and Charles Woods started in the absence of the four cornerbacks on Sunday. The latter, who had been questionable with a shoulder injury of his own, nearly picked off the first pass attempt of the afternoon and soon timed up a pass breakup on third down to go with a tackle for a loss of three yards. After beginning with a three-and-out, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak’s offense tied things up at 7-7 on the heels of six plays, four first downs and a subpar throw that became defensive pass interference. The next two drives gave way to punts before a missed field goal clanked off the left upright from 49 yards out and a fumble recovered by Las Vegas brought things to intermission. The Raiders took a 14-point deficit into halftime. By game’s end, the visitors stood with 5.4 yards per play while going 5-of-13 on third down, 0-of-2 on fourth down and 2-of-3 in the red zone. No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza stepped on in relief for his first NFL snaps under center. The Patriots were viewing Brock Bowers as the No. 1 wide receiver heading into the matchup. title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints loss to the Vikings
summary: The Good: Causing fumbles The only real moments of excitement in this game were two fumbles caused by the Saints in the red zone. Khristian Boyd punched the ball out of Aaron Jones’s hands and it was scooped up by Chase Young and returned 27 yards to set up an eventual touchdown drive. Later in […]
full_text: The Good: Causing fumbles The only real moments of excitement in this game were two fumbles caused by the Saints in the red zone. Khristian Boyd punched the ball out of Aaron Jones’s hands and it was scooped up by Chase Young and returned 27 yards to set up an eventual touchdown drive. Later in the third quarter Pete Werner and Martin Emerson Jr. caused receiver Myles Price to fumble which was returned 87 yards for a game tying touchdown by Jonas Sanker. The Saints would miss the extra point to leave the game tied, but these two forced fumbles and returns by the defense set up every point the Saints would score on Sunday. The Bad: Keeping the QB in the pocket Kyler Murray looked like his old self on Sunday, as the Saints allowed him to scramble around the field with impunity. Murray ran for multiple first downs, many of which on third down, and extended multiple plays leading to completions. Murray ran 10 times for just 51 yards, but it seemed like every time he ran it was impactful, either moving the chains or avoiding pressure and completing a pass. The Saints have struggled with this for a while, and did not make any adjustments during the game to mitigate the impact Murray was able to make with his legs. The Ugly: The offense The Saints offense gained just 142 yards against the Vikings. Minnesota does have the league’s top defense, but still we should have seen more. Tyler Shough had his worst game of the year, throwing for just 96 yards and 2 interceptions. The run game did nothing outside of a few good runs by Kendre Miller in the first quarter, and Chris Olave was held under 50 yards. The Saints offense did not have a play of longer than 20 yards, and every drive aside from the one scoring drive either finished in a 3 and out or a turnover/turnover on downs. The Vikings defense is great, but still it was an ugly game for the offense in a game that they could have won if they were able to put together just two more scoring drives.

title: Game Recap: Saints host Vikings in Week 5 matchup
summary: The New Orleans Saints were hoping to avoid falling to 0-3 at home when the Minnesota Vikings visited the Crescent City on Sunday. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter Minnesota received the opening kickoff, and Kyler Murray got the Vikings offense off to a quick start. He converted all 5 of his […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints calls a play at the line of scrimmage against the Minnesota Vikings during an NFL football game at Cesars Superdome on October 11, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints were hoping to avoid falling to 0-3 at home when the Minnesota Vikings visited the Crescent City on Sunday. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter Minnesota received the opening kickoff, and Kyler Murray got the Vikings offense off to a quick start. He converted all 5 of his throws on the opening drive, including a throw to Tai Felton for 23 yards. But a sack by Carl Granderson and an illegal formation penalty meant the visitors had to settle for a field goal. Will Reichard converted from 40 yards to establish a 3-0 lead. The Saints then went three-and-out, and the Vikings offense returned and continued to move the football. Murray converted a 3rd down near midfield with a 19-yard pass to Justin Jefferson. Aaron Jones proceeded to find some yards on the ground before he fumbled on a 3rd-and-short in the red zone. Chase Young recovered the ball for the black and gold. Shough found Chris Olave for 14 yards as the Saints offense found its first first down of the game. Second Quarter CJ Donaldson and Alvin Kamara split carries as the hosts drove down the field, and Shough converted a pair of fourth downs with short throws to Olave and Devaughn Vele. It was then Kendre Miller getting inside the red zone with a number of runs, before also running in a 2-yard touchdown for a 7-3 Saints lead. Both teams proceeded to go three-and-out twice, and the Vikings got the ball back with just under two minutes to go. Three completions for 41 yards by Murray helped Minnesota into field goal range before halftime, and Reichard converted again from 54 yards. Third Quarter Leading 7-6, the Saints received the second-half kickoff. But Jayden Price fumbled the ball on the return, and Minnesota took over with a short field. Murray took advantage, taking off for an 18-yard scramble shortly before throwing a 15-yard touchdown to Justin Jefferson to give the visitors a 13-7 lead. Shough returned and got the ensuing Saints drive off to a promising start, but he was then picked off at midfield by Byron Murphy. Minnesota looked poised to score with another short field position as Murray ran into the red zone with a 14-yard scramble. However, Myles Price fumbled after a catch, and Jonas Sanker returned it 87 yards to the house for the black and gold. Daniel Carlson missed the extra point wide left, so the score remained 13-13. The Vikings responded effectively, though. The opening plays of the ensuing series were a 32-yard connection from Murray to Jeshaun Jones and an 18-yard run from Aaron Jones. Fourth Quarter After more gains on the ground from Murray and Jones, the latter ran in an 8-yard touchdown to restore the Vikings’ lead at 20-13. New Orleans then went three-and-out at a bad time, and the visitors proceeded to find more success running the football as time ran off the clock. Colby Wooden did force the ball out from Jefferson after a catch, but Murray fell on it for the Vikings. Nonetheless, it helped hold Minnesota to a field goal attempt, which Reichard nailed again from 55 yards. Trailing 23-13, the Saints turned it over on downs near midfield. Minnesota then went three-and-out, but it wouldn’t matter. Shough was sacked on the opening play of the ensuing drive and threw another interception into the hands of Murphy two plays later. After Jones ran for their only required first down, Murray was able to kneel out the rest of the clock to secure the 23-13 Vikings victory. The Saints now hit the road for a Week 6 trip to New York to face the Giants on Sunday.

title: Jameis Winston is, and should be, the NY Giants quarterback
summary: Can we stop now with the breathless drum-banging for J.J. McCarthy to replace Jameis Winston as quarterback of the New York Giants sooner rather than later? The Giants unquestionably lose Sunday’s game against the Washington Commanders without Winston’s heroics — 254 yards passing and three touchdowns, two of those in the final eight minutes of […]
full_text: Jameis Winston | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Can we stop now with the breathless drum-banging for J.J. McCarthy to replace Jameis Winston as quarterback of the New York Giants sooner rather than later? The Giants unquestionably lose Sunday’s game against the Washington Commanders without Winston’s heroics — 254 yards passing and three touchdowns, two of those in the final eight minutes of regulation to erase a 14-point deficit, and the first 50+ pass game of his 12-year career without an interception. Albeit, the last fact comes with help from a questionable call. Winston, as he reminded reporters recently, is the Giants’ starting quarterback. With Jaxson Dart gone for the season, he deserves to be. The Giants, trailing 12-3 and with just 77 yards of total offense in the first half, changed things up after halftime. They went with more no-huddle, and put the game on Winston’s right arm. He went 26 of 38 after intermission and had the Giants in position to win the game twice in overtime. The Giants scored three touchdowns and a field goal on their four third- and fourth-quarter possessions. Had the Giants lost in the extra session on Sunday, that would not have been on Winston. Over the final 40 minutes of play, he did everything a quarterback can do to give his team a chance to win. In overtime, Dominic Zvada’s 46-yard missed field goal and Cam Skattebo’s untimely fumble denied the Giants a chance to get to 4-1. “I thought he [Winston] was amazing in the fourth quarter. I thought he was amazing in the second half,” said head coach John Harbaugh. “I thought his ability to come out and change like that. And I felt we changed our offense up, we tried some different things, and he really settled into the things we did offensively. And he was amazing. “First half, he wasn’t. He’d be the first to tell you that, but that’s on everybody. I tell the guys, nothing good is all the one person. We’re all responsible for all the good, and we’re all responsible for all the bad or the not good. And so, he’s right in the mix with everybody else that way. I called him up, broke the huddle, I said, what he showed out there was really remarkable.” Winston was matter-of-fact about the performance. “I think when your back is against the wall, you have to depend on your playmakers, and I think we did a good job of doing that, getting the guys the football, and mixing up on them, and kind of just threw them off schedule,“ Winston said. “We never give up, and our focus is to do whatever is required for us to win a football game. And I’m just grateful that the guys rose to the challenge, and we put on tape what we’re capable of doing if the game has to go the other way. However, we still have to, you know, focus on the things that we can control, and the things that we can control are us being our very best on every single play.” Winston is now 2-0-1 in three games replacing Dart. Even after Sunday, he was again asked about the skepticism in some quarters that he should be the starting quarterback. “I always focus on what my heart desires, and I say this over and over again, my desire is to be the New York Football Giants Super Bowl-winning quarterback. My desire is to be a great starting quarterback in the NFL. I dreamed of this, and this is who I am, and I know that I’m going to continue to get better and find ways to help this team win football games.” The Giants are an imperfect team. Their flaws are evident each time they play. You can easily argue that that they are a few twists and turns from being 1-4 instead of 3-1-1 and in first place in the there-for-the-taking NFC East. In some ways, Winston is the perfect quarterback for the Giants in this place and time. He is obviously imperfect. There is always an element of ‘which team is he going to throw it to?’ when Winston drops back to pass. Sometimes, his eyes look like saucers ready to pop out of his head. He looks awkward when he starts to move around the pocket. Especially with two hands wrapped around the ball, with the obvious intent of trying to protect it. His facemask somehow makes him look like he should be playing the 1960s. Yet, Winston, like these Giants just keeps playing and keeps slinging the rock, mistakes or no mistakes. “It’s faith. When you have unwavering faith, you’re not phased by the circumstances, conditions, and facts. That’s something that I am continuing to share with the guys, I say ‘let’s not get phased’,“ Winston said. “Russell Wilson used to always say this thing, and one of his good friends wrote a book called ‘Remain Neutral’. I think Russ did an incredible job that no matter the highs or the lows, he remained neutral. I was happy I was able to pick that up from him. Also understanding, biblically, one of my favorite verses, Philippians 4:13 says ‘I can do all things through Christ, through him who strengthens me’. Before that, Paul (an apostle) is in jail. He’s talking about being happy with a lot and being happy with a little. At the end of the day, he’s learned the secret to being content. That is: taking whatever you get, do what you can with what you have, where you have it, and making the most out of it.” Winston and the Giants have been doing that no matter the circumstances thus far. Maybe the time will come when Winston plays his way out of the starting quarterback job. Right now, though, he is the starting quarterback. And there is no reason for that to change. A few other quick ‘things I think’ The chatter that the Giants’ pass rush stinks needs to stop. The Giants defense had a 2.14 average time to pressure against the Commanders That is the fastest time to pressure for any team in a game this season and is in the 98th percentile since 2016, per @SumerSports — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) October 12, 2026 These two numbers, which I dropped into ‘ Kudos & Wet Willies ’, are insane. I have to trace them to the belief Harbaugh has instilled in this team that if they just keep going, they will have a chance. — Per the FOX broadcast, the Giants had lost 24 straight games when trailing at halftime. Well, at least now they have not lost 25 straight. — From ESPN Insights , comes this unbelievable nugget. Entering today, the Giants were 0-230 since 1970 when trailing by 14+ points in the final 8 minutes of regulation. They’re now 0-230-1. “The one thing that has become very evident is what is inside of our players. Their heart, their grit, their mental toughness, their ability to overcome adversity is A plus, plus, plus. And that showed up today, so I’m very proud of that. And I’m also very excited for the fact that we can improve so much. We improved throughout the game, we did a lot of really good things … So, proud of the guys though, for their fight. Would have wanted the outcome to be a win, and we’ll talk about that now, I’m sure. But there’s a lot to be proud of.” Until overtime on Sunday, the run-blocking was horrid. I can’t help but think that sometimes teams need running backs who can make players miss, and who make their blockers right. I’m not sure the Giants have that. It’s why they had interest in Kenneth Walker and Jeremiyah Love this offseason. If I’m Commanders owner Josh Harris, I would be seriously considering firing Dan Quinn this morning. You simply cannot botch the clock management at the end of the game, giving your quarterback conflicting — and wrong — guidance , as a veteran head coach and not find your job in jeopardy.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Giants-Commanders quotebook: What they’re saying about the final play
summary: Here is how both teams reacted to the crazy finish of the 27-27 tie Sunday between the New York Giants and Washington Commanders. Giants coach John Harbaugh on the end of the game … “Well the time ran out. That was what I saw, so that’s what happened. It wasn’t expected … ‘Was it a […]
full_text: Here is how both teams reacted to the crazy finish of the 27-27 tie Sunday between the New York Giants and Washington Commanders. Giants coach John Harbaugh on the end of the game … “Well the time ran out. That was what I saw, so that’s what happened. It wasn’t expected … ‘Was it a win?’ No. ‘Was it a loss?’ No. It was a tie. ‘How does that make you feel?’ I’m happy it wasn’t a loss and I’m sad it wasn’t a win. So that’s how I feel. It’s a tie. It’s a heck of a lot better than a loss, but it’s not as good as a win. So I know that just sounds so obvious, but that’s kind of how you feel. I mean, we’ve had a lot of these conversations over the years. We’ll take it. We’ll take it right now. We were down 14. Came back, and we got a tie, alright? … “I wanted to get off the field before they could take it away from us, I guess. I was surprised. I was surprised. I can’t say that I wasn’t. It was a pretty shocking end there.” Jameis Winston on the result … “I’m really just grateful that it was a tie. That’s the first time that I’ve been a part of. So, it’s just really good to know that we can just get so much better and just eliminate the negatives and build on the positives emotionally. And I’m just grateful that we found a way to persevere and make it a game … I was just thankful. Thank you, Lord. Thank you, Lord.“ Abdul Carter on the final play … “I’m just shocked, honestly. I seen the clock winding down, it was like two, three seconds left. I’m like, ‘all right, they gonna get a snap’. Then I seen they were still laying on the ground. I was like, ‘oh, game over.’ … I felt grateful, honestly. Just grateful.” Jevon Holland on the wild finish … “Man, it’s emotional. I mean, it’s like left and right, left and right, [and] kind of just trying to stay resilient. Like whatever happens, happens. Whatever happened in the game, happened, and you can’t control it anymore. How can we win the game? You know what I mean, finish the game? Coming out of the half, [and] overtime, we’re going to just do everything to win the game. Then even the swing at the end, [New York Giants RB Cam] Skat [Skattebo] fumbled. We’re like, ‘we’ve got to go back out.’ Some guys on the sideline were going to take their gloves off. It was crazy. And then for it to run out, I mean, even when the clock ran to zero, there was a second where I was like, ‘is it going to go to the second overtime?’ I don’t know if it was two overtimes or not. I’ve never been in an overtime tie like this. Yeah, that was crazy. They were just like, ‘game’s over,’ and I was like, ‘oh, sure.’” Cam Skattebo on his fumble … I” fumbled the ball. We can’t have that. I understand that. I’m going to go into the film room and get it fixed. I felt like I had good protection on it. The kid made a hell of a play. I think in that situation what I think I could do differently is try not to get the extra yards because we’re already in a good position and continue to take care of the ball. If I get tackled for a loss at one yard, then I get tackled for a loss at one yard. I’m the player that tries to fight for as many yards as possible for this team. It kind of bit me in the ass there. I got to make sure I protect the ball for this football team. We win that game if I do.” Skattebo on the game ending in a tie … “It was a sigh of relief. I probably won’t get reamed as much, but I’m still going to get reamed. At the end of the day, like I said, my number was called. I gave the ball up. If that happens again this year, I promise you it won’t happen.” Washington coach Dan Quinn on the ending … “Leaving tonight, with a tie feels like a loss. And the last sequence, we throw it out of bounds, we clock it, you give yourself a chance to kick it. And we pride ourselves on those moments at the end of the game. And after the first down run, still trying to gain more for the kick. The right call is honestly like we can go clock it early and don’t put ourselves in that spot and that is my responsibility. Nobody else’s. I’m gutted for our team.“ Quinn on Jayden Daniels’ responsibility on the final play … “The sequencing of that does not fall on him. It’s an outside throw or a clock. You know, those are the two, out of bounds throw or a clock. And that has to come from me. I don’t even have to put him into that spot. I can do that earlier and we can finish the kick early. We don’t need to gain more yards, so that’s on me. Yeah, I’m saying we don’t need to gain anymore. We were just trying to gain more and we don’t need to. Like it’s easy enough to say, ‘Hey man, let’s clock it right here. We’re early enough and go get it.’” Jayden Daniels on the end of the game … “We just have to be better. We all have to be better. Situational football. Starts with me. Everybody will say the same thing, but we have to be better at situational football. “We have to stop the clock. We have to know the situation. We have to relay that as an offense. It starts with everyone, top down. Ultimately, it’s on me.” Washington wide receiver Terry McLaurin on the final play … “I’m not quite sure what the call was over the headset. I think in that situation we practice to try to maybe center the ball. But, I mean, obviously we didn’t have it executed or communicated right, as an offense, because that’s what happened. That just can’t happen. So, we got to take that, and that’s a bad lesson to learn. You got to be better at the NFL level. But, we just gotta move on.”

title: NY Giants news: A tie is, well, good enough
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! The Giants did not win Sunday. They didn’t lose to the Washington Commanders, either. Sunday’s hard-to-comprehend 27-27 tie leaves the Giants alone in first place in the NFC East, and leaves the Commanders searching for answers. NFC East standings Giants 3-1-1Philadelphia Eagles 2-3Dallas Cowboys 2-3Commanders 1-3-1 Commanders’ Daniels takes […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! The Giants did not win Sunday. They didn’t lose to the Washington Commanders, either. Sunday’s hard-to-comprehend 27-27 tie leaves the Giants alone in first place in the NFC East, and leaves the Commanders searching for answers. NFC East standings Giants 3-1-1 Philadelphia Eagles 2-3 Dallas Cowboys 2-3 Commanders 1-3-1 Commanders’ Daniels takes blame for botched final play in OT | ESPN The Washington Commanders were in position to attempt a game-winning overtime kick to beat the New York Giants. But all they ended up kicking was themselves after botching the final play in overtime preventing a potential field goal attempt. Quarterback Jayden Daniels was tackled for no gain with eight seconds left in overtime and, with no timeouts, the Commanders could not stop the clock. So rather than a potential Drew Stevens 42-yard field goal, they were left trying to explain what appeared to be inexplicable in a 27-27 tie with the New York Giants. “We have to stop the clock,” Daniels said. “We have to know the situation. We have to relay that as an offense. It starts with everyone, top down. Ultimately, it’s on me.” Giants Report Card: Offense, Defense Rally for 27-27 Tie With Commanders | Giants on SI Big Blue View isn’t the only site that does post-game grades. Who knew? Why the Giants’ 27-27 tie with the Commanders proved they’re finally different | SNY John Harbaugh summed it up perfectly, or at least he tried to, after the Giants traveled to Washington, played the Commanders in a monsoon, and tied. There were moments of dysfunctional, unsightly football. Excitement and euphoria. Super highs. Gut-wrenching lows. Culminating in a 27-27 final. “I’m happy it wasn’t a loss,” said the coach. “I’m sad it wasn’t a win.” The truth really is somewhere in the middle. For the Giants, though, it’s hard not to err more on the side of optimism. They are not Super Bowl contenders. They are not ready to run away with the wide-open NFC East. They have their flaws. But it’s very clear, through the first five weeks, they aren’t the team they’ve been the past few years. That’s truly all that matters. Heroes, zeros from Giants’ tie with Commanders: Jameis Winston powered comeback | NY Post Heroes and zeros? I still like the sound of ‘Kudos and Wet Willies’ better. Magic Johnson calls out Commanders for clock management debacle vs. Giants | The Big Lead After the game was over, Johnson did not mince words about the debacle that was the end of the Week 5 game. “I’m in total disbelief my Commanders had such poor clock management in today’s overtime game against the Giants,” Johnson said. “All we had to do was kick the field goal and we would have won the game!” Johnson even added the “face palm” emoji for good measure. From Big Blue View Giants-Commanders ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’: Plenty of credit, and blame, to go around 4 things we learned during the Giants’ 27-27 tie with the Commanders Commanders’ bungled clock management lets grateful Giants escape with tie Giants-Commanders instant grades: Washington gets ‘F’ for clock management Giants-Commanders, Week 5: Giants and Commanders finish in overtime tie BBV mailbag Have a Giants-related question? title: NY Giants vs. New Orleans Saints odds: Opening lines for Week 6 matchup
summary: The New York Giants will enter their Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints as 1.5-point underdogs despite being home at MetLife Stadium, per FanDuel. The Giants emerged from Week 5 with a 3-1-1 record and extended their lead in the NFC East after a 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders The Saints, meanwhile, […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo carries the ball against the New Orleans Saints | Getty Images The New York Giants will enter their Week 6 matchup against the New Orleans Saints as 1.5-point underdogs despite being home at MetLife Stadium, per FanDuel . The Giants emerged from Week 5 with a 3-1-1 record and extended their lead in the NFC East after a 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders The Saints, meanwhile, are 1-4 following a 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. The Saints won 26-14 when two teams met last year, with the Giants committing five turnovers. The Giants will enter their third-straight game as underdogs against a team with 1 (or fewer) wins, despite not having lost since their Week 2 disaster against the Los Angeles Rams. Of course, it’s difficult to say that any of the last three weeks have been “inspiring”. Rather than “Big Blue”, we should probably be calling this team “Code Blue” as they’ve waited until the last possible second to snatch a win away from the jaws of defeat in recent weeks. In Weeks 3 and 4 that meant Red Zone interceptions in the closing seconds, by Jevon Holland and Deonte Banks, respectively. As we all remember, Week 5 ended with the Giants’ defense slowing the Commanders’ offense enough that time expired in their disorganization. That does speak to the team’s resilience and there have been flashes of excellence on both offense and defense. The Giants have overcome deficits in each of the last two weeks and have shown a willingness to fight through the final whistle. However there has also been too little down-to-down consistency from the Giants on both sides of the ball. On the flip side, the Saints are last in the NFC South by both their point differential and 0-1 divisional record. Their offense has largely been more efficient and consistent than the Giants’ attack, but their defense has been much worse. It’s worth noting that Tyler Shough threw for just 96 yards, averaging just 3.8 yards per attempt with two interceptions and a sack against the Vikings hyper-aggressive blitzing defense. title: NY Giants will reportedly work out DE/OLB Yannick Ngakoue
summary: The New York Giants are bringing in veteran DE/OLB Yannick Ngakoue for a workout on Monday, per a report from Jordan Schultz. Ngakoue, 31, was originally drafted out of Maryland by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the third round (69th overall) of the 2016 NFL Draft. He’s a familiar face for Giants head coach John Harbaugh, […]
full_text: Ravens outside linebacker Yannick Ngakoue tackles Washington Commanders tight end Zach Ertz. | Getty Images The New York Giants are bringing in veteran DE/OLB Yannick Ngakoue for a workout on Monday, per a report from Jordan Schultz . Ngakoue, 31, was originally drafted out of Maryland by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the third round (69th overall) of the 2016 NFL Draft. He’s a familiar face for Giants head coach John Harbaugh, who coached him in two separate seasons with the Baltimore Ravens. Ngakoue was with the Ravens in both the 2020 and 2024 seasons. Ngakoue only had 1.5 sacks in 2024 — all of which came with the Ravens, and his full sack was of Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels — and was ultimately waived by both the Ravens and New England Patriots. Ngakoue suffered a season-ending broken ankle in 2023 that required surgery to repair. He sat out the 2025 season to fully recover from the injury, which he felt hampered his performance with the Ravens (and Patriots) in 2024. Harbaugh likely wants to check in to see Ngakoues’ status after a year off. The veteran is a versatile defender who is both familiar with, and could fit well, in Dennard Wilson’s defense. Ngakoue is listed at 6-foot-2, 245 pounds and has played both outside linebacker and defensive end over the course of his career. He could not only help fill the void left by the loss of Chauncey Golston, but also help keep the Giants’ outside linebacker rotation and spell both Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux. The Giants have resolved to explore every avenue to improve their roster, and Ngakoue’s 71.5 career sacks and 243 career tackles certainly warrant a look.
