title: 4 things we learned from the NY Giants’ 27-27 tie with the Commanders
summary: Ordinarily we would think of a New York Giants – Washington Commanders matchup as a contest for positioning in the top 10 of the next NFL Draft. This season, though, has looked different. After the Dallas Cowboys’ face plant against previously winless Tampa Bay, and with the Eagles’ core talent level increasingly suspect after retirements, […]
full_text: Isaiah Likely celebrates a touchdown on Sunday. | Getty Images Ordinarily we would think of a New York Giants – Washington Commanders matchup as a contest for positioning in the top 10 of the next NFL Draft. This season, though, has looked different. After the Dallas Cowboys’ face plant against previously winless Tampa Bay, and with the Eagles’ core talent level increasingly suspect after retirements, trades, and injuries to key players and three consecutive losses, Giants-Commanders suddenly looked like a game with possible NFC East title implications. On second thought, after watching these two teams play Alphonse and Gaston in overtime, maybe the NFL will decide to ban all NFC East teams from the playoffs. What did we learn from this unbelievable, ridiculous 27-27 tie? Do too many cooks spoil the play-calling broth? I’m not sure how the dynamic among offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, passing game coordinator Brian Callahan, and run game coordinator Greg Roman operates, but so far I am not crazy about the results on the field. The Giants seem more predictable than they were during the Daboll years. Lots of runs on first down, and I think on second down, too, not many out routes at intermediate depths, lots of running plays between the tackles and not much outside. We saw J.J. McCarthy enter the game briefly. Nothing wrong with that, but the guy is a quarterback. If you’re going to put him into the game, let him throw the ball instead of just running RPOs and handing the ball off. Brian Daboll and Mike Kafka did the same thing last year with Jaxson Dart in the first three games. What does this accomplish? If I can predict what they are going to do, won’t the opposing defense know, too? Finally, to me Jameis Winston is a much better quarterback operating from the shotgun than under center. I know there are advantages to runnning dropback, but Jameis is not a young guy you are developing. He’s a veteran who is obviously more comfortable and capable getting the ball and immediately scanning the defense. The offensive line is good at pass blocking, but lousy at run blocking I know John Harbaugh wants to grind it out and wear teams down with the run game. But message to Harbaugh: There are no Marshal Yandas, Ronnie Stanleys, or Tyler Linderbaums on the Giants’ offensive line, and there are no Derrick Henrys running the ball either. As a result, the Giants’ running backs are rarely getting to the second level before contact. The one running back they do have with any ability to make defenders miss, Tyrone Tracy, was sent to football Siberia after his fumble in Game 1. At least they gave him the ball three times Sunday and passed to him three times as well. Meanwhile Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris have gotten the bulk of the play. Harris fumbled last week and is a 3-yards-cloud-of-dust guy, and Skattebo had his fourth – yes, fourth – fumble of the season Sunday, and at the most inopportune time, costing the Giants a win (that they didn’t really deserve, anyway). It could be worse – your quarterback could let the clock run out in field goal range, for example – but it wasn’t good. I like Skattebo, but Tracy has to become a bigger part of the mix to give them a breakaway threat. Isaiah Likely is amazingly consistent and Malik Nabers is back The Giants have had a fairly prolific receiving game these first four weeks, but it mainly runs through two people. I have to admit that I didn’t see it coming with Isaiah Likely. He was a “nice” player for the Ravens. For the Giants, though, he has quickly become their go-to guy in the receiving game. Likely had 2 TDs today, giving him four for the season, and he’s now up to 33 receptions in five games. He averaged 36 per season with the Ravens. Of course, in Baltimore he was TE2 behind Mark Andrews, but you never know whether a player will be able to step up once he becomes TE1. Likely has been everything you could hope for. He only has one drop on the season (in the wind and rain of the Tennessee game) and he is clearly the go-to guy in this offense. Likely is on pace for 965 yards. Meanwhile, the real Malik Nabers seems to be back. He should be happy with his 18 targets today, and he corraled 11 of them for 121 yards and a TD, his second consecutive 100-yard game. His drop today was his first of the season, and he’s on track for 1,119 yards. He has yet to catch any deep balls, but hopefully with Jameis Winston at quarterback those will be forthcoming. Dennard Wilson should keep blitzing The blitz has this reputation of being a gimmicky type of approach to defense, a crutch to rely on when your defensive personnel can’t win straight up and an unsustainable long-term strategy for a winning team. Brian Flores, though, has been on a Make Blitzing Great Again campaign in Minnesota and is 5-0 to show for it. The Giants used blitzing to great effect last week against Arizona. I assumed they wouldn’t do the same today with the much more mobile Jayden Daniels at quarterback. My guess was that he would use Arvell Reese to spy on Daniels, but I didn’t notice that happening. Daniels hurt the Giants with his legs, to the tune of 103 yards and two TDs, but Wilson started to bring the blitz again anyway, on 25 of 37 Daniels dropbacks. Daniels was moderately successful when blitzed with 129 yards, but for only 13 of 20 and 6.5 yards per attempt, compared to 14.0 yards per attempt when not blitzed. Abdul Carter did have another good game today getting to the quarterback, with five pressures including a sack, and D.J. Reader and C.J. Okoye had really good games as well. But given the limitations of the secondary, and the talent of Dru Phillips, who rushed seven times and got five pressures including two sacks, this seems like it should become a staple of what the Giants do on defense.
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: 7 winners, 4 losers in NY Giants-Washington Commanders tie
summary: If I were writing this from a Washington Commanders’ angle, the brutal clock management by Washington at the end of Sunday’s overtime tie would receive a massive “Wet Willie.” I’m writing from a New York Giants angle, though, so maybe it should get “Kudos.” You decide. I’m flummoxed. As, I think is everyone else with […]
full_text: Malik Nabers (1) and Jameis Winston. | Getty Images If I were writing this from a Washington Commanders’ angle, the brutal clock management by Washington at the end of Sunday’s overtime tie would receive a massive “Wet Willie.” I’m writing from a New York Giants angle, though, so maybe it should get “Kudos.” You decide. I’m flummoxed. As, I think is everyone else with how Sunday’s 27-27 game ended up. Before we get to the ‘Kudos & Wet Willies,’ a couple of absolutely wild numbers. Per the FOX broadcast, the Giants had lost 24 straight games when trailing at halftime. Well, at least now they have not lost 25 straight. From ESPN Insights , comes this unbelievable nugget. Entering today, the Giants were 0-230 since 1970 when trailing by 14+ points in the final 8 minutes of regulation. They’re now 0-230-1. Now, here is your ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ review. Kudos to … Jameis Winston — After an uninspiring Week 2 game in his first start, even Winston was wondering if he could still throw the ball. Well, umm, he can. After a 7 of 16 first half that included a costly sack/fumble, Winston finished 33 of 54 for 326 yards, and three touchdowns. The Giants scored all four times they touched the ball in the second half (three touchdowns, a field goal) and would have scored both times they had the ball in overtime had Dominic Zvada not missed a field goal and Cam Skattebo not fumbled with the game seemingly in hand. After halftime, Winston was 26 of 38 for 54 yards. He made big throw after big throw, though it is fair to mention that the Giants did get bailed out by a ticky-tack defensive pass interference call that negated a third-quarter interception at the goal line by Washington’s Amik Robertson. Still, credit to Winston. Without a running game to speak of until a 19-yard run by Skattebo in overtime, the veteran quarterback carried the Giants’ offense with his arm and some veteran savvy. The Giants have emphasized ball security with the always-willing-to-take-a-risk Winston. Sunday, per NextGen Stats, this happened: Winston’s 54 pass attempts were the most in a game in his career in which he did not throw an interception. Winston had thrown at least one interception in each of his prior eight career games with 50-or-more pass attempts. Isaiah Likely — During the first couple of games after Jaxson Dart’s season-ending injury, the connection between Likely and Winston looked uncertain. Not Sunday. The talented tight end caught a career-high 11 passes on 13 targets for 94 yards and 2 touchdowns. The second touchdown, which pulled the Giants within 27-20 with 7:20 to play, came on a 17-yard pass where Likely barely got across the goal line before fumbling the ball. NextGen Stats had some details on how Likely did what he did on Sunday: Isaiah Likely ran 87.0% of his routes from the slot in Week 5, catching 9 of his 11 targets for 78 yards and 2 touchdowns when doing so. Likely now leads all tight ends with 195 receiving yards from the slot entering the afternoon slate. Likely also added an 11-yard reception from a tight alignment and a 5-yard reception from the backfield. Dru Phillips — Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson was dialing up the pressure, especially as things got dire late in the game. Phillips ended up with two sacks and a big impact on the passing game. From NextGen Stats: Andru Phillips rushed the passer seven times in Week 5, generating four pressures and two sacks. All four of Phillips’ pressures came in under 2.5 seconds. Entering today, Phillips had rushed the passer just 9 times this season, generating two pressures and no sacks. 2 sacks & then some for Dru 💥 pic.twitter.com/vlAqfQngxl — New York Giants (@Giants) October 11, 2026 Malik Nabers — The star wide receiver wanted the ball thrown his way more often, and on Sunday Winston and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy made sure that happened against the Commanders. Nabers was targeted an astounding 20 times. It wasn’t always perfect as Nabers missed a couple of opportunities, including a second-half deep ball that might have been a touchdown. Still, Nabers caught 11 passes for 121 yards. He made a nice grab across the middle for a game-tying 17-yard touchdown with 1:43 to play. He also had receptions of 16, 17, and 20 yards. This is back-to-back 100-yard receiving games for Nabers. Abdul Carter — Carter got a sack when he chased down Jayden Daniels from behind. He forced a fumble. Pro Football Focus credited Carter with four hurries. The second-year edge defender was impactful, as has become customary. Dennard Wilson — So much for the thinking that because of Jayden Daniels’ ability to make huge plays with his legs, which he showed with 38- and 26-yard touchdown scrambles, that blitzing was a bad idea. With the Giants trailing in the second half and needing to force things to happen, Wilson threw caution to the wind with Cover Zero blitzes again and again. How often? This often: The Giants blitzed on 62% of dropbacks vs the Commanders, their highest rate so far this season, per @NextGenStats . Jayden Daniels went 11/18 for 131 yards and a 38-yard scramble TD — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) October 11, 2026 Personally, I loved it. And, it helped the Giants stymie the Commanders’ offense late in the game. Wilson simply seemed to decide that if the Giants were going to go down, they would go down throwing the biggest haymakers they could. And it worked. Somewhere, Wink Martindale is smiling. And maybe cursing, or lifting a glass, in approval. Cam Little and the Jacksonville Jaguars — I just can’t help jabbing the Philadelphia Eagles a little bit after a 19-17 loss on a 57-yard Little field goal. A game the Eagles took a lead in with :08 to play, only to give up a long kickoff return that put Little in position to be a hero. Wet Willies to … Cam Skattebo — Ball security. Ball security. Ball security. John Harbaugh has emphasized it again and again. Sunday, Skattebo’s inability to protect the football at a key time cost the Giants a victory in a football game they had in their grasp. Skattebo fumbled with the Giants at the Commanders 24-yard line with a first down and the game in their hands. Until the ball fell out of Skattebo’s. This simply cannot happen: CHAOS IN OVERTIME Cam Skattebo fumbles, and Washington recovers! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/LeMXcD6EOI — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 11, 2026 That is four fumbles for Skattebo this season, the most of any running back in the league. That negated two big runs by Skattebo on that last Giants’ overtime drive, a 19-yarder on third-and-2, and a 9-yarder to put the ball in clear field goal range at the Washington 29-yard line. Washington’s clock mismanagement meant Skattebo’s fumble did not cause the the Giants to lose, but it certainly prevented them from winning. Tyler Nubin — Multiple coaching staffs (three defensive backs coaching groups) have tried to address Nubin’s propensity to take horrible angles against ballcarriers in the open field. None have succeeded. For the second time this season, Nubin took an awful angle on a run play that went for a touchdown, but should not have. This time it was a 33-yard run by Jacory Croskey-Merritt on Washington’s first drive. Nubin found himself on the bench in favor of Ar’Darius Washington before the end of the first half. Nubin did return to action in the second half, but his job is clearly in jeopardy. As it should be. The rushing “attack” — Head coach John Harbaugh said during the week that the Giants were “ just not good enough yet ” running the ball. They certainly did not get any better on Sunday. The Giants ran the ball 28 times for 103 yards, 3.7 yards per carry. That was helped massively to overtime runs of 19 and 9 yards by Skattebo. There was also a 15-yard Winston scramble in there. For the entirety of regulation, there was really no place for Skattebo, Najee Harris, Tyrone Tracy, or J.J. McCarthy to go. Some will point the finger at offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, and I understand…
author: Ed Valentine

title: Commanders’ bungled clock management lets grateful Giants escape with tie
summary: The New York Giants and Washington Commanders are both shaking their collective heads after a 27-27 tie in Week 5 at Northwest Stadium. In the final 30 seconds of overtime, the Commanders were in field goal range and had a chance to stop the clock and kick a field goal from a reasonable range to […]
full_text: Washington fans weren’t the only ones stunned at the end of the game with the Giants on Sunday. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants and Washington Commanders are both shaking their collective heads after a 27-27 tie in Week 5 at Northwest Stadium. In the final 30 seconds of overtime, the Commanders were in field goal range and had a chance to stop the clock and kick a field goal from a reasonable range to win the game. Washington’s poor clock management, however, led to the game ending in a tie as they never even got the field-goal unit on to the field as time expired. “Was it a win? No. Was it a loss? No, it was a tie. How does that make you feel? I’m happy it wasn’t a loss, and I’m sad it wasn’t a win. That’s how I feel,” Giants head coach John Harbaugh said postgame. “It’s a tie. It’s a heck of a lot better than a loss, but it’s not as good as a win. I know it sounds obvious, but that’s how you feel. We’ve had a lot of these conversations over the years, and we’ll take it. We’ll take it right now.” Giants running back Cam Skattebo, who fumbled on the team’s final offensive drive that could have led to a New York victory, was visibly relieved on the sidelines following the end of the game. He went into further detail during his post-game press conference. “Skattebo says I’ll take the tie and get out of town.” @The_ChrisMyers sums it up. pic.twitter.com/Al69bQjTks — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) October 11, 2026 “It was a sigh of relief. I probably won’t get reamed as much, but I’m still going to get reamed. At the end of the day, like I said, my number was called, and I gave the ball up. If that happens again this year, I promise you it won’t happen,” Skattebo said postgame. A tie is the same result for both teams, but it definitely stings a little more for the Commanders, who had a win in their grasp in the final moments and couldn’t bring it home. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn took full responsibility for the clock mismanagement. With the team, I thought this was a hard-fought game that went to the wire. Leaving tonight with a tie feels like a loss. “In the last sequence, we threw it out of bounds, and we clocked it. That gave us a chance to kick it, and we pride ourselves on those moments at the end of the game. After the first-down run, we were still trying to gain more for the kick. Honestly, the right call is to clock it early and not put ourselves in that spot. That’s my responsibility, not anybody else’s,” Quinn said. There probably isn’t anyone in the Commanders’ locker room who feels worse about the loss than Jayden Daniels himself. Daniels returned to the field after two weeks away with an elbow injury, but he ran for two touchdowns during the game and showcased some growth that hadn’t been seen in his sixth season as of yet. However, that growth will be overshadowed by his late-game antics. “We have to stop the clock,” Daniels said. “It starts with everybody from top to bottom, but ultimately, it’s on me.” Big Blue View community, what are your thoughts on the end of that game? Let us know in the comments section below.
author: Jeremy Brener

title: Giants-Commanders instant grades: Washington gets ‘F’ for clock management
summary: The New York Giants were frustrating in Week 5 against the Washington Commanders. They were inefficient on the ground, made terrible defensive lapses, and the Jameis Winston Experience kept raising questions about who should start at quarterback. Despite all of this, the Giants tied the game in the fourth quarter — the team doesn’t go […]
full_text: Jameis Winston and the Giants escaped with a tie on Sunday. | Getty Images The New York Giants were frustrating in Week 5 against the Washington Commanders. They were inefficient on the ground, made terrible defensive lapses, and the Jameis Winston Experience kept raising questions about who should start at quarterback. Despite all of this, the Giants tied the game in the fourth quarter — the team doesn’t go away! Jameis Winston and the Giants’ offense put together 150 yards in the fourth quarter to tie the game with 1:43 left. Some may point to the Giants benefiting from officiating, specifically on the negated Amik Robertson interception, but Washington also committed terrible penalties throughout the game that put their offense into disadvantageous situations — they were playing sloppy football. New York had the football in field goal range to win the game in overtime, but Cam Skattebo fumbled the football. And then — AND THEN — Washington, without a timeout, ran a play and time expired, giving the Giants a 27-27 divisional tie against the Washington Commanders. “Skattebo says I’ll take the tie and get out of town.” @The_ChrisMyers sums it up. pic.twitter.com/Al69bQjTks — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) October 11, 2026 Quarterback I entered halftime thinking: is it J.J. McCarthy time? The Giants offense had 77 yards in the first half. It was lifeless, couldn’t run the football, and the Jameis Winston experience was not enjoyable…up until the fourth quarter. Jameis Winston led three consecutive touchdown drives to send the game into overtime. It was, once again, the Jameis Winston Experience. Winston finished 33 of 54 for 326 yards and three touchdowns. The Giants used a J.J. McCarthy package to leverage his athleticism, but it didn’t work. Some plays had elements where McCarthy would enter the mesh point, but Washington was all over the package. Although the offense looked inept for much of the game, it finished with 408 yards of total offense and would have scored more than 30 points if it weren’t for a rookie kicker and a costly Skattebo fumble. Grade: B- Running back At times, I asked, “Where is Cam Skattebo?” The Giants used a heavy running back rotation. Tyrone Tracy Jr. operated as the third-down back, and he received several opportunities throughout the game. Najee Harris started the second Giants’ drive and was involved. Harris finished with five carries for 9 yards with a 7-yard long — there was little to no rushing room. Tyrone Tracy Jr. had three carries for 6 yards and he caught two passes for 25 yards. Skattebo effectively ran in overtime as the pendulum of this game kept swinging. That was until Skattebo fumbled in field-goal range, giving Washington the ball with 1:55 left in overtime. Skattebo finished with 13 carries for 59 yards and one MASSIVE fumble. Grade: D Wide receiver Malik Nabers had two opportunities at the end of the first half to make a play; both were difficult catches to secure, but Nabers failed to secure them. The second – a nine-route in one-on-one action near the goal line – was more difficult but would have given the Giants a much-needed spark. Nabers was critical to the Giants’ comeback, catching 12 of 21 targets for 120 yards with the game-tying touchdown. Darnell Mooney only secured seven of 14 targets for 14 yards with a bad third-down drop. Malachi Fields secured both of his targets for 20 yards. The Giants have a concentrated target share within the receiver room, but Nabers is the engine. Grade: A – Tight end Isaiah Likely is such a reliable weapon for this Giants’ offense; so many of the plays are scripted for Likely. Theo Johnson made an impressive adjustment on a seam pass, but a bad route almost led to an overtime interception by Jameis Winston. Likely hobbled off the field at the end after catching 11 of 13 passes for 94 yards and two touchdowns. Let’s hope he’s okay. Grade: A Offensive line The Giants are not getting push at the point of attack. Their running game has been flat-out bad and inefficient for most of the season. Winston was sacked twice but wasn’t under constant pressure. Overall, the pass blocking was adequate. The offense had pockets and time to throw throughout the game. But the inefficient rushing attack is a problem, though the crack-toss on third down in overtime was an elite play, going 19 yards to Skattebo, as well as a few other holes that were opened up and assisted by quality play calling by Matt Nagy in overtime. Grade: B Defensive line The Giants defense tightened up after a terrible start. D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris continue to perform well on the line of scrimmage: STOPS, balls batted out of the air, sound gap responsibility – they’ve exceeded their expectations through five weeks. C.J. Okoye was removed off the line of scrimmage on Washington’s opening touchdown, which led to a much wider hole for Carter to constrict and the linebackers to fit. Jihad Ward saw snaps and will be worked into the rotation now that Chauncey Golston is injured. Grade: B- Edge Abdul Carter made an impact early. He sacked Jayden Daniels on a second-and-9 play that resulted in a punt on Washington’s second drive. Carter then forced a fumble in overtime, but the Giants could not recover, although it forced Washington to punt. The game featured few pure drop-back-and-pass situations. The edge defenders also weren’t making many plays against the run. We haven’t heard Kayvon Thibodeaux’s name much this season. Grade: B+ Linebacker The entire defense was locked up on Jacory Croskey-Merritt’s 33-yard touchdown run. However, the defense hunkered down and began to bottle up the rushing attack. Dennard Wilson’s blitzes incorporated the linebackers and the defensive backs, and it did harass Daniels and slow down the offense. Jayden Daniels had 38- and 26-yard touchdown runs against man coverage that seemed to be without a spy. Edmunds and Reese both made impressive plays, but the run defense wasn’t consistent. Grade: B Cornerback Washington wasn’t slinging the ball around the yard in the wet conditions through much of the game. The cornerbacks weren’t challenged much other than quick slants that Greg Newsome II and Tae Banks struggled to defend. The tackling in overtime was less than desirable. Dru Phillips made an important third-and-10 sack in the first half and another in the fourth quarter. The coverage downfield seemed solid late in the game when Daniels struggled to find open options. Grade: B Safety Tyler Nubin was left in the dust by Croskey-Merrit on the second-year back’s 33-yard touchdown scamper. Nubin’s athletic deficiencies continue to plague him from depth, but he did have a valuable tackle near the line of scrimmage early in the fourth quarter. Unfortunately, however, Nubin left the game with an injury to his neck/head area. Jevon Holland missed a tackle in the alley that resulted in a 22-yard gain. The safeties were tested much through the air, but they both struggled to effectively fit the run. Holland was in the area against Antonio Williams under route that converted on third down. Overall, the Giants did not receive much from their safety position. Grade: C Special teams Dominic Zvada is human. He missed a 50-yard field goal to start the game and then sent a 57-yarder wide left at the end of the first half. Zvada also missed the overtime field goal, which is obviously not ideal. He did, however, hit his 51-yarder later in the first quarter and a 56-yarder to start the second half. Jordan Stout booted a 59-yard punt and continues to be an asset when his number is called. Jack Kelly JUST missed blocking a punt deep in Washington’s territory. Charlie Jones had 52 yards on four punt returns and 130 yards on five kickoff returns; Jones gives the Giants some burst and excitement at returner. Grade: C

title: Jets vs. Browns: Winning Ugly
summary: Sometimes in the NFL it’s really about surviving. There are weeks where your team desperately needs a win. It doesn’t matter how you get that win. You just have to get it, someway, somehow. The Jets faced one of those moments in Week 5 against the Cleveland Browns. A loss would have sent the team […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; New York Jets defensive end David Bailey (31) sacks Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson (4) during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Robert Deutsch-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Sometimes in the NFL it’s really about surviving. There are weeks where your team desperately needs a win. It doesn’t matter how you get that win. You just have to get it, someway, somehow. The Jets faced one of those moments in Week 5 against the Cleveland Browns. A loss would have sent the team to a 1-4 record. The season would be spiraling out of control. The discussion would start to turn to the 2027 NFL Draft and coaching candidates for next season as both the team’s and Aaron Glenn’s respective fates would seem sealed. Amazon’s Al Michaels was mocked on Thursday night for saying Dallas’ game against Tampa Bay wasn’t a “must win” but it was a “can’t lose.” Silly though it might sound, I viewed this game for the Jets as more of a “can’t lose” than a must win. I don’t know that this victory turns the 2026 season around. I hope it will. It might. It’s just more that the team could not afford to lose to the Browns because of everything that would have brought. It wasn’t always pretty, but the Jets found a way to get the win that they so desperately needed. They might have committed 10 penalties. They might have thrown for only 120 yards after their first possession. The winning score might have been set up by a colossal Cleveland special teams miscue. But when the clock hit 0:00 in the fourth quarter, the scoreboard showed the Jets with more points than the Browns. Of course that isn’t to say this was a poor performance across the board for New York. The defense had a stellar day a week after an embarrassing effort in Chicago. Everything was better for the team on that side of the ball. The standout performance came from rookie David Bailey who had a breakout game with 3 sacks, a quarterback hit, and 7 to 8 pressures depending on what tracking website you want to use. Bailey was a target of criticism all week in the media. It was difficult for me to understand why. Through the first four weeks, the Jets were not generating enough pressure as a defense, but Bailey was right at the top of most pressure stats among rookies. For whatever reason, Bailey took the blame over major free agent signing Joseph Ossai, who has done nothing, or fourth year player Will McDonald, whose feast or famine production is well-known, or a defensive tackle group that hasn’t shown an ability to collapse the pocket. The number two pick in the Draft has high expectations, but listening to the New York media, you would have thought it was a catastrophe that Bailey wasn’t Lawrence Taylor within his first four games. Even more puzzling was the implication that the Jets made a massive blunder passing on Bailey for Arvell Reese. Reese, of course was an outstanding prospect, who is likely to be an excellent player for the crosstown Giants. But his success is coming in a role where he is not primarily rushing the passer. If the problem was a lack of a pass rush from a first round pick, it’s difficult to understand how Reese, who just had his first sack yesterday in Week 5, was going to fix that. In any event, Bailey quieted his critics against Cleveland. Many of those critics will undoubtedly declare Bailey a superstar off this performance. Once again, this will be premature. Bailey is a talented prospect who is producing. His game, particularly his pass rush moves, still needs refinement. He’s right on the trajectory where you want a highly drafted rookie to be. He’s doing things well with room to grow. That’s how he should have been viewed before the game. It’s how he should be viewed now. Another star of this game for the Jets was Braelon Allen. Allen has been an afterthought for most of his three year career, essentially receiving his carries in short yardage situations and when Breece Hall needs a rest. The Jets might want to start reconsidering his usage. This isn’t about one big game for Allen, who ran for a career high 116 yards and a touchdown on 24 carries. It’s about the skills he brings to the table. Allen is a true North-South runner who falls forward and picks up positive yardage almost every time he runs. Hall is a homerun hitter but inconsistent in reading his blocks and prone to too much dancing behind the line of scrimmage. None of this is to say that Hall is a player the Jets should trade to make room for Allen. But Allen’s ability to keep the Jets offense on schedule is something valuable that merits a heavier workload. In many ways, Allen’s strengths are Hall’s weaknesses and vice versa. This has the makings of a very effective running back duo if the Jets can see clearly. All in all there were many standout performers in this one. T’Vondre Sweat, Jamien Sherwood, and Darrell Jackson Jr. were among the other standouts for a Jets defense that shut the Browns down for most of the game and finished with 8 sacks. As mentioned earlier, the game wasn’t pretty. The Jets committed 10 penalties. The temptation will be to rebut this by noting how poor the officiating is. And to be clear, it was both poor and one-sided in Cleveland’s favor. However, aside from a shaky fourth quarter flag on Brandon Stephens, the blown calls in the Browns’ direction tended to be on plays where Cleveland committed clear penalties, and the officials refused to throw the flag. The calls against the Jets were largely correct, an indicator of sloppy play that must be cleaned up. The Jets’ passing game was also an issue for a second consecutive week. There is no easy answer as to what is not working when the Jets throw the ball. The poor conditions surely played a role. The offensive line struggled in pass protection, particularly Joe Tippmann, who had maybe his worst game as a pro. The receiving group reached a depth emergency level once Kenyon Sadiq left the game with a concussion. All of the injuries have left the Jets with nobody other than Garrett Wilson showing the ability to produce a big play. And for a second straight week, Geno Smith showed an inability to function in the pocket. Smith can be forgiven for a lack of explosive passing plays given everything just mentioned, but a 14 year veteran needs to be able to navigate the pocket much better, find his outlets, keep the offense on schedule, and avoid taking bad sacks at a rate much better than we have seen from Geno the last two weeks. So there are clear things that need to be cleaned up. The Jets need to cut down on the penalties and get more from their passing game if they want to beat higher caliber opponents going forward. For this week, though, they got just enough to win. This was one of those weeks that was all about survival, and survive they did. Wins are precious things in the NFL. The Jets got one in Week 5, and that should be celebrated.

title: Jets vs Browns: Barrage of sacks, Braelon Allen’s career game lead the Jets to win over Browns
summary: In the New York Jets’ fifth game of the 2026 season, on a miserable rainy day at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, the Jets defeated the Cleveland Browns, 17 – 12. The game opened with the Jets on defense. They had a nice start to the game with a three and out, forcing […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 11: Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns is tackled by David Bailey #31 of the New York Jets during the first quarter of the game at MetLife Stadium on October 11, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the New York Jets’ fifth game of the 2026 season, on a miserable rainy day at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, the Jets defeated the Cleveland Browns, 17 – 12. The game opened with the Jets on defense. They had a nice start to the game with a three and out, forcing a Browns punt. The Jets took over on offense and Garrett Wilson got going early with three receptions on the Jets’ first possession. The third went for a touchdown and an early 7 – 0 Jets lead. The Browns came right back, putting together a long drive helped by two Minkah Fitzpatrick 15 yard unnecessary roughness penalties. The Jets finally stopped the drive inside the 10 yard line. The Browns settled for a short field goal and the Jets led 7 – 3 late in the first quarter. The quarter ended with the Jets still holding a 7 – 3 lead with the Jets driving on their own 34 yard line. The Jets were forced to punt and the Browns put together a short drive ending in a field goal. The score was Jets 7, Browns 6 with a little more than 10 minutes left in the first half. After a Jets three and out Austin McNamara shanked a punt for just 33 yards, giving the Browns excellent field position at their own 37 yard line. David Bailey’s second sack of the game brought the Browns drive to a halt and the Jets took over on offense. They looked to put something together after getting stonewalled following their opening touchdown drive. Unfortunately the Jets again went nowhere. A Jets punt gave the Browns the ball at their own 10 yard line with a little more than a minute left in the half. A short Browns drive was thwarted well short of scoring position and the half ended with the Jets still leading the Browns, 7 – 6. The Jets opened the third quarter on offense. They advanced into Browns territory before they were forced to punt, continuing a scoreless streak for the Jets since the opening drive. An Austin McNamara punt pinned the Browns down inside their 10 yard line to start their first drive of the second half. The Jets defense forced a three and out, forcing a Browns punt out of their own end zone. The Jets took over in Browns territory within shouting distance of their first score since the opening drive. The Jets took the ball inside the Browns 10 yard line before Kenyon Sadiq lost a costly fumble and the Browns took over at their own 7 yard line. The Jets forced another Browns three and out, the Browns punted and the Jets took over at their own 37 yard line. A scoreless third quarter ended with the Jets still clinging to a 7 – 6 lead, driving inside Browns territory. The Jets didn’t go far, but it was just far enough. Jason Sanders drilled a 54 yard field goal to give the Jets their first points since the opening drive and a 10 – 6 lead early in the fourth quarter. On the ensuing Browns drive David Bailey sacked Deshaun Watson for his third sack of the game. The Jets forced a Browns punt and the Jets took over on offense at their own 31 yard line. After the Jets were forced to punt the Browns took over on their own 14 yard line. The Browns proceeded to put together a long drive culminating in a Deshaun Watson touchdown pass to Denzel Boston. The touchdown gave the Browns their first lead in the game with a little more than six minutes left in the fourth quarter. Isaiah Williams got a nice return on the ensuing kickoff and gave the Jets great field position at their own 45 yard line. A couple of Garrett Wilson catches gave the Jets the ball inside the Browns’ 40 yard line, looking for a game winning score. Alas, it was not to be. Geno Smith was sacked and lost the ball. The Browns recovered the fumble and they had the ball at their own 43 yard line, looking to run out the clock with a little over four minutes left. The Jets defense got a three and out, forcing another Browns punt. A high snap turned into a Browns fumble. The Jets ended up the ball already in field goal range at the Browns 23 yard line with a little less than four minutes left in the game. A couple of plays later Braelon Allen broke through the line of scrimmage and took it to the house, giving the Jets a five point lead at 22 – 17 with three minutes left. All the Jets defense needed to do was keep the Browns out of the end zone and the Jets would have the victory. A Jets three and out forced a Browns punt and gave the Jets the ball back just prior to the two minute warning. One Jets first down would seal the win. The Jets played it extremely conservatively, running three straight times, leading to a punt and one last chance for the Browns to win the game starting at their 20 yard line with 1:48 left. The Jets defense, once more into the breach, turned back the Browns offense, ending the game with a strip sack of Deshaun Watson. Final score: Jets 17 Browns 12. The victory brought the Jets’ record to 2-3. The Jets go on the road next week to take on a suddenly red hot New England Patriots team, looking to get to .500 for the year.

summary: I think it’s fair to say that Jets fans were feeling pretty good heading into the Week 4 game against the Chicago Bears. full_text: New York Jets Head Coach, Aaron Glenn, is shown during the second quarter, Sunday, October 5, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co I think it’s fair to say that Jets fans were feeling pretty good heading into the Week 4 game against the Chicago Bears. The team’s 1-2 record obscured what looked like legitimate progress through the first three weeks of the season. Each week we take a poll of Jets fans about their confidence in the team’s direction. Prior to the Chicago game 71 percent of fans who voted expressed confidence. It was easy to tell that the number would drop after an ugly loss to the Bears, but the effect is striking. Even by the standards of these polls, however, a 53 point swing in a single week is staggering. It’s clear Jets fans hold coaching responsible to a large extent. This week we asked fans what the team should do with Aaron Glenn. A vast majority said the second year head coach should be fired either now or after the season. There is one positive for Glenn and this team. If a bad week can lead to a large swing in a negative direction, a good week against Cleveland might have a similar impact in the other direction. title: New York Jets: A more disciplined defense is missing less tackles
summary: Missed tackles. They are a frustrating fact of life in the NFL. Every team misses multiple tackles per game, but some are worse offenders than others. The New York Jets have been egregious in this fundamental facet of the game for years. Different sites will give slightly different figures. Working with Pro Football Reference numbers, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 04: Dane Belton #6 of the New York Jets tackles Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Missed tackles. They are a frustrating fact of life in the NFL. Every team misses multiple tackles per game, but some are worse offenders than others. The New York Jets have been egregious in this fundamental facet of the game for years. Different sites will give slightly different figures. Working with Pro Football Reference numbers, the Jets have been among the NFL’s least efficient tackling teams. In the six years from 2020 through 2025 the Jets ranked in the top half of the NFL just once, and they ranked in the bottom six four times. Yikes! That’s not good. Here are the Jets rankings in the NFL in missed tackles since 2020: 2025 – 27th 2024 – 28th 2023 – 24th 2022 – 14th 2021 – 27th 2020 – 30th 2026 has been a different story thus far. The Jets have missed just 17 tackles in their first four games this season. That number makes them the NFL’s 10th best team in tackling. Bringing in sound tacklers appears to have been a Jets priority in the 2026 offseason, and it is paying dividends early this season. We have seen more wrapping up and less rolling into guys with the shoulder this season. It’s been great to see, but surprisingly it is a bit difficult to find much correlation in missed tackles to a team’s record. Three of the top six teams this season in missed tackles are the Arizona Cardinals, Tennessee Titans and Miami Dolphins. They have combined for a 1-11 record this season. In fact, of the top ten teams in 2026 for missed tackles, just two teams have a winning record. Going back to 2025, seven of the top 16 teams in missed tackles had losing records. It is a somewhat puzzling thing, but missed tackles don’t appear to be much of a factor in wins and losses. Nonetheless, if given a choice, a team would certainly prefer not to miss tackles. For the first time in a long while, the Jets have actually been good at this. If nothing else, it makes the defense more fun to watch. Perhaps it also is a leading indicator that the Jets are finally instilling a more disciplined approach on a team that has been badly in need of it for years. It may not amount to a big deal, but perhaps it’s a small silver lining in what has been a disappointing start to the Aaron Glenn era.

title: Jets make roster moves ahead of Browns game
summary: The New York Jets have waived receiver Jamaal Pritchett, activated receiver Tim Patrick and elevated linebacker Jaden Keller from the practice squad ahead of their game against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. If the 6’ 5”, 210 pound Patrick plays on Sunday he will add a large, physical presence to the depleted Jets receiver group. […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 14: Tim Patrick #17 of the New York Jets looks on prior to the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at MetLife Stadium on August 14, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets have waived receiver Jamaal Pritchett, activated receiver Tim Patrick and elevated linebacker Jaden Keller from the practice squad ahead of their game against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. If the 6’ 5”, 210 pound Patrick plays on Sunday he will add a large, physical presence to the depleted Jets receiver group. Last season Patrick racked up 15 receptions for 187 yards and three touchdowns playing for the Jacksonville Jaguars. For his career Patrick has 191 receptions for 2590 yards and 18 touchdowns. Patrick has not had a 400 yard season since 2021. He will turn 33 years old in a little over a month, and his best years are long behind him, but perhaps Patrick can turn back the clock a bit and contribute to a Jets receiver group that is in need of some assistance. Patrick will take the place of Jamaal Pritchett among Jets receivers. The 23 year old, 5’ 8”, 190 pound second year receiver out of South Alabama made his NFL debut last week after the Jets signed him off their practice squad. Pritchett played just three special teams snaps and returned one kickoff in his first taste of NFL action. As often happens with fringe back of the roster players, that taste of the NFL was short-lived. Pritchett was waived to make room for Patrick. Perhaps he will be re-signed to the practice squad in the coming days. Jaden Keller is a 23 year old, 6’ 3”, 235 pound linebacker out of Virginia Tech. He went undrafted in 2026 and the Jets signed him as an undrafted free agent before releasing him prior to the start of the regular season and adding him to the practice squad. Like Pritchett, Keller made his NFL debut last week when the Jets elevated him from the practice squad. Last week Keller played 14 special teams snaps against the Chicago Bears. During the preseason, Keller had 10 total tackles and a pass defended.

title: Jets vs Browns Pre-Game Ball
summary: Plenty of people hand out game balls after the game. That’s easy. Watch the game, see who does well, give them the game ball. We’re doing something a little different. We’re handing out a pre-game ball. Before we watch the game, let’s settle on a player or players we think might be a decisive advantage […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 20: Braelon Allen #0 of the New York Jets scores a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers during the second quarter of the game at MetLife Stadium on September 20, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images Plenty of people hand out game balls after the game. That’s easy. Watch the game, see who does well, give them the game ball. We’re doing something a little different. We’re handing out a pre-game ball. Before we watch the game, let’s settle on a player or players we think might be a decisive advantage for the Jets in the upcoming game. Occasionally we might hand out a pre-blame ball. If we think the Jets are going to get slaughtered, we’ll try to identify a prime culprit. One caveat: the quarterback is off limits. Nothing personal against quarterbacks, but they are obviously the most important players on the field. We could give out a pre-game or pre-blame ball to the quarterback virtually every week, but that would be boring, so we’re not going to do it. We’ll try to identify somebody besides the quarterback for the glory or the ignominy. This approach comes with the obvious drawback that predictions are difficult, especially about the future. We’re destined to get many of these wrong. No matter. We’ll have some laughs along the way. Let’s get to it. The Jets pre-game ball for the Jets game against the Cleveland Browns goes to (drum roll please) – Braelon Allen! The Jets are a bit of a mess on offense going into this game. They are missing starting running back Breece Hall, starting guard Dylan Parham and three receivers – Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper Jr and Arian Smith on offense. In addition, the weather is likely to be a mess, with the game expected to be played in a driving rain storm. All of this makes the Jets’ passing offense carrying the day a bit unlikely. Consequently the team may need the the running game to step up and carry the offense. Fortunately for the Jets the Browns have struggled defending against the run. They rank 24th in the NFL in yards allowed per rushing attempt at 4.6. In addition, the Browns have struggled to run the ball on offense, ranking 25th in the NFL with 3.7 yards per carry. Braelon Allen has never had more than 81 yards from scrimmage in any game in his NFL career. He has rarely been given the opportunity to carry the load for the Jets. Sunday seems like a great day to change that. Bad weather games were made for big bruising backs. In bad weather against a Browns team that struggles to defend against the run the Jets may see Allen as the best path to victory. If they can find some success in running the ball early the Jets will probably ride Allen as far as he can take them. Braelon Allen, come on down! Your breakout game awaits. You get your opportunity on Sunday. Let’s see you run with it. What about you? Who would you give the pre-game ball to? Let us know in the comments.

title: Eagles-Jaguars Takeaway: Nick Sirianni isn’t helping
summary: It’s a good thing there are more important things in life than the Philadelphia Eagles. If that wasn’t the case, Sunday’s stunning 19-17 loss in London to the Jacksonville Jaguars might have plunged you into a deep, dark depression. The Eagles had somehow overcome a myriad of injuries and, as seven-point underdogs, flown across the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on prior to the game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s a good thing there are more important things in life than the Philadelphia Eagles. If that wasn’t the case, Sunday’s stunning 19-17 loss in London to the Jacksonville Jaguars might have plunged you into a deep, dark depression. The Eagles had somehow overcome a myriad of injuries and, as seven-point underdogs, flown across the Atlantic Ocean and stunned a superior Jags team with a unclean-but-effective effort to move to 3-2 on the season. Until they hadn’t. The 2026 Eagles roster is not nearly as talented as preceding years, and it’s even less so with all their banged-up players. Now, more than ever, the coaching staff has to do everything in its power to put the players they have in the best positions to succeed. Nick Sirianni cannot be a reason the Eagles are losing games. On Sunday in London, he was. Sirianni admitted this publicly, and to the team, following their heartbreaker of a defeat. “I didn’t make the right decision, and I lost us that game. And that’s what I told the guys,” he said. After Jake Elliott drained a go-ahead field goal with eight seconds left in the game to put the Birds up 17-16, Sirianni and special teams coach Michael Clay decided to have Elliott place the ensuing kickoff inside the target zone for a return rather than through the end zone. A touchback would have put the ball at the 35-yard line, about 20-25 yards away from field goal range for Jacksonville’s outstanding long-range kicker, Cam Little. Sirianni was undoubtedly hoping his special teams unit (which had given up a touchdown on the opening kickoff of the game that was called back due to penalties) would tackle returner Ameer Abdullah while at the same time burning most of the remaining time off the clock. In 99 instances out of 100, that’s probably exactly what happens. But with many of the team’s special teams players forced into action on offense and defense due to injuries, that unit was more inexperienced and undermanned. As a result, Abdullah received the kickoff at the 5-yard line and ran it 53 yards into Eagles territory, setting up Little’s stunning 57-yarder with one second left. It probably goes too far to say Sirianni single-handedly lost that game for the Eagles. The offense’s second half struggles (no touchdowns and one field after halftime over the last three weeks) and injuries throughout the roster took their toll. But every fan watching this game was thinking the same thing prior to the kickoff: “Just kick it through the end zone. Just kick it through the end zone.” It’s always fascinating when the fanbase watching a sporting event is all screaming for one strategy while the coaches/managers on the field are thinking something entirely different. It’s also fascinating how often the fans are right, and the best football minds in the country get it so very wrong. Sirianni doesn’t call plays on offense. In fact, Sirianni’s offense doesn’t exist. There isn’t one. He has nothing to do with the defense. His entire job as CEO head coach is to be in charge of in-game decisions exactly like this one. And yet, Sirianni has not executed this part of his job well. Undoubtedly, he looked at recent events around the NFL in making the decision to kick it short of the end zone. On September 27 when the Cowboys lost the Ravens on a last second field goal, the Cowboys had just tied the game with a field goal with under 10 seconds left. Dallas kicked the ball into the end zone, giving the Ravens the ball at the 35-yard line. Lamar Jackson hit Zay Flowers with a 27-yard pass and called a timeout with one second remaining. Baltimore then kicked a shocking game-winning field goal, just as Jacksonville did on Sunday. But Baltimore had a timeout remaining. They could throw the ball in the middle of the field and stop the clock. The Jags were out of timeouts, and would have had to force a long completion outside the hash marks and get out of bounds to stop the clock. That’s an enormous difference that Sirianni and Clay should have factored into the equation. They also seemed to ignore the fact they almost gave up a kickoff return for a touchdown earlier in the game, and were undermanned in that unit. These were all thoughts fans were thinking in the moment. Why wasn’t Sirianni? Why wasn’t someone else? New kickoff rules are admittedly making late-game decisions more difficult for head coaches. Touchbacks used to be at the 30-yard line until last year, when they were moved up to the 35 in order to convince more coaches to encourage returns. And now, with kickers allowed access to special kicking balls before the games, we are seeing more field goals of 55+ yards being made throughout the league. It’s no longer necessary to get the ball to the opposing team’s 35-yard line for a realistic shot at a field goal. Most kickers can hit from 55+ with relative ease, and some can go from 60. The league is happy because endings like Sunday’s in London is exactly what the NFL wants. It was exciting, if you weren’t an Eagles fan. But this is the reason Nick Sirianni is still employed by the Eagles. He can’t run an offense. He can’t run a defense. He’s supposed to have mastery over in-game decisions like this. He’s supposed to know when to go for it on fourth down and when not to. And, no, he’s not going to get every decision correct, simply because he’s asking other grown men to execute his decisions for him. Sometimes, they’re going to fail, even if it is the right decision. No one thought this was the right decision. Not in real time and certainly not in hindsight. Sirianni didn’t let us in on his thought process after the game. It would be helpful for us to know why he did what he did, but he is not required to tell us. He owned the decision, and that’s that. The 2026 season is shaping up to be his most difficult and challenging yet, and there is little margin for error. There is not enough talent on this roster to paper over mistakes by the head coach, especially ones that every fan in the Delaware Valley could see as it unfolded in front of them. The Eagles need Nick Sirianni to be a force multiplier. They need him, as CEO, to give them an edge. Too often this season, he’s done the opposite. If he cannot improve in this most important part of his job, it’s going to be difficult to argue he should continue for much longer.

title: Eagles-Jaguars snap counts: Darius Cooper played the most of any wide receiver
summary: The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars are in. Let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE DEFENSE SPECIAL TEAMS DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Tanner McKee, John Ojukwu INACTIVE: Hollywood Brown, DeVonta Smith, Saquon Barkley, Marcus Epps, Jonathan Greenard, Lane Johnson, Drew Kendall
full_text: Philadelphia Eagles' Darius Cooper celebrates a touchdown during the NFL London Games match at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, London. Picture date: Sunday October 11, 2026. (Photo by Ben Whitley/PA Images via Getty Images) | PA Images via Getty Images The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars are in. Let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE Jordan Mailata is the only player on offense who’s played 100% of the Eagles’ offensive snaps this season. Lining up at center, Jake Majors logged his first career start in his first regular season game played. Lining up at left guard, Willie Lampkin made his first career start. Darius Cooper, WR1! In terms of snaps played, at least. But he also led the Eagles in receiving with 71 yards. And this despite only seeing three targets. Safe to say the Eagles should be more intentional about getting him involved. He’s a good player. Dontayvion Wicks ranked second among pass-catchers in snaps played, targets, and receiving yards. Makai Lemon set career highs in snaps played, targets, receptions, and receiving yards. Making some progress. Will Shipley started the game at running back but he left the game due to a foot injury. Dameon Pierce, previously RB4, filled in as RB1. Playing behind a less than stellar offensive line, his 11 carries resulted in just 14 yards. And his five (?!) targets resulted in two catches for negative two yards. That’s 13 total touches for 12 yards. Not great. Tyler Steen missed some snaps due to a shoulder injury but he was able to return to the game. Fred Johnson filled in at right guard during Steen’s absence. Dallas Goedert saw a smaller playing time workload than usual in his first game back from a knee injury. He did log a team-high eight targets, which produced six receptions for 38 yards. Johnny Mundt continues to be TE2. E.J. Jenkins was TE3 … ahead of Zach Ertz, who was TE4. Ertz saw two targets that resulted in zero catches. Ertz’s eight targets over the last three games had produced three receptions for 22 yards. Is he still getting adjusted to the game after coming off last year’s injury? Or might the 35-year-old be cooked at this point? Elijah Moore has yet to see a target this season and he doesn’t contribute on special teams. Wonder if he might be gone if/when DeVonta Smith and Hollywood Brown get healthy. Seems like they could probably get him back on the practice squad. DEFENSE Another game where the defense had to be on the field a lot because the offense simply can’t sustain drives. This unit logged 7o snaps in Week 1, 72 in Week 3, 84 in Week 4, and 72 once again in Week 5. They’re going to get worn out at this rate. By contrast, the Eagles’ defense only had to play 53 snaps in Week 2. The NFL lead in opponent plays per game last year was 65.5. Vic Fangio’s defense is seeing 70.2 so far. Zack Baun played his normal workload in his first game back from a concussion. Quinyon Mitchell appeared to be banged up after his interception but he did not miss any playing time. Baun revealed that Jihaad Campbell and Jeremiah Trotter Jr. were set to rotate at linebacker in this game. But that plan was obviously scrapped after Trot Jr. got ejected on the opening kickoff that didn’t even actually count due to penalties. Curious to see what this rotation looks like moving forward. Is it a 50/50 split? With Jalyx Hunt leaving the game with ankle/knee injuries that didn’t look so good, Nolan Smith was easily the Eagles’ top edge rusher. Kenny Moore II saw a decent amount of action due to Michael Carter II suffering an abdomen injury that prevented him from returning to the game. Moro Ojomo saw his second-lowest snap count percentage of the season. Arnold Ebiketie became the Eagles’ second edge rusher after Hunt left the game. He logged a team-high four pressures, according to Pro Football Focus charting. He also missed two tackles. Jordan Davis tied his second-highest snap count percentage of the season. He logged his first quarterback hit of the season in this game. It’s his first QB hit since Week 14 last year. Hunt got hurt on the final play of the second quarter. A.J. Epenesa saw some more snaps than usual with Jonathan Greenard out and Hunt getting hurt. Jonathan Jones was the extra defensive back in the Eagles’ dime packages. Ty Robinson has a tiny role on defense each week. SPECIAL TEAMS Carson Steele was limited to special teams duty in his Eagles regular season debut. Could’ve been nice to find him a touch or two after he had some success in the preseason. Especially since he showed more as a pass-catcher than Dameon Pierce, who inexplicably logged five targets. Rookie quarterback Cole Payton, who moved up to QB3 on the depth chart with the Eagles releasing Andy Dalton, made his NFL regular season debut by playing on special teams. He served as the punt protector. Britian Covey had a productive game with 136 total return yards on three kick returns and four punt returns. He was only 96 yards shy of tying the Eagles’ total yards on offense. The Eagles notably went with Fred Johnson instead of Micah Morris at guard when Steen got hurt. The coaching staff doesn’t appear to trust the rookie to play on offense just yet. As previously noted, Trot Jr. was ejected after the opening kickoff that didn’t even count due to penalties. DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Tanner McKee, John Ojukwu INACTIVE: Hollywood Brown, DeVonta Smith, Saquon Barkley, Marcus Epps, Jonathan Greenard, Lane Johnson, Drew Kendall McKee was reportedly promoted to QB2 last week. There’s no doubt that he’s Jalen Hurts’ backup now that Andy Dalton is gone (for now, at least). Ojukwu was temporarily elevated from the practice squad to give the Eagles an eighth offensive lineman but they didn’t need him to play. Brown, Smith, Barkley, Epps, Greenard, and Kendall all missed the game due to injury. At least some of these guys might be able to play in Week 6. Johnson was not announced among the Eagles’ inactives by the team … but he’s included in this game log. In case you missed it, the recently retired Johnson is reportedly set to remain on the Eagles’ roster for the rest of the season . While understandable due to financial implications, it’s not really ideal that the Eagles will now be working with a 52-man roster (instead of the normal 53) the rest of the way in 2026.

title: Eagles News: “It really hasn’t been a good year for Nick Sirianni”
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles need more from their head coach. He’s not providing answers on offense and the game management just hasn’t been good. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Roob’s Observations as Eagles suffer unimaginable London loss to […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on prior to the game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! The Eagles need more from their head coach. He’s not providing answers on offense and the game management just hasn’t been good. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Roob’s Observations as Eagles suffer unimaginable London loss to Jaguars – NBCSP One thing about Nick Sirianni. He’s accountable, and after the game he told his players that this loss was entirely on him because he didn’t have Jake Elliott kickoff into the end zone with eight seconds left. “I didn’t make the right decision,” Sirianni said. “Bad job by me. I lost this game for the team. I cost us this game. I put the loss fully on me. I should never have put them in that situation. I take full responsibility for that.” He’s entirely right, and it’s good that he said it but it really hasn’t been a good year for Sirianni. Whether it’s making the wrong calls on some key fourth downs or this decision at the end of the Jaguars game, he’s had a rough time with these basic decisions. When you’re a head coach that doesn’t call plays, you better get the other stuff right, and he just hasn’t. Nick Sirianni: “I lost us that game” – BGN The Eagles struggled throughout Sunday’s game against the Jaguars, but it was their end-of-game management that drew the most criticism. During his post-game press conference, head coach Nick Sirianni took full accountability for the decision-making that led to the loss, and also talked about the team’s continued second-half struggles. Eagles-Jaguars Postgame: Last-Second COLLAPSE Buries Eagles In London – PHLY Eagles Podcast The Eagles lost to the Jacksonville Jaguars in the most gutting way imaginable. Wasting a game-winning drive from Jalen Hurts and a clutch kick from Jake Elliott, the kickoff coverage unit set up a last-second field goal for the Jags that may not send the Eagles season into a spiral. EJ Smith is joined in-studio by Vinny Curry and Brandon Lee Gowton, a well as Anthony Gargano and Bo Wulf LIVE FROM LONDON to break down Jalen Hurts’ performance and everything else from the game. 3 reasons why the Jaguars beat the Eagles – Big Cat Country Let’s get one thing straight: the Jaguars should have lost this game. Not because Philadelphia were particularly impressive, but because Jacksonville seemed determined to sabotage themselves at every available opportunity. There are bad performances, there are frustrating performances, and then there is whatever the hell the Jaguars served up in North London. Thirteen penalties for 100 yards told only part of the story. Jacksonville’s offense repeatedly found ways to turn promising situations into disasters, with questionable playcalling and sloppy execution threatening to undo everything Trevor Lawrence and company had worked for. The most glaring example came in the fourth quarter, when the Jaguars had first-and-goal at the one-yard line. Three procedural penalties later, they had somehow turned a golden opportunity into a turnover on downs. Considering the way the first half ended in similar circumstances, it was enough to test the faith of even the most ardent fan. Handing out 10 awards from the Eagles-Jaguars game – PhillyVoice Ebiketie should have never had a chance to make that mistake. If Nick Sirianni had Elliott kick the ball through the back of the end zone, the Jaguars would have had the ball at their own 35-yard line, and they would have needed to complete a long-ish pass while also getting out of bounds, and do it in seven seconds or fewer since they were out of timeouts. That was the clear strategy. Instead, Sirianni opted to allow a return, despite the Eagles missing several core special teamers (Jeremiah Trotter, Michael Carter, etc.), and in a game in which the Jags had already returned a kickoff for a touchdown (that was called back because of a hold). Sirianni took blame for the loss after the game. “Our guys fought their butts off today,” Sirianni said. “The defense had an outstanding game, keeping us in that game. The offense did enough at the end to go win us that game. Special teams did a nice job of kicking it there. I didn’t make the right decision and I lost us that game, and that’s what I said to our guys. “What hurts there is that the guys fought so hard and then I don’t make the decision that I should make at the end of the game, and I cost us that game and I put that fully on me.” Sirianni doesn’t call plays, and it’s not fully his offense anymore. This is the kind of mistake that he cannot afford to make. Oh the Agony – Iggles Blitz Plenty of people are going to scream about firing Sirianni. I certainly get the frustration. That was an ugly finish. Others are simply ready to give up on the season. I get that as well. This team feels like a mess right now. I want to see how this team looks when somewhat healthy. Get Saquon, DeVonta and Drew Kendall back on offense. Get Jonathan Greenard back on defense. Let me see that group for a week or two. If they still stink, then the season is basically over. We saw enough good things on Sunday that I’m still holding out some hope. And remember the three teams that the Birds just played. Wulf: For Jalen Hurts, game management “not his place” as he fights make sure Philadelphia still is – PHLY Eagles “It’s not my place,” he repeated when asked about the end-of-game sequence again. “We’re prepared, I’m prepared as a quarterback to not worry about those things. I’m honoring the playcaller, honoring the things that are coming in the game. When I’m up at night, I might think about, ‘Should I have said something? Should I have took a step back and said, ‘Wait –’’ But ultimately, there’s a commitment to that in going out there and executing. This was one where it did not work in our favor.” Several players in the locker room insisted the nature of “the ultimate team game” means that Sirianni was not alone in blame for Sunday’s loss. The running backs combined for 20 rushing yards on 16 carries. Hurts and Wicks were unable to connect on an uncovered would-be touchdown. Drew Mukuba was left flailing on Parker Washington’s 51-yard touchdown. But all anyone will remember are the game’s final few plays. “That’s gotta be a question for coach,” Elliott said when asked about his final kickoff, later adding: “I always think you want to end the game with a kick there and not have to go out there and try to cover a kick, but that’s not how it played out unfortunately and go back and look at it and learn from it. It didn’t work this time. It sucks. You come all this way. You think you’re in the driver’s seat to win a big game and now we’re feeling pretty down.” Nick Sirianni’s anemic Eagles offense is a bigger problem than his game management – Inquirer But last season was a step back and this one is starting to look like further regression. And a lot of it points back to Sirianni’s inability to maintain continuity on offense. Hurts is part of that equation. General manager Howie Roseman is, as well. And when the Jimmys and Joes aren’t quite what they used to be, the X’s and O’s matter more, and the Eagles just don’t have the schematic answers right now. Sirianni, ultimately, is responsible, and that will decide his team’s fate more than a few game-management blunders. “That’s going to hurt for a while,” Sirianni said, “but I’m going put my chest out, and I’m going to stick my head up, and I’m going to get better from it.” And, doggone it, the Eagles like him. How long will that carry him through? Nick Sirianni took the blame in London. title: Nick Sirianni: “I lost us that game”
summary: The Eagles struggled throughout Sunday’s game against the Jaguars, but it was their end-of-game management that drew the most criticism. During his post-game press conference, head coach Nick Sirianni took full accountability for the decision-making that led to the loss, and also talked about the team’s continued second-half struggles. “It’s gonna hurt for a while. […]
full_text: The Eagles struggled throughout Sunday’s game against the Jaguars, but it was their end-of-game management that drew the most criticism. During his post-game press conference, head coach Nick Sirianni took full accountability for the decision-making that led to the loss, and also talked about the team’s continued second-half struggles. “It’s gonna hurt for a while. But I’m gonna put my chest out, stick my head up, and get better from it. I’m gonna own it, and move forward.” Here’s what else the head coach had to say: On the late-game decision making “I didn’t make the right decision, and I lost us that game. And that’s what I said to our guys. What hurts there is that the guys fought so hard, and then I don’t make the decision that I should make at the end of the game and I cost us the game. I put that fully on me.” He didn’t want to get too much into whether the kickoff decision was pre-established and doubled down saying that he is to blame for the bad decision, and that it’s going to stick with him for a long time. “I’m not going to go too much into that. I don’t really want to get into exactly what that is. At the end of the day I didn’t make the right decision, and it cost us the game. There’s no other way around it. There’s nothing really else to say about that. It’s just I didn’t do my job good enough in that situation.” The head coach also explained the plays leading up to Jake Elliott’s field goal, and how they would hope to kick with less time on the clock. “You would like to have it with 3 seconds left. You know, in that situation they used their timeouts. We ran the ball at the end. You’d love to pick up a first down there and be able to call a timeout and grandfather timeout, call it at about five seconds. They stopped us there, and we weren’t able to do that. In that situation, them holding onto their timeouts helped them to get that last play, but it should have never came down to that.“ Sirianni went on to explain that they didn’t want to do anything that might lose additional yards, because it was already a long field goal attempt for Jake Elliott. He noted that he does watch a lot of film from similar situations around the league, and also used their experience against Tennessee, when making that decision. On second-half struggles Sirianni said that they played halftime a little bit different this game, and it wasn’t quite good enough. “We’ve gotta figure out our second-half offense, because we’ve put together some nice first-half offense, and have a lot of opportunities to put games away, and we haven’t been able to do that.” He went on to say that they shouldn’t have been in a position for the last play call to matter, but they were, and it’s an area they need to improve or it will keep biting them the rest of the season. “I think you have a team that’s together. And, I think you have an extremely mentally tough, physically tough football team that fought and played their butts off. So, those are the positives. We’ll have to watch the tape, there will obviously be other things, but I just thought the guys fought like crazy and picked themselves up after last week’s tough loss.” Other notables Sirianni said he wished he was in a better mood post-game, but was really appreciative of the environment and to London for hosting the team. He also thanked the Eagles fans that traveled there, pointing out how loud it got and how much they affected the game. He said it’s important for him to take accountability with the team, and he has, because that’s how they build trust with one another. The head coach said that being accountable is one of their core values, and it’s something he is compelled to do.

(Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images After losing in London on Sunday, the Philadelphia Eagles must shift their focus to hosting the Carolina Panthers in Week 6. The Birds are 1.5-point home favorites, according to FanDuel . Home teams are normally listed as 2.5-point or three-point favorites in a game between two evenly matched teams. So, while the Eagles are favored in this matchup, it’s the Panthers who are drawing more respect. And understandably so. The Eagles have lost three straight. Their defense has played better over the past two weeks but their undermanned offense is abysmal. The Panthers, meanwhile, have a much more functional offense. Carolina’s defense is more middle of the pack. That unit ranks 16th in EPA per play and 12th in success rate. Heading into the Week 5 matchup, the Eagles had six […]
full_text: Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images | DeFodi Images via Getty Images The Eagles had another ugly loss this week , although this time the collapse happened across the ocean in London. The list of injuries heading into the international matchup against the Jaguars was already incredible, but the number of players sidelined during the game, was staggering. Heading into the Week 5 matchup, the Eagles had six players inactive due to injury : DeVonta Smith (hamstring) Saquon Barkley ( Week-to-week hamstring injury ) Hollywood Brown (ankle) Drew Kendall (knee) Marcus Epps (groin) Jonathan Greenard ( Day-to-day ankle injury ) These injuries don’t include the offensive line being without RT Lane Johnson , who retired earlier in the week , and C/G Cam Jurgens , who was traded to the Ravens . Not to mention RB Tank Bigsby was put on IR to recover from core muscle surgery . Things continued to spiral out of control in London, pretty early in the game. First, LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr. was ejected for a fight on the opening kickoff , and then injuries continued throughout the matchup, including: Will Shipley (foot) – was ruled out Jalyx Hunt (ankle/knee) – was ruled out Michael Carter III (abdomen) – was ruled out Jalyx Hunt was seen in a walking boot after the game, and despite being able to return, both RG Tyler Steen (shoulder) and CB Quinyon Mitchell (shoulder) had injury scares that sidelined them briefly. There are also a handful of players who have been on IR, with some uncertainty about when they’ll be back with the team: Landon Dickerson (knee) Eli Stowers (hamstring/quad) Grant Calcaterra (back) Jakorian Bennett (knee) Andre’ Sam (foot — ineligible to return this season) Johnny Wilson (knee — ineligible to return this season) Overall, the Eagles have huge depth issues at positions throughout the offense and defense, and things aren’t looking up.
