title: 49ers News: Victory Monday + Go Bills
summary: Fleet Week was this past weekend in San Francisco. When the Blue Angels really get rocking with their aerial tricks, it’s such an overwhelming combination of power and precision. They go so fast and turn so tight and everything feels both explosive and hyper-accurate.  That’s what it felt like watching Mike Evans play today. I’ve […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers makes a catch against Josh Jobe #29 of the Seattle Seahawks during the fourth quarter at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Olivia Vanni/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fleet Week was this past weekend in San Francisco. When the Blue Angels really get rocking with their aerial tricks, it’s such an overwhelming combination of power and precision. They go so fast and turn so tight and everything feels both explosive and hyper-accurate. That’s what it felt like watching Mike Evans play today. I’ve always known him as an amazing player, but to sit through the whole arc of the game and experience the highest stake moments was something else. The way he just physically dominates his match-up, grabbing the ball through dudes, reaching those Go-Gadget arms into the cosmos in a tightly-coordinated sequence…. he looks like a freaking fighter jet out there. Today revealed to us that the sky’s the limit for the 2026 49ers. This is it. They’re here. Their biggest opponent is the medical tent. Otherwise, I’m officially on board the full hype train. This team is a rocket ship. What a wild ride. 49ers’ Brock Purdy could have buckled vs. Seahawks. Instead, he found Mike Evans (paywall) “Purdy said he kept an eye out for situations in which Evans was matched with single coverage, and the Seahawks obliged on the biggest drive of the game. What’s more unusual is that the quarterback also looked Evans’ way when he was double-covered. Purdy admitted he’s had to readjust his programming with Evans on the roster. Usually, if a target is doubled, he automatically moves onto the next option. Evans, however, is so powerful and trustworthy when the ball is in the air that the quarterback has learned to fight his instincts and give him a chance.” Grading 49ers’ statement Week 5 win over Seahawks as Mike Evans stars in victory “The 49ers’ defensive line has been much better than expected, and a lot of that is because Morris has made the pieces fit with their nine-man rotation. Morris’ biggest influence has been with the play of the secondary. The 49ers’ corners and safeties are playing with extreme confidence because of how they are being coached up.” Kawakami: What’s different about the 2026 49ers? Mike Evans. It’s all Mike Evans (paywall) “It’s really cool to get new guys who come in and they just continue to up the standard that the Niners have built for so long,” Christian McCaffrey said. That’s a big statement from a player who rarely gushes about anything. But this might communicate even more: When McCaffrey walked to the podium immediately following Evans, he glanced at Evans, shook his head dramatically and said one sentence. “That guy is unbelievable.” Mike Evans is a difference maker generally; very specifically, he’s what the 49ers are all beginning to sense and enunciate: On Sunday and maybe for a lot more games, he was the difference between beating the Seahawks and not beating them. And the value of that in this division and this league is just about everything.” Mike Evans stars in 49ers’ win: ‘Exactly why he’s here’ “I’m on the sideline watching him do crazy stuff,” Warner said. “I’m like, we have Mike Evans. I can’t believe it. And he’s unreal. He really doesn’t say anything. He just shows up every week and just works and then goes out there on Sunday and just dominates you.” Evans was even on point when it came to his trash talk. In a moment that went viral during the game, Evans was seen going back and forth with Seahawks cornerback Trevon Diggs. After exchanging words, Evans turned Diggs’ shoulder to take a look and see who, exactly, he was talking to. “I was blocking him to the whistle and then he said something like, ‘I’m doing extra,’ or something like that,” Evans said. “And I didn’t know that was him at first because I played against him a few times and we always been cool. He was a good player. And I honestly didn’t know it was him because in the helmet, it’s hard to tell sometimes. And we were talking trash and I think I pushed him and then I was like, ‘Who are you?’ I looked to make sure, ‘Oh, it’s f—ing Diggs.” And then he mushed me. It should have been a penalty. But yeah, it is what it is.” 49ers win a thriller over the Seahawks to remain undefeated “Are you not entertained? This was the most San Francisco 49ers-Seattle Seahawks game you’ll see.”

title: 49ers beat the Seahawks on the road to be undefeated through five weeks and 3-0 in the NFC West; today was a good day
summary: I’m going to be taking something from the Fooch intellectual property by posting an oldie by a goodie: Get that rolling on your speakers. While we’re at it, I’ll keep at it with playing the hits and stealing from Fooch’s IP: The 49ers beat the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 in a type of game they most […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers catches a pass against the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’m going to be taking something from the Fooch intellectual property by posting an oldie by a goodie: Get that rolling on your speakers. While we’re at it, I’ll keep at it with playing the hits and stealing from Fooch’s IP: View Link The 49ers beat the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 in a type of game they most likely would have blown three, or even two, years ago. Actually, this is a game they may not have won last year. Was it pretty? No. But divisional games rarely are. Brock Purdy’s 19 for 29 (65 percent completion) isn’t exactly earth-shattering, and his first three sacks of the season came today. Say what you want about Brock Purdy, and I’m sure they will; he showed up when he needed to to win the game. That touchdown drive, in that stadium, was something else. Intentional grounding, offensive pass interference, and some bonehead play calls are not going to stop him from scoring a touchdown, and then the two-point conversion. And if you think his play might have hurt his MVP odds, FanDuel Sportsbook currently has him tied with Josh Allen with the best odds to win. So the 49ers are now 5-0 and return to Santa Clara to host the Washington Commanders. The Seahawks suffered their first loss to the Commanders, so the 49ers could help in a tiebreaker scenario by taking a win there. But we can look at the bigger picture here: The 49ers are 3-0 in the NFC West, taking victories from each of their opponents. They are set up perfectly for their divisional rematches. Overall, they have a two game lead over the Seahawks. Provided things don’t completely fall off, they are in a great position to take the division—and possibly the first seed. Oh, and there’s one more thing: They. Aren’t. HEALTHY. On offense, Mike Evans has that rib injury, Kyle Juszczyk is out, and it’s a bit until De’Zhaun Stribling returns. On defense, the 49ers were without Nick Bosa or Marques Sigle. If they can get those pieces back without suffering more injuries in the meantime (asking a lot, I know), this could be something special. Beyond the Brock Purdy discussion (which will probably dominate this week), how about that defense? Not only did they generate two (2) interceptions, but they also limited the Seahawks from doing explosive Seahawks things. And…uh…this play that might be a first down, actually: Two great teams. It came down to this. pic.twitter.com/RyJ1y4Nbnq — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 11, 2026 Maybe it was a first down, maybe it wasn’t. The explanation on the broadcast made sense. But if that’s a first down, then Brock Purdy didn’t have intentional grounding called on him, nor was there an offensive pass interference call; hey, even the Deebo Samuel fumble can be changed (he fumbled). Regardless of the officiating, the defense doing what it did Sunday without those pieces I mentioned means it can only get better. But it’s still a long season. Right now the 49ers are 5-0, and they have three divisional wins as well. Undefeated is nice, but undefeated with that divisional record is huge. Today was a good day. Even though three hours of it raised our blood pressure.
author: Patrick Holloway

title: 3 quick takeaways from the 49ers win over the Seahawks: Game of the Year candidate?
summary: In a thriller that went down to the final minute, the San Francisco 49ers outlasted the Seattle Seahawks 29-26 on the road to improve to 5-0 on the season. It wasn’t a pretty game on either side, as both teams combined for seven turnovers, while neither side topped 300 yards in a hard-nosed, physical game. […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers runs with the ball after a catch against the Denver Broncos in the fourth quarter at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images In a thriller that went down to the final minute, the San Francisco 49ers outlasted the Seattle Seahawks 29-26 on the road to improve to 5-0 on the season. It wasn’t a pretty game on either side, as both teams combined for seven turnovers, while neither side topped 300 yards in a hard-nosed, physical game. Ultimately, the 49ers had a great fourth quarter, as the team gritted out a gutsy victory over a division rival. With the win, the 49ers are now one of two 5-0 teams in the NFL and are also 3-0 in the division. Here are three quick takeaways from the win over the Seahawks on Sunday. Brock Purdy’s finish Just like last week, Sunday wasn’t Brock Purdy’s best game. He had a couple of turnover-worthy plays and a rough interception on a bad read and throw. Purdy finished the game with 189 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception on 19 of 29 passing attempts, while being sacked for the first three times this season. There were times Purdy just held on to the ball too long earlier in the game. But he continued to fight and finished out the game strong once again, leading the 49ers to another victory. It was the Brock Purdy to Mike Evans show, as the 49ers star receiver gutted out seven catches for 113 yards and a touchdown despite clearly dealing with an injury once again. On San Francisco’s 12-play, 74-yard touchdown drive to start the fourth quarter, Purdy was 7 of 8 for 89 yards, including a seven-yard touchdown pass to Brandin Cooks that gave the 49ers a 29-26 lead. In addition, he also found a way to extend the play on the two-point conversion, finding Mike Evans to give the 49ers the three-point lead. Then, with under seven minutes left, Purdy and the 49ers went eight plays and 43 yards for the go-ahead field goal. That fourth-quarter touchdown drive was an MVP-level drive, and it came at exactly the right moment for the 49ers. Purdy wasn’t close to perfect on Sunday. He had probably his toughest game of the season and made a few uncharacteristic decisions. But he delivered when his team needed him to, and the 49ers are 5-0. Points off turnovers It was a turnover-laden day for both teams, and the 49ers had their fair share with a Brock Purdy interception, Jacob Cowing punt muff, and a Deebo Samuel fumble. But San Francisco was also the beneficiary of four takeaways, and they were able to make the most of those opportunities, which directly led to the win. The 49ers had 21 points off turnovers in the first half alone. While they weren’t able to capitalize on Sam Darnold’s interception to start the second half, those three easy touchdowns off turnovers were a big factor on a day that offense was going to be hard to come by. Seattle also did well off turnovers with 17 points, but that difference between a field goal and a touchdown was a big one. Also of note, the 49ers scored touchdowns on all three of their red zone drives, while the Seahawks went just two of three. Those two slight advantages (21 to 17 on points off turnovers, 3 red zone touchdowns vs. 2) ended up being huge for the 49ers in a big battle. Mike Evans is him My biggest concern coming into the game was the 49ers receivers outside of Mike Evans. They struggled last week, which made things a bit more difficult for Brock Purdy in the passing game. Here, the 49ers were in a similar situation against an even better defense. Well, no receiver outside of Mike Evans had more than 25 receiving yards. Deebo Samuel, Jacob Cowing, and Brandin Cooks combined for four catches and 37 yards. But it didn’t matter because a beaten-up Mike Evans outplayed whoever Seattle threw at him, making several tough catches en route to 7 receptions for 113 yards and a touchdown on 10 targets. Still laboring from his rib injury, Evans came up often, especially in big moments, serving as the key target for Brock Purdy. We’re really starting to see Purdy grow with a true WR1 after the 49ers didn’t really have that guy in 2025. And Evans’s hands were incredible: he caught a ton of contested targets and was a factor in the red zone once again.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers win a thriller over the Seahawks to remain undefeated
summary: Are you not entertained? This was the most San Francisco 49ers-Seattle Seahawks game you’ll see. The 49ers started with a three-and-out. Punter Corliss Waitman pinned Seattle deep in their territory. Three plays later, Renardo Green stepped in front of a route to intercept Sam Darnold. Gifted with terrific field position, Brock Purdy found Mike Evans […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after a touchdown reception against the Seattle Seahawks during the first quarter at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Are you not entertained? This was the most San Francisco 49ers-Seattle Seahawks game you’ll see. The 49ers started with a three-and-out. Punter Corliss Waitman pinned Seattle deep in their territory. Three plays later, Renardo Green stepped in front of a route to intercept Sam Darnold. Gifted with terrific field position, Brock Purdy found Mike Evans on 3rd and 7 for 13 yards. Then threw a slant to Evans to give the 49ers an early 7-0 lead. After the defense got off the field again in three plays, Jacob Cowing muffed a punt, returning the gift to Seattle. The Seahawks converted a 3rd-and-5 to Cooper Kupp, who was defended by Deommodore Lenoir. Emmanuel Wilson punched it in to tie the game at seven. The teams would trade punts on the next three possessions. Late in the first quarter, Jaxon Smith-Njigba ran by Lenoir for a 38-yard gain. JSN made Malik Mustapha miss on a screen pass for 16 yards. Seattle wouldn’t gain another yard on the drive. Jason Myers’ 49-yard field goal made it 10-7 for Seattle. After the offense punted, Fred Warner used his patented peanut punch to jar the ball loose from Emmanuel Wilson. Malik Mustapha pounced on the ball, giving the 49ers possession on Seattle’s 11-yard line. Christian McCaffrey scored on the next play, and the Niners were up 14-10. The next drive would prove costly for the 49ers. Dre Greenlaw hit Sam Darnold out of bounds, then headbutted a Seahawks player to compound the mistake. Gracen Halton picked up his first career sack. Osa Odighizuwa had his first sack as a member of the Niners. The defense stood tall and held Seattle to a field goal, making it 14-13. The 49ers had an opportunity to score before the half. Brock Purdy found Mike Evans for a 23-yard gain. But on 3rd-and-12, Purdy was sacked, taking the team out of Eddy Pineiro’s range. Corliss Waitman’s punt was downed at the one. Waitman had been excellent up until this point. Trying to run out the clock, George Holani couldn’t hold onto the ball in the end zone. Halton made a miraculous forced fumble. He not only reached back but also had the awareness to find the ball. His fumble recovery and touchdown gave the Niners a 21-13 lead. Renardo Green undercut an Elijah Arroyo route to intercept his second pass of the day. That must have felt great for a player who was benched in the same stadium less than a year ago. Unfortuantely, the offense didn’t do anything with it. To make matters worse, Pineiro pulled the kick wide left. And just like that, Seattle had the ball as if nothing happened. The Seahawks picked up a couple of first downs, but Keion White’s tackle for loss helped stall the drive. Myers kicked a 43-yard field goal to make it 21-16. Purdy was a little off leading up to this play, but he made a poor read on 3rd and 7. He threw the ball late and behind Jacob Cowing, and the Seahawks cornerback took advantage for an interception. JSN made Warner and Mustapha miss in the open field on 3rd and three en route to a touchdown, giving Seattle a 23-21 lead. Deebo Samuel hurt his hamstring at the start of the next drive. As he went down, Samuel did not hold on to the ball. That gave Seattle another short field. To their credit, the defense did not falter. Myers kicked another field goal, this one from 48 yards out. That gave the Seahawks a 26-21 lead. Mike Evans caught a 15-yard pass on 1st and 20. Later in the drive, he caught a nine-yard pass on 2nd and 5, then picked up 23 yards on 3rd and 10. Then, on 2nd and 21, he caught a 28-yarder. Evans kept the 49ers’ offense on the field single-handedly. Brandin Cooks scored a touchdown, but Mike MacDonald called a timeout. After the timeout, Purdy scrambled and found Cooks in the end zone to make it 27-26. Evans was interfered with on the two-point conversion. The Niners had another shot and went right back to Evans. He caught this one, giving the 49ers a 29-26 lead. Purdy went 7-for-8 on the drive for 89 yards, with Evans doing most of the work. He bounced back after the turnover and didn’t shy away from being aggressive. Could the defense hold? They had all day, but they also needed to prevent Seattle from scoring with just under 11 minutes remaining. Rahshid Shaheed picked up 22 yards to put Seattle in field goal range. But Keion White had a stop and picked up the fifth sack of the day for the defense. Myers added another field goal to tie the game 29-29. Christian McCaffrey picked up 8 and 13 yards to begin the drive. He made a defender miss in the backfield to stay out of a negative play. Kaelon Black gained 11 yards on the next play. The 49ers were in field goal range with a little more than four minutes remaining. Kaelon Black lost a yard on 3rd and 1 after Byron Murphy blew the play up by beating Connor Colby. Pineiro’s 44-yard field goal attempt was good with two minutes to play, to give the Niners a 32-29 lead. It looked like Jordan James drew a holding penalty on the ensuing kickoff to back up Seattle on the 15-yard line. But Smit-Njigba picked up 35 yards on the first play from scrimmage to give Seattle the ball at midfield. On 3rd and 10, JSN beat Jack Jones, but inexplicably dropped the ball. The game came down to a 4th and 10. Cooper Kupp made Upton Stout miss, but was called out of bounds shy of the first-down marker. Ballgame. 49ers win-32-29. For the third time, the 49ers are 5-0. title: 3 keys to a 49ers win over the Seahawks: Is this the Brock Purdy revenge game?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are taking on the Seattle Seahawks on the road in Week 5, with the winner moving to first in the NFC West. San Francisco has started off the season strong, going 4-0 with several convincing wins. They’ve beaten two playoff contenders, while handling business against two struggling teams as well. Seattle, […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers runs for a first down in the third quarter against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are taking on the Seattle Seahawks on the road in Week 5, with the winner moving to first in the NFC West. San Francisco has started off the season strong, going 4-0 with several convincing wins. They’ve beaten two playoff contenders, while handling business against two struggling teams as well. Seattle, on the other hand, has started getting into form with Sam Darnold healthy, and they’re going to be the toughest challenge the 49ers have seen so far. Heading into the game, the 49ers are 3-point underdogs. How can they pull off the victory on the road? The third down battle I mentioned in the predictions piece earlier this week that this feels like a physical, rugged battle that could have a similar tune to last week. Both teams could play with a slower pace, and both teams will look to establish the run, and that makes extending drives that much more important. That battle becomes even more challenging when you see the stark differences between the two teams. The Seahawks are the third-best defense on third downs, allowing opponents to convert at only a 28.6 percent clip. Meanwhile, the 49ers are the clear leaders in the NFL in third-down conversion rate at above 57 percent, while averaging 0.45 EPA per play on third down, an elite rate and good for second in the NFL. If the 49ers can find a way to stay on the field, they’ve got a really good shot at controlling the pace and winning this game. Meanwhile, on the flip side, Seattle has been atrocious on third downs, converting at just a 31.1 percent rate. That provides a big opportunity as well for the 49ers, but it also depends on the next part… Who can run efficiently enough? Both of these teams will want to run the ball. San Francisco and Seattle both rank in the top 10 in rush rate, but there is a difference in how they run. The 49ers are ninth in rush EPA per play with their high-octane offense, while the Seahawks are all the way down at No. 26 under new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury. Now, the 49ers do drop to 14th in the first half, but the Niners are also eighth in success rate compared to 21st for the Seahawks. The trench battle will be pivotal. The 49ers will have to find a way to beat the Seahawks defensive line enough on the ground, but it’s the other side of the battle that could be the more difficult side. Seattle’s Emmanuel Wilson had a productive day running behind his offensive line last week. The Seahawks could try to operate similarly to try to move the ball on the ground, which can open up the play-action game. This 49ers defense has played well despite its banged-up personnel. But this will be a tough matchup on both sides for efficient running. Can either team break that open? Brock Purdy Brock Purdy has had some really good and really rough games against the Seahawks in his career. The game script is pointing to a ton coming on his shoulders. The receivers are banged up. Mike Evans and his busted-up ribs looked hurt last weekend. Kyle Juszczyk adds a personnel issue with his injury. And it’s the Seahawks defense that loves to tee up on opposing quarterbacks. Purdy is going to have to take care of the football. He hasn’t against the Seahawks in the past, but has done an exceptional job of playing clean football this season. There were times, Kyle Shanahan noted, that Purdy wasn’t patient enough last week in letting plays develop. He’ll need to really read the field clearly against Mike Macdonald’s crafty defense, and just needs to execute the offense on Sunday. If the 49ers win, though, Purdy is probably a big part of it.

Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Daily Slop – 12 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles ESPN NFL Week 5: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday’s games How devastating was this collapse? This was the worst collapse under coach Dan Quinn. The Commanders are now 1-3-1 and 0-2-1 in a bad NFC East. They could blame other losses on being short-handed or without their starting QB. But not Sunday. They held a two-touchdown lead in the fourth quarter, and quarterback Jayden Daniels showed his dynamic ability. But it all fell apart. Now, life could get awfully tough with their next games against the 49ers, Eagles and Rams. Washington badly needed a win, especially against an NFC East rival. Having Daniels back will always provide hope, but the defense again struggled to defend the pass. Trend to watch: Washington’s second-half defense continues to struggle. The Commanders allowed a combined 85 points in the past four games combined. That included 17 to the Giants on Sunday, wiping out a two-touchdown lead. The pass rush simply did not bother quarterback Jameis Winston enough, as he threw for 254 yards and two touchdowns after halftime. — John Keim Next game: at 49ers (Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET) To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Download the SB Nation app Commanders fans, take command of game day! Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Chat live during every game Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . ESPN Judging overreactions to NFL Week 5 This might be disrespectful to the 3-1-1 Giants, and I apologize if it is. But not having quarterback Jaxson Dart or star edge rusher Brian Burns for the rest of the season is going to be tough to overcome. Their schedule still includes trips to Houston, Philly, Seattle and Detroit, along with home games against the Jaguars and the 49ers. The Cowboys’ defense looks no better than it did last season. Dallas has December road games against the Seahawks and the Rams and home games against the Jaguars and the 49ers. The Eagles are without their top three running backs and are also missing four of their Week 1 starting offensive linemen, and their final four games of the season include a home contest versus Seattle and a game at San Francisco. The Commanders — well, after Sunday, I think we can just say we aren’t going to give them much of a shot. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Ringer The Winners and Losers of the NFL Week 5 It was the worst decision of Daniels’s young career, and what followed was one of the most embarrassing end-of-game sequences in recent NFL history. Daniels went to the ground with eight seconds left, then lounged on the grass for roughly five seconds , seemingly oblivious to the situation he had just created. His teammates scrambled to pull him upright and get the offense lined up for a spike, but by then, it was too late. The clock hit zero before the Commanders could take another snap, and the game ended in a 27-27 tie. A made field goal would have put Washington at 2-3, even with the flailing Eagles and Cowboys and one game behind the Giants. Daniels deserves the largest share of the blame for the final play. A starting quarterback has to know that he cannot go down in bounds there. But Quinn doesn’t get to separate himself from the embarrassment either. Quinn entered 2026 with his seat already warm, and this is the kind of failure that can erode whatever confidence remains in his leadership. Coaches can explain injuries and personnel deficiencies away, but an error of this magnitude is much harder to excuse. And it could end up being the point of no return. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Bad decisions come in threes? If you thought Tampa Bay Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles’ curious choice not to kick a chip-shot field goal that would have given his team a three-possession lead in Thursday night’s game against the Dallas Cowboys would be the most scrutinized move of the week — well, it may go down only as the bronze medalist of baffling, thanks to a couple of not-so-smooth moves by men in headsets on Sunday. First came Nicki Sirianni’s decision to pass late in the Eagles’ game against the Jags, with the ensuing incompletion ensuring that Jake Elliott’s eventual go-ahead field goal would leave eight seconds on the clock, rather than zero. Then Sirianni chose to have Elliott kick the ball into the landing zone, setting up Ameer Abdullah’s 53-yard return and Cam Little’s 57-yard walk-off field goal . “I didn’t make the right decision and I lost us that game,” Sirianni said, after Philly (2-3) dropped its third straight. He wasn’t wrong, but given that he came into the game with an NFL-best record of 35-15 in one-score games, we’ll give him a little grace. Besides, embattled Washington coach Dan Quinn later accepted responsibility for an even more egregious collapse: With 12 seconds left, no timeouts and the ball at the Giants’ 24-yard-line, Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels inexplicably scrambled and went down inbounds , leaving no time for a field goal attempt. Though Daniels clearly goofed, Quinn, who threw his headset to the ground in disgust, shouldered the blame for taking the risk of running another play, saying, “It falls on me.” Will something else soon fall on Quinn? With a Monday night road game against the undefeated 49ers coming up for the Commanders (1-3-1), followed by a bye week, he has ample reason to be concerned. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) The undefeated NFL teams are exactly as nobody predicted Coach Dan Quinn took the blame , and he’s ultimately responsible for the operation. But the game management coach said this looked like a case of quarterback error. “Decisions made in real time are seldom perfect, but I can assure you of one thing: Dan Quinn and his staff told the quarterback no sack or scramble,” the coach said. “You can’t do that. You throw it away, and if you have eight seconds, throw it away again, get it to four seconds. There are three errors by the quarterback: scrambling, taking the sack and not getting up fast.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Front Office Sports It’s time for NFL Networks to hire ‘clock management’ specialists It was so laughable that ProFootballTalk’s Mike Florio called it a “firing offense.” No wonder, since Washington minority owner Magic Johnson sounded off about the blunder on X/Twitter. “I’m in total disbelief my Commanders had such poor clock management in today’s overtime game against the Giants,” tweeted Johnson. “All we had to do was kick the field goal and we would have won the game!” The Magic Man wasn’t alone. Fox play-by-play announcer Chris Myers and color commentator Jonathan Vilma couldn’t believe what they were seeing as the Commanders QB Jayden Daniels danced around with no timeouts instead of clocking the ball and attempting a game-winning field goal inside of 40 yards. “They don’t have a timeout. What are they doing?” asked Myers. “They’ve got to get up and spike this. They’re not going to be able to get this done in time! It’s gonna run out on them! The clock ran out as Daniels ran the ball!…Unbelievable. A comedy of errors late.” Vilma agreed. “Chris, that’s inexcusable!” he said. “It was just supposed to be, you go, you take a knee, set up, clock, and then get out of there.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE…

title: Commanders report card: Team grades in NFL Week 5 tie with Giants
summary: We have already written a ton about that fateful end-of-game sequence that concluded Sunday’s game with the New York Giants in a 27-27 tie that sure felt like a gut-wrenching loss.   There will be some mentions of it here, but we’re not going to break it down on a granular level. We’ve already done […]
full_text: We have already written a ton about that fateful end-of-game sequence that concluded Sunday’s game with the New York Giants in a 27-27 tie that sure felt like a gut-wrenching loss. There will be some mentions of it here, but we’re not going to break it down on a granular level. We’ve already done that in the stories linked below. It’s also fair to mention the Commanders should’ve secured victory well before that. They were up 14 points with roughly seven minutes to go . The Giants ended regulation with 14 unanswered points, finishing with two touchdown drives that sandwiched a Commanders three-and-out. That’s all bad. Not everything that happened on Sunday was terrible. Let’s breakdown how the Commanders looked in every phrase in this Week 5 report card. Rushing offense The Commanders running game totaled 202 yard on 30 carries, a quality number that shouldn’t be discounted by the fact Jayden Daniels rushed for more than half of them (and two touchdowns) on nine carries. That still left a 4.7-yards-per-carry average for the running backs, paced by Bill Croskey-Merritt’s 82 (and a TD) on 11 totes. It sure helps the run game to have Sam Cosmi back and Lucas Patrick’s clear upgrade at center. Some better second half work would’ve sustained drives and iced the game, but that didn’t happen. While that last play was technically a run, that doesn’t impact this grade. That was a lapse in judgement. Grade: A-minus/B-plus Passing offense Daniels completed 17-of 25 passes for 199 yards, not a massive total but still at eight yards per attempts and a 91.9 rating. He also had some clutch throws to Terry McLaurin and Treylon Burks down the stretch. Chig Okonkwo started fast and then fizzled. The Commanders were able to move the ball through the air, but the passing game wasn’t dominant. And, can Washington stop throwing Dyami Brown the ball? Only bad things happen. The pass protection was an issue, especially with left tackle Brandon Coleman dealing with Abdul Carter and blitzers from his side. He struggled mightily. It’ll take the All-22 to analyze the protection completely, but five sacks and seven hits on Daniels is too many. Grade: C-plus Rushing defense The Commanders defensive line is looking stout these days, and holding the Giants to 3.7 yards per carry is decent despite NYG exceeding 100 overall. Getting that Cam Skatebo fumble in overtime was huge (until it was negated). Letting Jameis Winston run at important times can’t happen, though. Washington shut down the zone-read. Overall, this phase remains the defensive hallmark. Grade: B-plus Passing defense The Commanders let a backup quarterback, albeit a veteran in Winston throw for 326 yards. All those blitzes worked early until they didn’t. Amik Robertson got robbed of an interception at the goal line by a brutal pass interference call that was a game-changer. He had a tough assignment against Malik Nabers and held his own. Washington got a key sack-fumble from K’Lavon Chaisson but only two sacks overall. Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely went off — Nabers was better when Robertson wasn’t on him — to an unacceptable point. The secondary is a complete mess outside of Robertson and the occasional Rasul Douglas pass defensed. The Commanders have personnel problems at safety and cornerback right now and it’s costing them dearly, as it did during that late-game Giants run, when Winston had a (no joke) 131.7 passer rating . Grade: F Special teams Drew Stevens made both of his field-goal attempts and should’ve been given a third to win but never got it. Punter Tress Way dropped two of his six punts inside the 10-yard line and averaged 52 yards per punt. That’s, you know, good. The Commanders clearly miss Jaylin Lane returning punts and kicks. Grade: B Coaching Clock and game management are on coaching. Always. Quinn took blame for that disastrous end-of-game sequence and he should’ve considering what happened. The play call was for Daniels to hit someone quickly on the sideline or throw it out of bounds — why did he tuck it? — but Quinn should’ve said to clock it on that play, even if he had to overrule OC David Blough to do so. It was a makable field goal. Stevens should’ve had a chance to attempt it. Also, all these pre-snap penalties fall on coaching, too. They were drive killers in a few instances. While Quinn’s taking most of the blame here, Daronte Jones ’ game plan worked until it fell apart in the second half. He just kept sending the house and Winston just kept completing passes. The Commanders have been conceding second-half points in high volume. Jones needs to find things that work for the talent level available, though he desperately needs secondary help. Overall, though coaching committed some unacceptable mistakes in this one. It was a disaster through and through. Grade: (Wish there was a grade lower than) F How would you grade the Commanders in each phase of this game? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Inside the end-of-game sequence that led to Commanders tie with Giants
summary: The Commanders worked their way into comfortable field goal range with Jayden Daniels’ pass to Treylon Burks, who went out of bounds at the New York Giants’ 26-yard line with 1 minute, 2 seconds remaining.   Washington kept pushing for yards despite it being just a 43-yard field goal attempt. They ran Rachaad White to […]
full_text: The Commanders worked their way into comfortable field goal range with Jayden Daniels’ pass to Treylon Burks, who went out of bounds at the New York Giants’ 26-yard line with 1 minute, 2 seconds remaining. Washington kept pushing for yards despite it being just a 43-yard field goal attempt. They ran Rachaad White to the right despite having no timeouts. He gained two yards on a play that ended with 55 seconds left. The Commanders had plenty of time to discuss everything and ultimately decided to try one more play to make it a shorter field goal. As we all know by now, this is what happened next: A wild finish to Giants-Commanders game pic.twitter.com/0QvJGVIPbG — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 That led to a 27-27 tie against the New York Giants on Sunday at Northwest Stadium that left everyone stunned at what they just saw. It was a brutal sequence and awful display of situational awareness that cost Washington a win. After the game, head coach Dan Quinn and quarterback Jayden Daniels explained what went down in a moment where everything fell apart. “Leaving tonight with a tie feels like a loss,” Quinn told on-site reporters in his postgame press conference . “The last sequence – you throw it out of bounds, you clock it, you give yourself a chance to kick it. We pride ourselves on those moments at the end of the game. After the first down run, we’re still trying to gain more for the kick.” According to Quinn, the play called for Daniels to connect with a receiver on the left side – it looked to be tight end Ben Sinnott – or immediately throw it away if he wasn’t open. That didn’t happen. The ball was snapped with 12 seconds left and, instead of throwing it to Sinnott or out of bounds, Daniels moved around the backfield, never threw it away and was tackled as seconds ticked away. The Commanders frantically tried to clock it at that point – most of their receivers were down the field — but never got set before time expired. The game ended in a shocking tie. Daniels was asked after the game what he was supposed to do in that spot. His answer didn’t directly address that. “We have to stop the clock,” Daniels said. “We have to know it’s an o-zone situation. We have to relay that as an offense. It starts from everybody, (from) the top down, but ultimately, it’s on me.” Jayden Daniels addresses the clock management on Washington's final possession that led to a tie against the Giants pic.twitter.com/WuHIjnyxNd — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 11, 2026 Hindsight being what it is, Quinn said that play never should’ve been run. “The right call, honestly, is to clock it early and don’t put ourselves in that spot,” Quinn said. “That’s my responsibility, nobody else’s. I’m gutted for our team.” That would’ve been the correct sequence. And, with as much time as was on the clock after White’s run, Quinn could’ve heard and killed that final play call and simply let kicker Drew Stevens try to end it with a field goal from a makable distance even with wet conditions. “We were trying to gain more (yards),” Quinn said. “We don’t need to. It’s easy enough to say, ‘let’s clock it right here.’” The Commanders didn’t, and then the quarterback didn’t throw it away. It was a situation overcomplicated unnecessarily that very likely gave a win away. “The sequencing of that does not fall on (Daniels),” Quinn said. “It’s an outside throw or a clock, those are the two (options). Out-of-bounds throw or a clock, that has to come from me. I don’t have to put him in that spot. I can do that earlier. We can finish with a kick. We don’t need to gain more yards.” Quinn calls performance under pressure “winning time moments,” and the Commanders thrived in those situations during a 2024 campaign that ended with a trip to the NFC title game . The Commanders generally haven’t been good in those situations since, and were awful there at the end of Sunday’s game. “Finding a way to nail that moment and that play – we have to do that 100 out of 100 times,” Quinn said. “That falls onto me.”

title: Key takeaways from Washington Commanders tie with New York Giants
summary: BOX SCORE The Commanders started slow, with three losses in their first four games. That’s a messy situation to be sure, especially with the injuries piling up.   The NFC East, however, did Washington a favor. Dallas lost on Thursday night. Then the Philadelphia Eagles lost an early game in London.   That left Washington […]
full_text: BOX SCORE The Commanders started slow, with three losses in their first four games. That’s a messy situation to be sure, especially with the injuries piling up. The NFC East, however, did Washington a favor. Dallas lost on Thursday night. Then the Philadelphia Eagles lost an early game in London. That left Washington with a golden opportunity to match those teams at 2-3 with a victory over the New York Giants on Sunday. Beating the Giants would bunch the NFC East to the point that all four team would be within a game of each other. The key to all that, obviously, was a Commanders victory over the Giants. They had Jayden Daniels back and Terry McLaurin was able to play despite a hamstring. Could they get the job done? They did not. But they really, really should’ve. The Commanders should’ve at least set up a last-second field goal attempt, but ran when they had to clock it and ended up in a 27-27 tie as time expired. That was an unreal blunder in a game the Commanders should’ve won in regulation if not for blown leads, and should’ve won in overtime with a makable field goal. Instead, this game ends in a tie and a completely blown opportunity to beat the Giants and hop out of last place in the NFC East and into the thick of the division race. Honestly, that’s as bad as it gets. What we just watched was unbelievable. Here’s the play: A WILD ENDING IN WASHINGTON! With no timeouts remaining, the Commanders can't spike the ball before time expires, and the game ends in a tie! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/GgTTHtyRVC — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 11, 2026 Let’s examine at some key takeaways from this crucial Week 5 contest: Jayden Daniels runs wild , embracing the brace Daniels felt pressure from his left midway through the first quarter and moved to avoid it. He wasn’t able to, as Giants edge rusher Abdul Carter closed the gap and tackled Daniels by the ankles. The quarterback twisted towards the turf, falling in a way where he could have used his left hand to ease his fall. Daniels didn’t do that. He kept twisting and landed on his right hand, avoiding an awkward landing like what dislocated his elbow in Week 2. Abdul Carter sacked Jayden Daniels. This is the kind of takedown where a QB can brace himself with his left hand. Whether consciously or unconsciously, better for Daniels he didn’t. pic.twitter.com/0i1qztzZVi — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) October 11, 2026 Daniels was wearing a custom-fitted brace to protect his left elbow and avoid another dislocation, starting in a Week 5 game that was also his return to action. Washington’s quarterback threw the ball well and wasn’t afraid to run and was aggressive when his team needed it. Daniels completed the game and finished this one and was an explosive player despite the unflattering conditions. Overall, he was 17-for-22 passing for 199 yards, with nine carries for 103 yards and two touchdowns. His dynamic playmaking ability was clear in the third quarter, when Daniels tucked it and ran away from everyone on a 38-yard touchdown run that put Washington up two scores. Jayden Daniels is so back! pic.twitter.com/dkndjPP3Ce — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) October 11, 2026 That wasn’t the only time Daniels did that. He broke free early in the fourth quarter for a 26-yard touchdown run where he was untouched. Jayden Daniels does it again! pic.twitter.com/xp58VYsYTz — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) October 11, 2026 Daniels didn’t have a massive day passing, but was smart and effective throwing the ball while finding moments to run wild. While there were several points where the Commanders were in firm control, Washington kept needing to lean on Daniels. That was true once this game went to overtime. He couldn’t lock down a score on his first OT series, and then got Washington into position with huge passes to Terry McLaurin and Treylon Burks and a big 16-yard run. Then disaster struck with a mental blunder by the quarterback or the entire offense that let the clock go out without a field goal attempt. Close calls go against Commanders Amik Robertson intercepted a Jameis Winston pass just before the goal line and returned it 25 yards. He immediately started celebrating in the opposite end zone, unaware that a flag had been thrown. Fellow cornerback Rasul Douglas eventually told him. Officials called for pass interference, which is tough to identify upon replay. They called pass interference on Amik Robertson for THIS! 🤦🏻‍♂️ What a weak, BS call!!! Negated a huge INT pic.twitter.com/C3rA8fvxFZ — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) October 11, 2026 Robertson couldn’t believe it. Commanders fans couldn’t believe it either, as the reaction to the play suggests. Was it defensive holding? Either way, the officials got that call wrong. The Giants were given a first-and-goal and Isaiah Likely eventually turned the opportunity into a touchdown. It was a clear momentum shift in this game, and cut Washington’s lead to six. Daniels’ big touchdown run took it back, but many will play those seven Giants points shouldn’t have been scored. Especially with how close this game was at the end. That’s why the impact of that PI call looms so large. Later in the game, Jameis Winston completed a fourth-down pass to Likely, who had the ball punched out right near the goal line, but he was ruled (after replay) to have crossed the plane before losing possession. Isaiah Likely gets the TD before Rasul Douglas punches the ball out. Washington gets the ball back up 27-20 pic.twitter.com/8VKgFxQdPF — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) October 11, 2026 That kept things close late in a game where Washington twice had two-score, second-half leads. The Giants eventually took the lead with 14 unanswered points late in the fourth quarter to tie it at 27-27 on a Malik Nabers touchdown catch that ultimately sent it to overtime. The Giants missed a field goal on the overtime’s opening drive and lost a fumble on the second, leaving Daniels to drive the team into position for the decisive points. Daniels hit a big run and then an important completion to Treylon Burks with roughly a minute left. Burks breaking tackles 📺 #WASvsNYG FOX pic.twitter.com/5XVvyy7CPU — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 11, 2026 Then the Commanders inexcusably didn’t clock the ball and Daniels ran as the time expired and without a timeout. That’s how this game ended in a tie. Defense falls apart, then stands tall Washington’s defense was in firm control of Winston and the New York Giants offense, which couldn’t do much in the opening two quarters. Things were going well, with just three points allowed, a takeaway and a solid pass rush going strong. Things were completely different in the second half. The Giants scored 24 second half points. We address some close calls going against Washington that we addressed above. The Commanders were penalized heavily during those stretches at inopportune times. The Giants started neutralizing the Commanders blitz and capitalizing on it down the field. Winston took control of the game late and had all the momentum entering the overtime period, with Likely and Nabers becoming difficult for a suspect Washington secondary to stop. The Commanders held in the first overtime series but not in the second, allowing Winston and Cam Skattebo to beat them again and again. Then, when they found a way to make a play. Odafe Oweh and Daron Payne were credited with a forced fumble of Skattebo that Shy Tuttle recovered deep in Commanders territory and well within field-goal range. That gave the Commanders one more shot to win the game, and somehow the Commanders didn’t even take it. Chig Okonkwo steps up, shows out The Commanders got tons of questions about tight end involvement during the week, and for good reason. The entire position group had 10 receptions for a league-low 65 yards on just 17 targets through four games. Big free agent signing Chig Okonkwo had been largely quiet early, and head coach Dan Quinn said that was due to…

The team announced that Jayden Daniels is back this week and will be starting with rookie Athan Kaliakmanis backing him up. Marcus Mariota got the start the last two weeks, but reinjured his MCL, and will miss a few weeks. Washington ruled out six players as their injury woes continue for another week. The Giants come to town as 3-1 division leaders, and they’re being led by QB Jameis Winston after Jaxson Dart was lost for the season. They’ve beaten the Cowboys, Titans, and Cardinals, but were blown out by the Rams when Dart went down. title: Making sense of the Giants-Commanders tie, the Texans' Marvin Harrison Jr. trade
summary: What were the Commanders doing in the final minute of OT? Why did the 1-4 Texans make an aggressive trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.? Let's try to find the logic.
full_text:
Two very different decisions -- one on the field and another off it -- had me asking the same question by Sunday afternoon on Week 5 : What are they thinking? 

 There were the Commanders, who bizarrely decided to run the clock late in overtime against the Giants in field goal range and saw the game end without ever getting a chance to attempt the game-winning kick. And there were the Texans, who won their first game of the season and celebrated by making a surprisingly aggressive move on offense, trading second- and sixth-round picks to the Cardinals for a seventh-rounder and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr ., who has underwhelmed during his pro career so far.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 I love trying to explain the inexplicable, so let's give it a shot. Why did a 1-4 Texans team -- whose playoff chances sit at 23.2% after Sunday's victory, per ESPN's Football Power Index -- trade a significant future pick to acquire a player at a position where it already has  Nico Collins ? And what on earth were the Commanders attempting to do at the end of that game?

 I'll try to answer both those questions today, starting with the decision to try to kick-start a frustrating season by trading for one of the league's most frustrating players.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 The 1-4 Texans traded for Harrison? 
 The Commanders let the clock expire? 

 
 

 

 The Texans' trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. 
 Of course, the simple explanation for why the Texans traded for Harrison starts with one simple argument. We're about two and a half years removed from Harrison entering the 2024 NFL draft as arguably the most exciting and polished wide receiver prospect of his generation. Even amid a legendary run of Ohio State wide receivers that includes the likes of Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Chris Olave , Garrett Wilson , Emeka Egbuka  and others, Harrison was seen alongside  Jeremiah Smith  as the two best pro prospects of the bunch.

 Our various draft analysts saw Harrison as  no worse than the third-best player overall  in the class of 2024. There just aren't many players with Harrison's sort of scouting reports and college pedigree to ever enter the league. They don't come available via trade very often, and it's even rarer to get a shot at acquiring them just after they turn 24 years old.

 The Texans have been through this under general manager Nick Caserio and don't regret their past decision. After drafting C.J. Stroud with the second pick of the 2023 draft, the Texans surprised everyone by trading two first-round picks and a second-rounder to the Cardinals to move up for edge rusher  Will Anderson Jr . with the third overall selection. It was a move that seemed overly aggressive for a team that projected to be among the worst in football the following year, but it turned out to be a masterstroke.

 

 The Texans were a playoff team with Stroud and Anderson, with the latter emerging as one of the most dominant defenders in all of football. Like Anderson, Harrison plays a premium position. And while we don't have access to Houston's scouting reports, this trade implies that it saw Harrison as a potential superstar entering the league after his run at Ohio State. Stroud, Harrison's college teammate with the Buckeyes, gave a glowing report to the organization and said that the wideout was "probably the hardest worker I've ever been around in my life."

 The difference, of course, is that in Anderson, the Texans were trading up for a player with a great college résumé who hadn't yet played at the pro level. With Harrison, the Texans are trading for a player who has been outright disappointing as a pro over a multiple-season sample. He isn't a bad player, but he has hardly been great. Since 2024, he ranks 70th out of 130 wideouts in yards per route run (1.54) and 44th in receiving yards per game (47.8). He hasn't had great quarterback play, but Harrison has been roundly outperformed by Trey McBride and Michael Wilson within the same offense.

 On one hand, Harrison's contract is extremely affordable, which is important for a Texans team that just paid Anderson and has deals for Stroud, Calen Bullock  and Kamari Lassiter to come over the next 12 months. Harrison will make just $776,000 over the remainder of 2026 and $5.6 million in 2027. Even if the Texans decide to pick up Harrison's fifth-year option in 2028, that deal projects to come in at only  $17.2 million .

 That's a total of $23.6 million over the next three years, which is just a tiny bit more than what Jakobi Meyers is making per year on his existing contract. That number rises if you factor in the surplus value of the draft picks sent to the Cardinals , which throws another $33 million onto the pile -- but even $56.6 million over the next three years would be reasonable WR2 money right now. It'll look even cheaper as the cap rises over the next two seasons.

 The Texans are obviously counting on Harrison delivering something more than solid WR2 performance and living up to his lofty predraft expectations. Will he get there? To answer that question, there were two places to look. First, I wanted to get a sense of why Harrison was struggling in Arizona to see whether a change of scenery might be likely to unlock the second-generation pro. Second, I looked back through history to find examples of highly drafted players turning things around in a second act with a new team.

 
 What went wrong in Arizona? 

 The simplest answer is the one that Texans fans would fear the most. While there are mitigating factors and potential excuses to be made, the reality is that Harrison just wasn't able to get himself open often enough to get the sort of target share or rack up the sort of receiving production his draft status suggested was coming. While anyone with access to All-22 film and a lot of free time can undoubtedly find plays where he was open and didn't get the football, that's also true for any starting receiver in football.

 

 During his time with the Cardinals, Harrison ranked last in the NFL among all wide receivers (with 50 targets or more over the past three years) in separation, averaging just 2.1 yards of separation when targeted, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Great receivers -- even ones that get plenty of attention from opposing defenses -- are typically able to create more space for themselves. The likes of Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson average over 3 yards of separation on their routes. In Arizona, McBride averaged 3.3 yards of separation on his targets during that time, while Wilson was at 2.5 yards.

 In part because of those separation issues, Harrison didn't have a lot of chances to bring in easy targets. His expected catch rate over the past three years, using the Next Gen Stats model, was only 53.7%. That's fifth-lowest among wide receivers since the start of 2024. I'll get to the four below him in a minute.

 By those expectations, the good news is that Harrison has roughly delivered about what the model would project given that low expected catch rate. He has caught 53.5% of his passes so far as a pro, almost exactly in line with the model's prediction. He has generated a total of 34 receiving yards over expectation across his 202 targets, which is also essentially a match for what the model suggests. You could make a case that Harrison has done an average job with below-average opportunities and hope that his expected catch rate will rise in Houston.

 But my concern is that Harrison is not separating because he hasn't been explosive enough. The four other wideouts with lower expected catch rates are Alec Pierce , Tyquan Thornton , Marquez Valdes-Scantling  and Christian Watson . Those are all deep threats who primarily make their money with their speed and ability to get open downfield. While they're going to draw targets that don't have great chances of being caught, the huge gains those receivers provide when they do bring in the football make up for the low catch rates.

 Next Gen Stats also…

title: 2027 NFL draft order projections for Round 1, chances for top pick, more
summary: ESPN's Football Power Index projects the 2027 NFL draft order for Round 1, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.
full_text:
The 2027 NFL draft is still months away, but with the 2026 season underway, we're starting to track pick order in Round 1. Which teams are in position to add elite prospects in the top 10 next April? What about the top five ... or even at No. 1?

 What follows is not the current draft order based on records. It is a projection of what ESPN's Football Power Index thinks the order ultimately will be by the end of the season. Each week during the season, the FPI projects the draft order by simulating the remainder of the season 10,000 times. Game probabilities are based primarily on the model's team ratings and game locations. The draft order is determined by the records the model projects for each team after 17 games, as well as each team's average draft position across the simulations.

 So where do things stand? Here are the full sortable projections, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.

 The Indianapolis Colts ' selection was dealt to the New York Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade .

title: NFL Week 5: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday's games
summary: Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering the biggest questions coming out of each Sunday game. Here's what we learned from Week 5.
full_text:
The Sunday slate for Week 5 of the  2026 NFL season  kicked off in London with a thrilling matchup between the Eagles and Jaguars.

 Back in the United States, the first tie of the season came between the Commanders and Giants. The Vikings stayed undefeated despite two fumbles in the red zone against the Saints; while the Texans got into the win column for the first time with a blowout victory over the Titans. The Steelers, led by a big performance from RB  Jaylen Warren , dominated against the Colts. And the Packers avenged last season's playoff loss to the Bears.

 In the late window Sunday, the 49ers eked out a win over the Seahawks despite losing  Deebo Samuel Sr . to injury in the third quarter. The Chargers fell to 0-5 after losing to the Broncos, and the Lions pulled off a comfortable win over the Cardinals. The Ravens finished things off with a gutty overtime victory over the Falcons on "Sunday Night Football."

 Our NFL Nation reporters reacted to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game and detailing everything else you need to know for teams that played Sunday. Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup.

 

 Let's get to it with the biggest lessons from Sunday's games.

 
 Jump to: 
 BAL-ATL |  SF-SEA |  DET-ARI | DEN-LAC 
 NYG-WSH | CLE-NYJ |  IND-PIT 
 HOU-TEN |  CIN-MIA | LV-NE 
 CHI-GB |  MIN-NO |  PHI-JAX 

 Catch up on Thursday's game: 
 TB-DAL 

 
 

 

 Baltimore 30, Atlanta 23 (OT) 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Ravens 
 Is the win streak without Lamar Jackson sustainable? Tyler Huntley has led the Ravens to three straight wins without Jackson dating to last season, but none as dramatic as Sunday night. Looking a little like the two-time NFL Most Valuable Player late in the game, Huntley delivered his first comeback win for Baltimore in four seasons. He completed his last 10 passes for 79 yards and converted two key third downs in overtime to set up his winning 1-yard sneak in OT. The Ravens' 14-play series was the longest overtime touchdown drive in the NFL since 2018. Thanks to Huntley's effort, the Ravens are 4-1 for the first time in five years and hold a one-game lead atop the AFC North.

 Trend to watch: Ravens kicker Tyler Loop has become automatic from long range. He hit two field goals from 51 yards, improving to 5-of-5 from 50 yards or longer this season. This is a major change from last season, when Loop was 1-of-4 from 50 or longer as a rookie. -- Jamison Hensley 

 Next game: at Browns (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Falcons 
 Should the Falcons remain optimistic with their current position despite a loss? Short answer is yes, pending Michael Penix Jr .'s health after he was knocked out of the game late in the fourth quarter. Tua Tagovailoa took over in overtime and threw a game-ending pick. But even though that wasn't the ideal result, nor is being 2-3 with two home losses, there is hope with a healthy Penix. The Falcons didn't light it up Sunday night as they did against the Packers and Saints, but they were in position to win their third straight game late in the fourth quarter. Now, they need to learn how to close out these games while hoping for good news on Penix's health. But they've proven that they can compete when he's playing.

 Key stat to know: The Falcons led 7-3 after the first quarter despite not having a pass completion or a passing yard in the quarter. That had not happened since 2017, per ESPN Research. Falcons safety Jessie Bates III returned a fumble for a touchdown to give Atlanta its TD. -- Marc Raimondi 

 Next game: vs. Bears (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: Drake London had 18.8 fantasy points Sunday night against Baltimore, catching seven of a team-high 11 targets for 118 yards. Over the past three games with Penix at quarterback, London is scoring 20.6 points per game. London should have perimeter matchup advantages in Atlanta's Week 6 game against the Beras, locking him in as a WR1 as long as Penix can play. -- Bowen 

 

 

 San Francisco 32, Seattle 29 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 49ers 
 Is WR Mike Evans the player who can finally put the 49ers over the top? After failing to score a touchdown in their final two meetings with Seattle last season, the Niners signed Evans to win games like this. Playing through a rib injury for the second consecutive week, Evans finished with seven catches for 113 yards and a touchdown. He delivered multiple clutch catches to will a sagging San Francisco offense to a huge road victory. Much still needs to fall into place for the 49ers to hoist the Lombardi Trophy again, but Evans has offered a strong answer to one of San Francisco's biggest offseason questions.

 What to make of the QB performance: Brock Purdy once again struggled against Seattle's vaunted defense though much of Sunday's game. But as he has many times throughout his career, he delivered when the Niners needed him most. Purdy led two late scoring drives to deliver the winning points, finishing 19-of-29 for 189 yards and two touchdowns with one interception.

 Best quote from the locker room: 49ers LB Fred Warner on the team's undefeated start, including road division wins against the Rams and Seahawks: "We're 5-0. We've found a way to win every game and at the end of the day, the goal is to continue to just be on the rise. We're not satisfied with just winning. Of course you want to win every game, but the goal is to continue to get better as the season goes. And I think that sets you up for the best chance to go do what you want to do at the end. I'm really proud of the group. Today was special. It was fun."  -- Nick Wagoner 

 Next game: vs. Commanders (Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET)

 

 
 

 Seahawks 
 Can Sam Darnold stop throwing interceptions? For the second week in a row, Darnold was picked on the opening possession. He threw another interception in the second half, as Seattle committed four turnovers that led to 21 points for San Francisco. Darnold (18-of-29, 195 yards, TD) has thrown five interceptions in three games since returning from the glute injury that sidelined him for most of the first two (compared with zero turnovers by Drew Lock in his absence). Darnold showed at the end 2025 that he could play clean football, with zero turnovers over the final four games (including the playoffs). That was after he led all players with 20 turnovers in the regular season despite Seattle having the fourth-lowest dropback rate.

 Most surprising performance: Seattle's running backs lost two more fumbles -- one apiece by Emanuel Wilson and George Holani . Jadarian Price fumbled twice before he went on IR last week. The Seahawks miss Price's explosiveness, so they're using receiver Rashid Shaheed in the backfield. They also miss Zach Charbonnet 's ball security, among the other things he does well. Mike Macdonald said the plan right now is that Charbonnet won't play Thursday night against Denver. 

 Best quote from the locker room:   Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught five passes for 102 yards and a touchdown, but he had two drops on the final drive, including one deep down the field on Seattle's second-to-last play. "At the end of the day, I had the chance to catch the ball. So really just catch the ball. Catch the damn ball football. ... I know I'll make the next one."  -- Brady Henderson 

 Next game: at Broncos (Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: 49ers WR Mike Evans is emerging as QB Brock Purdy's go-to guy. Evans' 10 targets boosted his seasonal share to 37%, and his 26.3 fantasy points gave him four of five games with at least 12. His matchup-oriented track record reminds us to always check his upcoming opponent, but he should have no problem against the Commanders in Week 6. -- Cockcroft

title: NFL Week 5 arrivals: Ravens trio channels early 2000s style ahead of 'SNF'
summary: NFL stars continue to turn game-day arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
Week 5 of the NFL season is here, and October is starting to bring a little more variety to the forecast -- and potentially to pregame fashion.

 With fall temperatures settling into parts of the country and lingering heat beginning to ease elsewhere, players have another opportunity to switch up their game-day looks. 

 California's early-October heat wave has weakened, while cooler conditions in the Northeast and a hurricane that brought heavy rain to parts of the South made for a mixed bag across the country this weekend. That leaves room for everything from lightweight fits to layered looks as players make their stadium entrances.

 Whether they're embracing the season with jackets and sweaters or sticking to their signature styles, NFL players are bringing another round of personality to the tunnel in Week 5.

 

 Primetime fashion 
 
The Baltimore Ravens turned back the clock with some early 2000s-inspired fashion ahead of their Sunday Night Football matchup against the Atlanta Falcons . Cornerbacks Chandler Rivers and Keyon Martin joined safety Keondre Jackson in rocking backwards throwback basketball jerseys, oversized shorts and nostalgic accessories. Rivers led the way in a blue Derrick Rose Memphis Tigers jersey, baggy denim shorts and wheat Timberland boots, while Martin sported Penny Hardaway's pinstriped Orlando Magic jersey and Jackson repped Carmelo Anthony and the New York Knicks . The coordinated looks brought a dose of Y2K nostalgia to the Ravens' arrival in Atlanta. 
 
 
 
 Sunday's best 
Throwback jerseys honoring New England sports legends were a theme ahead of Sunday's matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and New England Patriots . Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby arrived in a Larry Bird jersey, while Patriots safety Craig Woodson sported a Ty Law jersey as New England prepared to celebrate the 25th anniversary of its Super Bowl XXXVI championship.
 
 
 Thursday night drip 
 Dallas Cowboys teammates Cooper Beebe and Brevyn Spann-Ford  showed some love to the Dallas Stars ahead of "Thursday Night Football." Beebe arrived in a Jake Oettinger jersey, while Spann-Ford repped Stars legend Mike Modano.

title: Inside the NFL's wild endings and why coaches need to adapt
summary: Scoring too early and kicking the ball into the end zone can be costly, as the Cowboys learned.
full_text:
Editor's note: This story ran Friday, before the wild ending to the Eagles-Jaguars game , which became the first to feature two go-ahead field goals in the final 10 seconds of regulation in the Super Bowl era (since 1966). Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said it was a mistake to let the Jaguars return the kick with eight seconds left.  Ameer Abdullah  returned the kick 53 yards to set up  Cam Little 's 57-yard game-winning field goal. 

 The Indianapolis Colts appeared positioned for exactly the kind of finish that keeps NFL stadiums packed.

 Fourth quarter. Their ball. Down one point against the Houston Texans with 1:48 remaining. On the second play of what would be their final drive in Week 3, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones ripped a pass down the middle to receiver Laquon Treadwell for a 20-yard gain. Just like that, the Colts were cooking at the Houston 45-yard line.

 What happened next left some perplexed: The Colts began to display a sudden lack of urgency.

 They ran the ball on their next play. Next, they casually allowed the clock to tick down from 40 to 29 seconds before the following play -- that's when Houston, interestingly, called a timeout. Then, another run.

 Not until the Colts faced a third-and-6 did they make a more concerted effort to achieve a first down. Receiver Keenan Allen came up inches short after a 6-yard reception, so kicker Spencer Shrader came on and booted a 53-yard game-winning field goal with 21 seconds remaining.

 Why weren't the Colts more aggressive? And when did a 53-yard field goal become a slam dunk? The situation offered a prime example of how the traditional approach to late-game situations in the NFL has necessarily evolved at a time when more and more games are being decided late.

 In some instances, the "hurry-up" offense becomes more like "hurry up ... kinda."

 

 "That is real," Colts coach Shane Steichen said. "There's no doubt. When you have an opportunity to finish the game, you want it to be the last drive."

 Just ask the Dallas Cowboys , who can attest to it after losing a Week 3 game to the Baltimore Ravens on an inexplicable seven-second scoring drive.

 If it feels like there has been more last-minute scoring in the NFL lately, it's because there has been.

 Since the latest change to the NFL kickoff process last year, with the ball positioned at the 35-yard line after touchbacks, madness has ensued in the final moments of games. The number of drives starting in the final minute of halves culminating in a touchdown or field goal attempt skyrocketed by more than 50% relative to the 10 seasons before the changes.

 Meanwhile, the increasing strength and skill level of kickers, combined with underappreciated changes to rules governing how kicking balls -- known as K-balls -- may be manipulated by teams, has spurred a 60% increase in field goal attempts of 50 yards or longer in just five seasons. Many of those attempts are coming late in games and proving decisive.

 

 There were an NFL-record 12 field goal conversions of 60 yards or longer last season, including Jacksonville Jaguars kicker  Cam Little 's 68-yarder, the longest in NFL history.

 Subtle changes are translating into massive impacts on the game, and the trends seem unlikely to slow anytime soon.

 "Now you're seeing, I mean, chaos out there from some teams," Jaguars coach Liam Coen said. "And it's cool to watch."

 When a touchback can cost you the game 

 Of course, it's less cool if you're on the wrong side of the outcome.

 That brings us back to the Cowboys. There are a host of reasons they lost 34-31 to the Ravens on Sept. 27 in Rio de Janeiro, among them some curious coaching decisions and poor execution by players.

 

 But not to be overlooked was the role that today's kickoff rules played in the defeat. Had the Cowboys made the exact same miscues and been subject to the same circumstances just a few years ago, they likely would have held off Baltimore and pushed the game into overtime.

 One of the biggest variables in the loss was Dallas' decision to kick into the end zone after their tying field goal. With just seven seconds remaining, kicker Brandon Aubrey was instructed to aim for a touchback. But in the past three seasons, field position after touchbacks has been overhauled. After a 2024 change, teams were awarded the ball at the 30-yard line after touchbacks. (It was previously the 25-yard line.) A year later, in 2025, the rule was amended again, placing the ball at the 35.

 Ten yards of additional field position is priceless in an environment where kickers are capable of making field goals from near midfield.

 "There are so many yards at stake,"  Los Angeles Rams  coach Sean McVay said. "That's led to just so many more action plays in the kicking game in general. It's a big deal."

 Said Steichen: "You get the ball at the 35, and, shoot, someone hits an in-cut [route]. Next thing you know, they're at the plus-45 [yard line] and they kick a game-winning field goal."

 It's precisely what happened to Dallas, when quarterback Lamar Jackson hit receiver Zay Flowers for a 27-yard gain immediately after Dallas' kickoff. Baltimore called a timeout with one second remaining, allowing kicker Tyler Loop to convert a 56-yard field goal as time expired.

 Two-minute situations have been turned upside down by all of this.

 According to the Elias Sports Bureau, there were 49 game-winning drives that ended in the final two minutes of regulation in 2025, the most since 2000. Through four weeks of the 2026 season, there have already been 11 such drives. That puts this season on pace to match or exceed last year's total.

 "It used to be easy," said New York Giants coach John Harbaugh, who began coaching in the NFL when touchbacks translated to drive starts at the 20-yard line. "You kick a touchback and it's a gift. Good field position for your defense. They eliminated that because they want more returns, which I'm always for more."

 

 Adding to the issues is the complexity of today's dynamic kickoff process. Because the ball must land within the specified landing zone -- between the receiving team's goal line and the 20-yard line -- the possibility of a miss exists. When kickers are attempting to kick into the corners or hit kicks at specific angles to disadvantage kick returners, the odds of a miscue increase. The potential consequences are dire: The receiving team takes possession at its 40-yard line if a kick misses the landing zone or the ball goes out of bounds.

 The whole exercise is harder than it looks.

 "People don't get how hard it is for it to land just in the landing spot," San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said. "Not a touchback, not short and not out of bounds. It's not as easy as people think.

 "You want to kick it high in there, but you're a little amped up and [could be] a touchback and that's a big miss because it's already at the 35 now."

 Why manipulating K-balls for the kicker could be huge 

 It's a part of the game few fans concern themselves with: the origins of the footballs used on game day.

 But it's actually a huge aspect of game prep for teams, both in terms of the balls used by quarterbacks and those set aside for kicks and punts. That's why a little-discussed rule change in 2025 has seemingly played an important role in today's frenzied final minutes of games.

 The NFL years ago standardized kicking balls, putting a stop to the over-manipulation of balls by teams looking to achieve better ball flight. The balls were presented to teams by the officiating crew, fresh out of the box, 60 minutes before kickoff. Equipment managers could address the balls using water, towels and brushes, but time was limited.

 But that rule was rescinded last year. Now, teams have the freedom to address the balls to their liking throughout the week, just as they have been doing on behalf of quarterbacks for years.

 Whether it has made a tangible difference is difficult to prove. But it's hard to imagine…
