title: How to bet Bills-Rams on MNF: Analysis, tips and top prop plays
summary: Odds and analysis to help you bet Bills-Rams on "Monday Night Football."
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills ' defense has a lot to account for on "Monday Night Football." 

 Los Angeles Rams  star receiver Puka Nacua can hurt them across the middle.  Davante Adams can attack outside. And Kyren Williams has become a bigger part of the passing game, having posted 16 catches over the past two weeks, so Buffalo's linebackers have to handle the run and track Williams when he leaves the backfield. That can leave space behind them for Nacua.

 

 Buffalo needs James Cook III to make the Rams' defense respect the run. The Rams are allowing just 4.8 yards per pass attempt, so asking Josh Allen to carry everything through the air is a tough assignment. Cook can help draw the attention of defenders and open up play-action, while Allen's legs add another problem because coverage can hold up and he can still move the chains. If DJ Moore sits, Buffalo needs Keon Coleman to give Allen somewhere to go outside when the Rams crowd the middle.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 I would consider the Rams -3 because their scoring hasn't matched how well they've moved the ball. They're sixth in yards per play but average just 21.3 points per game. Turnovers explain part of that gap. Matthew Stafford already has six interceptions, after throwing eight all last season, and Los Angeles collectively has committed multiple turnovers in four straight games. I wouldn't assume that it suddenly disappears, but I also wouldn't treat this stretch as what we should expect every week.

 

 The Rams have faced San Francisco, Denver and Philadelphia, so the offense has had to work through some difficult defensive assignments. Buffalo presents a chance to turn that yardage into more points. The Bills are in the bottom 10 in points per play allowed. That's why the spread interests me; the Rams just need to stop giving possessions away and finish the opportunities they've already been consistently creating.

 Bet: Total points OVER 54.5 (-118) 

 I like the pace and the passing volume here. The Rams play at the fifth-fastest neutral pace, and Allen averaged 41.5 dropbacks when Buffalo was an underdog last season. That gives both offenses more opportunities to score, with fewer running plays draining the clock. The Rams can cover if they protect the ball, but turnovers could help the scoring if they give Buffalo short fields.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Matthew Stafford  rushing yards OVER 2.5 (+100) 

 Liz Loza: Having totaled a single rushing yard over the whole of the 2025 regular season, Stafford is certainly not known to be a mobile QB. That said, he has registered at least 10 rushing yards in each of his last two contests. Additionally, the Bills have allowed the fifth-most rushing yards to opposing QBs. C.J. Stroud , Justin Herbert , and Drake Maye all surpassed double-digit rushing yards against Buffalo, while Jared Goff contributed seven yards on the ground. The bar here is so low and the bet is juicy enough to bite.

 

 

 Davante Adams 70+ receiving yards (+123) 

 Eric Moody: Adams has cleared this line in two of four games this season, both coming with Puka Nacua inactive. Nacua commands a massive target share, but the Bills have allowed the fourth-most receiving yards to wide receivers. Stafford should also have time to find his playmakers behind a Rams offensive line that ranks sixth in pass block win rate. I believe both receivers can have productive games Monday night, especially with such a high game total.

title: How Bills QB Josh Allen has become a star on and off the field
summary: The Buffalo QB is racking up the endorsements and leaning on his Hollywood wife for advice.
full_text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- Here's a dirty little secret of the advertising industry: Professional athletes can be divas too.

 Athletes have been pitching products in TV commercials for almost as long as there have been TV commercials. They act. They sing. They dance. They toss their game-worn jerseys to well-meaning kids who have reminded them of their long-lost innocence and they laugh -- holding the product they're sponsoring label out, of course -- as choirs sing infectious jingles about how all the regular people at home wish they could be a little bit more like their heroes.

 One thing they don't do all that often in commercials is, well, play sports. There are plenty of reasons why this is the case, but one that's less talked about is that some athletes and their agents come on set with established constraints. It's why so many commercials for sports drinks and athletic wear consist of sluggers pointing their bats to the camera and basketball players setting up for slow-motion free throws.

 

 It's the way it is. Unless you're working with Josh Allen .

 "Some athletes will be like 'I'll give you three throws' or 'I'll kick the ball four times' or 'I'll run at no more than 50%' or whatever," said Alex Bower, former creative director at TBWA/Chiat/Day who wrote Allen's 2024 Gatorade campaign. "Josh, we shot him in L.A., it was a hot day. He gave us a lot of takes of him running lines and throwing the ball full pelt. He committed. We kind of used his shots heavily in the edit because it looked real because he was giving it 100%."

 Allen, the Buffalo Bills quarterback and betting favorite to win the NFL's MVP award (+280 on DraftKings entering Week 5), is a commercial star. He has endorsed Nike, New Era, New Balance, Nationwide and Natrol Sleep, and that's just the part of his portfolio that begins with "N." As the Bills (3-1) prepare for their "Monday Night Football" showdown at the Los Angeles Rams (2-2) at SoFi Stadium ( 8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN ), the prospect of having to perform in Hollywood for a national TV audience will hardly be novel for Allen -- who in addition to his commercial work is also CEO of his own production studio and is married to an Academy Award nominated Marvel superhero actress Hailee Steinfeld.

 "I just try to be myself," Allen said when asked if there's a trick to being a successful commercial actor. "I just kinda wing it."

 

 

 It's a Wonderful life 

 Wonderful Pistachios had its pick of three days.

 Between Allen's commitments to his new marriage, newborn daughter, practices, workouts and other work ventures, he had only six to eight hours on one of three summer days to be in Los Angeles to film a quartet of TV spots, which are set to debut during Monday's game.

 As Allen points out in the ads, his family owns a pistachio farm, making the partnership with Wonderful as much a business endeavor as a pitchman job. But ask Wonderful's chief creative officer Bobby Pearce and executive creative director Steve Yee, and they'll tell you Allen's behavior on set hardly portrays that of someone viewing this relationship transactionally.

 "He wasn't the kind of athlete or celebrity who as soon as he's done with his shot he's running back to his trailer," Yee told ESPN. "He's hanging out with us and sitting amongst us at Video Village. He's just really cool and chill."

 "He's just curious," Pearce adds. "He wants to look at the process. He's like 'Did I do that right? Did I give you what you need?'"

 

 If anything, the Wonderful cohort points toward Allen being a little too friendly on set. He gets to know cast and crew. He banters. In Year 1 of their partnership, Allen and his co-star spent so much time laughing with each other that the producers had to ask them to settle down.

 It would be one thing if this experience was unique to Wonderful. But it really isn't.

 "It's almost like he became buds with people on set a little bit, people we've worked with. Which is kind of unusual," Bower said. "Athletes, or talents in general, tend to be quite cloistered and separated off. It makes sense why that would be the case. But in the small moments between takes [Allen] seemed to be joking around and being friendly with regular people that were on set."

 "People will ask me after they know what I do 'Is this person really as nice as they seem on television?'" adds Rebekah Lyle, chief marketing officer for Vytalogy Wellness, parent company for Natrol. "I think Josh is one of those individuals where I'm always proud to say 'yes.' I think the person you imagine of who he would be is really genuinely who you get to interact with when you're with him on set."

 

 Allen's backstory says it all 

 Allen's family doesn't own a Gatorade bottling plant, so that partnership trades a little bit more in Allen's status as a football star. To Bower, Allen's origin story of emailing more than 1,000 college coaches and coordinators seeking a scholarship but received only two offers was his everyman hook before ending up at Wyoming.

 The campaign didn't traffic in mythological boasts about Allen's arm strength. Gatorade bet on Allen's persistence resonating with viewers who also believe greatness lies within them.

 

 Natrol went the other way. It identified Allen as a busy husband and father with a hectic life who prioritizes sleep and wellness, a superstar avatar for the workday public.

 And while Wonderful had no problem leaning into the farmer image, it also values him as a celebrity who it believes transcends sports. Pearce jokes that Wonderful founder Stewart Resnick knows only two athletes by name: Allen and LeBron James.

 Commercial shoots are hectic. Allen's most recent Wonderful shoot was interrupted first by a Bills superfan attempting to sneak onto set by posing as an ESPN reporter (his comically large collection of Bills hats and pins gave him away) and later by a police lockdown nearby that sealed off the 2-mile radius outside the studio and made it impossible for production assistants to go out on coffee runs.

 Amid all that, Allen played. Pearce swears by his theory that Allen took acting lessons between Year 1 and Year 2 of working with Wonderful. (He didn't, but he says his wife helped him out.) In one of the soon-to-be-released ads, Allen didn't know he would have to react to a surprise reveal of a blocking dummy wearing a jockstrap. Per Pearce, Allen's improvised reaction made it to the final edit.

 According to the Forbes list of the world's highest paid athletes in 2026, only Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes makes more money in off-field earnings ($28 million) than Allen does ($17.5 million) among NFL players. Per the Forbes report, no other NFL player made more than $5 million in off-field earnings. When factoring out international soccer stars and athletes who compete in individual sports like golf and tennis, Allen ranks as the 10th-highest paid athlete by off-field earnings in major American team sports.

 

 Factor in Allen's $55.1 million salary and Forbes has him ranked 22nd in the world for 2026, right between Ravens QB Lamar Jackson and YouTube star turned boxer Jake Paul.

 Based on internal research shared with ESPN, the ads are effective. Wonderful commissioned a third-party survey of 2,647 participants to evaluate the commercials. Two-thirds of participants rated Allen as a good fit for the brand and 41% of viewers said the ads made them more likely to purchase Wonderful Pistachios.

 Then there's the effect Allen had on the folks he worked with. Yee keeps a bobblehead of Allen riding a tractor in his office and a framed photo of Allen with the cast and crew on his desk.

 "What comes across for me with Josh is he looks like he's having fun," Yee says, trying to sum up why he's proud of the ads. "I think he is. That's a difference. A lot of times when a camera turns on, people freeze up. He's cool as a cucumber."

title: NFL Week 5 uniforms: Packers debut Rivalries look, Patriots wearing throwbacks
summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 5, led by the Green Bay Packers debuting their Rivalries look.
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers have had their fair share of alternate uniforms throughout their distinguished history. There were the 1950s all-green look and the 1923 classic threads unveiled last year. However, no Packers combination has ever been like the ones they'll wear this week.

 

 Green Bay will debut its "Rivalries" uniforms against the Chicago Bears on Sunday. It's a look that includes a desaturated vintage green jersey with alabaster pants and a matching matte helmet. The alabaster color is reminiscent of the aged paper of historic Packers stock certificates, according to the team . With the franchise being publicly owned, fans are able to become shareholders. More than 500,000 homes in Wisconsin include framed stock certificates, which inspired the uniform design. The alabaster jersey numbers feature an engraved treatment modeled after the lettering of paper currency -- a nod to financial support for the team. "Go Pack Go" runs on the back of the helmet, while "Making History Since 1919" is inside the collar. 

 In throwback fashion, the New England Patriots are wearing their "Pat Patriot" look versus the Las Vegas Raiders . The red uniforms include tricolored shoulder stripes with white numbers. White pants and helmets complete the look with the star of the show being Pat Patriot on the lid.

title: Disastrous NFC East Week 5 keeps Cowboys' hopes alive
summary: Somehow no NFC East team got a win, which helps take the edge off Dallas' rough start to the season.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- A Dallas Cowboys season that started with optimism finds itself in peril.

 Twelve games remain in the regular season, starting with Sunday's game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ). At 2-3, the Cowboys find themselves tied for second in the NFC East after Thursday's 24-16 loss to the previously winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers .

 Coach Brian Schottenheimer said the Cowboys "are just getting started" and time is on their side, but can they make the necessary improvement to be anything but a win-one, lose-one team?

 Schottenheimer is now 9-12-1 as the Cowboys' head coach. They have won consecutive games once in his tenure -- Weeks 11-13 last season, when they improved to 6-5-1 overall.

 Since then, Schottenheimer is 3-6.

 "You've got to think more about 'now' than you do 'future,'" owner and general manager Jerry Jones said on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas the day after the loss to the Buccaneers. "That's not in acquiring talent as much as it is how you address practice this week, how you address how we approach playing Green Bay. Now all of this you say, 'We need better answers' and 'We need answers that sound like it could solve it all.' That's just not there, not that answer."

 

 Jones has remained open to making more trades to bolster the roster, but the Cowboys have only four selections left in the 2027 draft (first-, second-, fourth- and seventh-round picks). They dealt their 2028 second-round pick to the Steelers to acquire  Joey Porter Jr . on Oct. 1.

 If they aren't stacking wins, would getting rid of more picks make sense?

 Schottenheimer said he "believes the solution is in the room."

 If it is, then the entire room will need to significantly improve.

 Despite the changes in coaching, scheme and personnel, the Cowboys' defense remains sieve-like. They have allowed at least 378 yards and at least 20 points in each of their first five games.

 Growing pains were expected in Christian Parker's first year as coordinator, but the defense in a lot of ways looks the same as the 2025 unit that finished near the bottom in every category.

 Situationally, the defense has had stunning moments, too, such as giving up a 27-yard completion with seven seconds left to set up the  Baltimore Ravens ' game-winning field goal in Week 3 and allowing the Buccaneers to convert on third-and-21, which led to a touchdown drive. Before that play, teams were 1-of-29 when facing third-and-20 or longer on the season.

 

 Offensively, the Cowboys have not met their own " Greatest Offense There Is " expectation. The run game delivered only 50 yards against the Buccaneers. Turnovers led to defeats in Week 1 (Giants) and Week 5 (Bucs).

 Schottenheimer's game management has come under question in each of the past three weeks, including his playcalling at the end of the Ravens loss in Rio and the decision to opt for a touchback instead of kicking short to run time off the clock; the 65-yard field goal attempt at the end of the first half against the Texans that was missed and led to Houston taking a 10-point lead; and the decision to go for two after the Cowboys cut Tampa Bay's lead to 24-16 with 5:26 to play.

 Analytically, some of the decisions might be correct, but they seem to be made independently of the flow of the game or how the Cowboys are playing defensively.

 "You certainly do react and you kind of see how the game's going," Schottenheimer said. "Sometimes when it's a low-scoring game, you might react a little bit differently than if it's a shootout or based on how you're playing. But it's a little bit of both. And what I can assure you is that the conversations are very, very strong during the week. And then on game day, it's more of a you have the conversation, you react based off of all the factors involved."

 As quarterback, a lot of responsibility on how the Cowboys respond falls on quarterback  Dak Prescott .

 His goal now is to make sure "guys don't lose belief in one another."

 "We control what we do, and whether it's offense, whether it's defense, whether it's just an individual and the way that he prepares and studies and takes care of his body and gives everything to this game," Prescott said. "So for me, it's just about being contagious and saying the right things to make sure my teammates understand that they control and we control our destiny."

 Perhaps the extra time between the Buccaneers loss and Sunday's matchup with the Packers will do the Cowboys' bodies and minds some good. They just played three games in 12 days over two continents, although nobody in the organization used that as an excuse for their poor performance against Tampa Bay.

 

 The saving grace has been the state of the NFC East.

 Week 5 was a disaster for the everyone in the division: The Cowboys suffered their first home loss to a team 0-4 or worse since 1975; the Eagles (2-3) lost after blowing a one-point lead with eight seconds left; and the Giants (3-1-1) and Commanders (1-3-1) played to a tie as Washington saw the clock run out before it could attempt a winning field goal.

 The Giants are atop the division but have lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season. The Eagles are battling injuries and lost right tackle Lane Johnson to retirement last week. The Commanders have already had to play without their quarterback, Jayden Daniels , who wore a brace Sunday in his return from a dislocated left elbow.

 "Thankfully, our division doesn't look like somebody has taken off and run with it, and everything's still in front of us. So that's the beauty of it and that's the unique part about an NFL season and these divisions. You know, we'd feel a lot worse if somebody in our division was 5-0 right now.

 "So, having pretty much everything still out in front of us, gives us, gives myself, all the guys in the locker room, a lot of confidence about what's in front of us."

title: Betting buzz: Who wants to win the NFC East?
summary: Week 5 was one to forget for the NFC East, and all four teams shared in the misery.
full_text:
Everything that happens in sports has additional context when viewed from a sports betting perspective. From season-changing injuries to record-setting moments and so much more, the sports news cycle will constantly and significantly affect the sports betting industry. 

 Our NFL betting buzz file, with contributions from David Purdum, Doug Greenberg and others, aims to provide fans a look at the sports betting stories that are driving the conversation throughout each week of the season.  

 Key links: NFL futures | Awards odds |  Sports betting home  |  DraftKings   

 
 Betting buzz: Who wants to win the NFC East? 
 By Doug Greenberg 

 Week 5 was one to forget for the NFC East, to say the least.

 It started Thursday night when the Dallas Cowboys lost outright to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers after closing as 8.5-point favorites, tied with four other games as the biggest upset of the season, according to DraftKings odds.

 Not only were the Cowboys heavily backed on the spread and in moneyline parlays at multiple sportsbooks, they were also the most popular pick in both ESPN Survivor (40% of the remaining field) and the $1,000-per-entry Circa Survivor (2,554 entries, 42.8% of the remaining field). It's the third time in the season's first five weeks that ESPN Survivor's most popular pick lost.

 

 But the misery didn't end there for the division. The Philadelphia Eagles led off the day in London by seemingly notching a winning field goal with eight seconds left against the Jacksonville Jaguars , giving them a 99.5% chance to win the game, per ESPN Analytics.

 Jacksonville returned the ensuing kickoff to the Philadelphia 35-yard line with one second left, allowing the Jags to kick a winning field goal as time expired. It was the first game in the Super Bowl era that featured two go-ahead field goals in the final 10 seconds of the fourth quarter, according to ESPN Research.

 Then, there was the most bizarre result of the week, possibly the season. The New York Giants and Washington Commanders played a mistake-ridden game into an overtime where neither team scored, including in the matchup's final moments when the Commanders somehow ran out the clock while in field goal range.

 "In the closing minutes and overtime, the live moneyline market was in complete chaos," Joey Feazel, Caesars Sportsbook head of football, told ESPN via email. "Every big play looked like it might decide the game and the book's fate, only for the final whistle to leave everyone staring at the screen wondering what had just happened. It was 90-plus minutes of drama, countless swings in perceived win probability, and in the end, nobody got the outcome they were expecting."

 That's right: None of the NFC East teams recorded a win in Week 5 ... despite two of the teams playing each other.

 Going into "Thursday Night Football," the Cowboys had been the +105 favorites to win the division and immediately dropped to +164 following their upset loss, tying them with the Eagles. After Week 5, Philadelphia is now the slight favorite for the division at +170 -- the longest odds for any division favorite in the league. Next comes Dallas at +180, followed by current division leader New York at +320 and Washington at +750. All of the teams in the NFC East show underdog plus-odds to make the playoffs ... even though one of them has to.

 The Eagles had actually been a top-six favorite for the Super Bowl at 17-1 going into the season, but that number has lengthened to 40-1. The Cowboys are now the Super Bowl favorite among NFC East teams at 30-1 after coming into the season at 25-1.

 The whole situation is made all the more disorienting by the fact that bettors had much higher expectations for this division going into the season. At BetMGM, Dallas is the biggest liability for the NFC championship, having attracted a $10,000 wager at 16-1 odds to win $160,000.

 The Giants provoked a $5,000 wager to win the Super Bowl at 66-1 odds, creating a potential payout of $330,000. New York is also the largest liability to win the NFC East at both BetMGM and DraftKings, with both books also reporting some action for the division on Dallas.

 "The Eagles/Commanders right now are the best-case scenario for the book with the Giants/Cowboys being the best-case scenario for the bettors," Feazel said, "but based on today's events we are not sure that any of these teams would like to win the division."

 

 Sept. 28: Betting buzz: 8.5 the magic number for underdogs 
 

 By Doug Greenberg and David Purdum 

 Big underdogs are having a historic start to the 2026 NFL season, and it's all revolving around one number.

 On Sunday, the Washington Commanders upset the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks after coming into the matchup as 8.5-point underdogs. In Week 2, the New Orleans Saints defeated the Baltimore Ravens outright as 8.5-point underdogs and the Cleveland Browns beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers as underdogs by the same number. And in Week 1, the Arizona Cardinals pulled off the first big upset of the season when they defeated the Los Angeles Chargers ... again, as 8.5-point underdogs.

 The four straight-up wins by underdogs of eight points or greater is the most through three weeks of a season since 1978 when five teams accomplished the feat, according to ESPN Research.

 Only one 8.5-point favorite has survived so far: the Jacksonville Jaguars , who won and covered against the Browns in Week 1. Additionally, the only two favorites of greater than 8.5 -- the San Francisco 49ers (-12.5) in Week 2 and the Kansas City Chiefs (-10) in Week 3 -- also won and covered, both against the Miami Dolphins .

 Because public bettors generally like to back big favorites -- via straight spread wagers, teasers or money-line parlays -- the underdog wins have been a boon to sportsbooks. At DraftKings, Washington's outright win against Seattle during Week 3 was "a good outcome for the book" after the Seahawks became the sportsbook's fourth-most-backed team of the day, pushing the line up from 6.5 earlier in the week, according to a sportsbook representative.

 "The Commanders' win was the most impactful result for the book," Caesars Sportsbook head of football Joey Feazel told ESPN over email. "The news throughout the week created a perfect storm for bettors to focus on Seattle. With Sam Darnold returning and Marcus Mariota starting for Washington, the Seahawks became the perceived 'free square' in parlays."

 Through "Sunday Night Football," underdogs are 7-8 outright in Week 3. If the Chicago Bears win Monday night, it will be the first time that underdogs have gone .500 or better in a week since Week 5 of 2025, according to ESPN Research based on DraftKings odds.

 For the third time in as many weeks this NFL season, the big underdog win also meant carnage for survivor pools: Seattle was the third-most selected team in ESPN Survivor with 11% of the picks, and the second-most selected in Circa Survivor at 12.9%.

 Lawrence's costly kneel 

 With nearly nine minutes remaining in the Jacksonville Jaguars' blowout win over the New England Patriots , quarterback Trevor Lawrence pulled a bizarre move when he took a knee at the 1-yard line, allowing running back Bhayshul Tuten to score on the next play. Lawrence's kneel cost his fantasy owners and benefited Tuten's, but some bettors in Florida really paid the price.

 At Hard Rock Sportsbook, Lawrence's odds to score a touchdown settled at +275 before the game and several bettors included him in long-shot parlays. One such parlay saw the first seven legs hit, and missed out on Lawrence getting in the endzone as the eighth and final leg. The $10 ticket would have paid out $11,323.72.

 Another saw a $2,000 five-leg parlay hit on only four of its legs, including Lawrence over 16.5 rushing yards, but missed on Lawrence anytime touchdown, denying a $33,339.20 payday. Ouch.

title: Judging overreactions to NFL Week 5: Time for Titans to look for another QB?
summary: Is Cam Ward already on the hot seat? Is the NFC East doomed to mediocrity (or worse)? We're judging Week 5 overreactions.
full_text:
Did we overreact to the Raiders' 3-0 start? To the Packers' rough beginning? To Drake Maye 's early-season struggles? Almost assuredly, yes.

 But that's OK. Early-season overreactions are like that. We jump in headfirst with either zero or minimal knowledge about who these teams are or what they're going to turn out to be, make our guesses and watch to see how we did every week as evidence piles up.

 Even now, five weeks in, the season is still a baby. We have some better ideas about how things might go. The Eagles look as if they could be in real trouble, given three straight tough losses and their ever-deepening roster holes. The Vikings might need to be taken more seriously if their offense is going to come around; the Cowboys might not.

 But everything we say here today could easily look silly five weeks from now. But that is part of the fun and is certainly not going to stand in the way of the Week 5 Overreactions column, where we look at five potential takeaways and judge them as legitimate stances or irrational exaggerations. Plus, we hit a few fantasy football overreactions at the bottom.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 NFC East winner will be below .500? 
 Titans looking for another QB in 2027? 
 Jaguars going to their first Super Bowl? 
 Bailey favorite for DROY? 
 NFC West has three best NFC teams? 
 Fantasy overreactions 

 
 

 

 The NFC East winner will have a losing record this season 
 The week opened with the Cowboys laying a major egg at home on Thursday against the previously winless Buccaneers to drop to 2-3. Sunday morning opened with Philadelphia giving the Jaguars everything they had but still losing a brutal heartbreaker in London to drop to 2-3. Then came a Giants-Commanders game no one wanted to win. The Giants fumbled on a promising drive late in overtime. Then Washington quarterback  Jayden Daniels brain-locked on the final play of overtime, seeming to forget his team had no timeouts and watching the clock run out even though the Commanders were in field goal range.

 That left the Commanders at 1-3-1 and the Giants in first place at 3-1-1 but down to their second-string quarterback for the rest of the season. The Giants have beaten the Cowboys and tied with the Commanders. Washington has lost to Dallas and Philadelphia and tied the Giants. The whole thing is a mess. And frankly, none of these teams looks very good.

 

 Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION 

 This might be disrespectful to the 3-1-1 Giants, and I apologize if it is. But not having quarterback Jaxson Dart or star edge rusher Brian Burns for the rest of the season is going to be tough to overcome. Their schedule still includes trips to Houston, Philly, Seattle and Detroit, along with home games against the Jaguars and the 49ers.

 The Cowboys' defense looks no better than it did last season. Dallas has December road games against the Seahawks and the Rams and home games against the Jaguars and the 49ers. The Eagles are without their top three running backs and are also missing four of their Week 1 starting offensive linemen, and their final four games of the season include a home contest versus Seattle and a game at San Francisco. The Commanders -- well, after Sunday, I think we can just say we aren't going to give them much of a shot.

 

 We do love when the NFC East is a big, jumbled, confusing mess, and that's exactly what it is. But it's tough to look at any of these teams and feel good about their chances of them winning more games than they'll lose.

 

 

 The Titans are going to be looking for a quarterback again in next year's draft 

 Tennessee selected Cam Ward  with the  No. 1 pick  in the 2025 draft. It  fired coach Brian Callahan during Ward's rookie season and replaced him this offseason with Robert Saleh, who brought Brian Daboll to be offensive coordinator . It's safe to say things haven't worked the way the Titans had hoped just yet.

 Tennessee is 0-5 after Sunday's listless 26-3 loss to the previously winless Texans. Through five games, Ward has completed 63.2% of his passes, with three touchdowns and three interceptions. He has been sacked 10 times. His QBR on Sunday was a season-low 12.8. Tennessee had high hopes after Ward finished last season strong, but he has not made progress, and Saleh was fielding questions about Ward's status as the team's starting quarterback after Sunday's outing. Saleh said Ward was safe. But there's a lot of season left, and the Titans would surely like to see some progress soon.

 

 Verdict: OVERREACTION 

 

 This was a close one, but I'm still going to give Ward and Daboll a chance to show more than they have. Ward wasn't a controversial No. 1 pick. Many people around the league believed at the time (and entering this season) that he had the tools and the makeup to be a franchise quarterback. He has had five lousy games in a new system, and I understand feeling discouraged. But the Titans have no reason to bench Ward. He gets 12 more games to show he can still be the guy they believed him to be when they drafted him. That's a lot of games. If you believed in Ward two months ago, it's too soon to give up.

 
 

 The Jaguars are going to the Super Bowl 
 It might have taken a late-game miracle, but Jacksonville beat the Eagles on Sunday in London to improve to 4-1. Dating to the middle of last season, Jacksonville has won 13 of 16. The Jaguars been good and consistent on both sides of the ball this season, and the success quarterback Trevor Lawrence has had under coach Liam Coen appears sustainable.

 Jacksonville has given Lawrence a wide receiver corps that fits his strengths. The Jags are still working on the run game, but it shows promise. They play in the AFC South, where the second-place team is the 2-3 Colts. Only four of the Jags' remaining 12 games are against teams that currently have winning records. Jacksonville is positioned to grab the top seed in the AFC playoffs if things keep going the way they have to start the campaign.

 Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION 

 The Chiefs could still have something to say about this. The Bills have looked good. The Patriots are rounding into form in a big way . The AFC North is going to produce at least one tough playoff team. I guess the Broncos could still make some noise. So, there are potential contenders in the AFC, for sure.

 But honestly, none of them has played better than Jacksonville since Week 9 last season. The public might not be inclined to take the Jaguars seriously as a contender, since they rarely have been throughout their three-decade-plus history. But the Jaguars use that skepticism as a chip on their shoulder. And while they should have lost Sunday, the teams that go all the way are the ones that figure out how to win games they should lose during the season. So, don't ignore what the Jaguars are doing; they're sticking around.

 

 

 

 

 David Bailey will be the Defensive Rookie of the Year 
 Hey, the Jets beat the Browns 17-12 on Sunday. It was kind of gross, but wasn't that what you were expecting? Bailey, the No. 2 pick in April's draft, had three sacks. He now has five on the season, putting him on pace for 17. And sure, New York faced this rickety version of Deshaun Watson and a Browns offense full of rookies, but that offense certainly wasn't a pushover entering Sunday's game. It was a strong defensive effort by the Jets, led by their star rookie. And now, New York is 2-3 ahead of a game at New England next week.

 Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION 

 Generally, the person who wins this award is a guy who gets a lot of sacks or a lot of interceptions. And I'm on the record in saying this Jets team is going to be OK this season; if so, that also will help Bailey's case. While I doubt the Jets will make the playoffs, I wouldn't be stunned if they did.

 

 New York's offense has mostly looked good, and the defense has shown it can play at a high level. Both need more consistency. But if the Jets hang around and continue to be a tough team to play…

title: Texans' win over Titans might have broken Terrible Towel curse
summary: After ripping a Terrible Towel following January's playoff win over Pittsburgh, Texans mascot Toro attempted to reverse the team's fortunes.
full_text:
The Houston Texans might finally be free of the Terrible Towel curse. After Texans mascot Toro ripped a Pittsburgh Steelers rally towel following Houston's 30-6 wild-card victory on Jan. 12 , things quickly went downhill.

 The Texans  lost 28-16 to New England in the divisional round and opened the 2026 season with four consecutive losses.

 But Sunday's 26-3 victory over the Tennessee Titans might have finally ended their bad luck.

 Toro appeared ready to make amends, posting a video of himself using tape and glue to piece the torn towel back together. The Texans aren't the first team in recent memory to experience a string of misfortune after disrespecting Pittsburgh's iconic rally towel. During the 2023 season, Jacksonville Jaguars safety Andrew Wingard grabbed a Terrible Towel and waved it in celebration during Week 8 victory over Pittsburgh.

 The Jaguars went 3-6 the rest of the way, missing the playoffs after a late-season collapse that also helped the Steelers secure a postseason berth.

 Whether Houston's victory over Tennessee officially ends the curse remains to be seen. But the Texans will have an opportunity to test the theory when they host the Steelers in Week 13.

 And this time, Toro might want to leave the towel intact.

title: How NFL pros such as Matt Stafford gain perspective from coaching their kids
summary: ESPN spoke to 16 NFL players about what it's like to coach their children and what it means to spend that time with them.
full_text:
IT WAS THE middle of April, and Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford was drawing up a play on a whiteboard on the sideline of a youth flag football game.

 He was surrounded by a group that included his three oldest daughters -- Chandler (9), Sawyer (9) and Hunter (8) -- as he described how to read a quarterback's eyes and attack the run.

 Stafford's daughters, who expressed interest in playing the sport after watching a girls flag football camp at the Rams' facility last year, were supposed to be coached by a local high school student. But after a conflict came up with the student's schedule, Stafford said all eyes turned to him.

 "Everybody just kind of looked at me and was like, 'I mean ... it should be you,'" Stafford told ESPN.

 Stafford's team won the championship, but he said his focus was trying to teach the players -- six girls and four boys -- the fundamentals of flag football.

 "I tried to keep it as simple as I possibly could," Stafford said. "We kind of just lined up and played the same defense all the time and tried to keep it simple for them so they could go play and have fun."

 Stafford is one of many current NFL players who coach their kids in sports that include football, soccer, baseball, basketball and golf. ESPN spoke to 16 of those players about what it's like to coach their children and what it means to spend that time with them.

 New England Patriots right tackle Morgan Moses said he gets recognized at games when coaching his sons -- Isaiah (11), Jeremiah (10) and Legend (8) -- in youth football during the spring.

 "It's funny because a lot of the parents from the opposing team are like, 'They're running NFL plays!'" Moses said.

 

 Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, said he didn't lean too hard on his NFL expertise.

 "I'm just a dad out there at that point," Stafford said. "I could scheme up some stuff, but can we execute it? Probably not.

 "I'd draw something up, we'd run the play, I'd look at my sheet and be like, 'That's not anything what I thought I was going to get,' but we score a touchdown on it."

 

 LOS ANGELES CHARGERS outside linebacker Bud Dupree  said he will never forget when his sons -- Jett (8) and Ace (6) -- told him that they wanted to play flag football. Jett was 4 when he joined a team rather than just playing around with his dad and brother.

 Dupree said it was important to him that he coached his sons because he has seen how much youth sports has changed from when he was a kid.

 "A lot of coaches are in it for the wrong reasons," Dupree said. "A lot of coaches are gambling on the games. They yelling at the kids that never played sports in their life.

 "So, I want to make sure that [when they're young what] they're doing is not necessarily focused on all wins. It's focused on maturing in the game, getting better at the actual sport and learning from the mistakes that they playing and understanding the actual game of football."

 Dupree created several teams called BD Elite. His sons play on the 8U team, but he also has 10U, 15U team and 18U teams.

 

 "I started it for my kids, but along the way, I just wanted to reach as many kids as I could, and I took upon that to make it stand, man," Dupree said. "Now, I'm trying to get kids in college, give them scholarships, taking on that. It's not only affecting my kids' life, but affecting other kids."

 Carolina Panthers long snapper JJ Jansen coaches sons Luke, 13, and Ben, 7, in baseball. Jansen called coaching his "greatest passion," saying, "[It] takes up a lot of my time because I want it to take up a lot of my time." For the past five years, Jansen said he has coached during the NFL season and spends time during the week thinking about how he can "positively impact" the kids on his team.

 "Everything from scripting practice, thinking through how they each should develop in their own way," Jansen said. "One of my absolute favorite things to do is scripting out practice and going through each player, thinking, 'What do they need? What are the skills they need to develop? What [are] the strategies they need to learn?' I spend way too much time on it, but I love it."

 When Jaguars quarterback Nick Mullens ' son, Luke, 7,  started his first season of coach-pitch baseball in Birmingham, Alabama, Mullens told the head coach of his son's team he was available to help if needed but didn't want too much authority.

 The offer was gladly accepted. The first part, anyway.

 "A week into practice, I was the second in command," Mullens said. "The first practice, I was timid, but three practices in, you're like, 'All right, listen up.' And the kids start listening to you a little bit, so I really enjoy that aspect of it. It's a lot of fun."

 Moses said his goal is simple: for the kids on his team to learn the fundamentals of football.

 "I told everybody I really don't care if we win or lose, I just want the kids to walk away knowing they learned great football strategy," Moses said. "So when they leave, and if they don't play on my team the following year, they have a set of fundamentals they can lean on."

 

 EVEN THOUGH MULLENS is entering his NFL ninth season (20 starts) and was coaching his son in Birmingham, Alabama, the town right next to Hoover, Alabama, where he grew up and attended high school, he didn't get recognized much by other parents or coaches. Which meant he was inevitably going to be asked, "What do you do for a living?" by those parents and coaches as the league is active in the NFL offseason.

 At first, he was reluctant to tell them he was a professional football player because he knew the conversation would then revolve around that, and he'd rather talk to the other parents and coaches about their professions. So, he'd sometimes ... embellish a bit about his career.

 Such as the time he told someone he worked for a logistics company. But that presented a different problem for him.

 "Then, they keep asking you questions. You've got to make stuff up as you go," he joked. "So I've been down that path, and it's like, 'Dude, you're better off just telling people what you do.'"

 Jansen has done most of his coaching with former Panthers tight end Greg Olsen, who gets more attention than Jansen.

 "I think my younger kids get a kick out of it," Jansen said. "My older kids, it's a little bit of, like -- it's not an eye roll. It's just sort of like, 'Oh, here we go again.'"

 

 Jaguars punter Logan Cooke said he gets recognized by parents at times when helping coach his 5-year-old Cooper play T-ball, but the fact that he's a Pro Bowl punter means absolutely nothing to the players.

 "I'm not Trevor Lawrence walking out there so there's always subtle comments about it, good luck this weekend, stuff like that," he said. "But the kids have no idea, and they wouldn't even care. They're so young."

 

 FORMER NEW ENGLAND Patriots quarterback Brian Hoyer  serves as the offensive coordinator for the freshman football team at Xaverian Brothers High School in Westwood, Massachusetts, where his son, Garrett, is the starting quarterback.

 Hoyer, who played in the NFL from 2009 to 2023, was helping coach the varsity team after former NFL quarterback -- and Xaverian alum -- Matt Hasselbeck convinced him to help out. Hasselbeck served as the team's quarterbacks coach while his son Henry was in high school. 

 But when a coaching change left the freshman team without an offensive coordinator, Hoyer was asked if he wanted to take over.

 "I could have never guessed what it was going to entail," Hoyer said. "That started with basically creating a whole new offensive playbook, but tailored to the freshman level.

 "Understanding what freshman football is -- it's been forever since I've been exposed to it. You have kids playing football for the first time. It's been an adventure."

 This season is the first time Hoyer has coached his son and said, "It's a little bit unique coaching him as a freshman in high school for the first time because…

title: NFL trade deadline grades: Marvin Harrison Jr. to Texans; Cam Jurgens to Ravens
summary: Will Marvin Harrison Jr. boost Houston's offense? Can Cam Jurgens fill the Ravens' hole at center? We're grading NFL trades ahead of November's deadline.
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which is Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for the first four deals of trading season:  J.J. McCarthy  to the Giants,  Joey Porter Jr . to the Cowboys,  Cam Jurgens  to the Ravens and  Marvin Harrison Jr . to the Texans. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 

 Cardinals trade WR Harrison Jr. to Texans 
 Texans get: WR  Marvin Harrison Jr ., 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Cardinals get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick

 Texans grade: C+ 
 Cardinals: A-

 Minutes after the Texans completed their 26-3 blowout win over the Titans, news broke that the rumored trade of Harrison, who was inactive Sunday because of the expected move, would be completed. The Cardinals sent him to Houston for a second-rounder and a sixth-rounder in 2027.

 Similar to a lot of trades for young players, there are two simple questions: How much of our opinion of Harrison should be shaped by the league's predraft opinion of him and how much should be based on what we've seen from him in the NFL so far?

 Harrison was considered a premier wide receiver prospect and was the first non-quarterback off the board with the fourth pick in the 2024 draft. But his production has fallen well short of those expectations to date, with Harrison amassing 1,578 receiving yards over 33 career games.

 That equates to 1.5 yards per route run, which is in the 46th percentile among wide receivers who have run at least 15 routes per team game in that span. That number has been even worse in a small sample this season: just 0.6 yards per route run with a much higher percentage of deep fades and go routes (24%) than the previous two seasons (13%). Harrison's player-tracking metrics have been mediocre but not awful during his first two seasons: 47 and 54 overall in ESPN's receiver scores (with slightly better open scores) in 2024 and 2025, respectively.

 

 Despite a rough start, the 1-4 Texans probably still believe they have a Super Bowl-caliber defense and a chance for a postseason run if they can get more talent around quarterback C.J. Stroud , who has been playing well. I don't think that's far-fetched despite their record. This is not the Texans' first attempt to upgrade at wide receiver. After second-year man Jayden Higgins suffered a torn ACL in August, Houston acquired   Kayshon Boutte from the Patriots. But Boutte has managed only 1.1 yards per route run despite Nico Collins missing two games .

 The Texans will get Harrison for cheap for the rest of this season and next year, and they will have a fifth-year option on him for 2028. But this move is not worth it if Harrison remains the same player he has been with the Cardinals because second-round picks have real value. Receivers who average 1.5 yards per route run can be found quite easily. The Texans are betting that Harrison can reach the upside he showed at Ohio State, including a breakout season in 2022 when Stroud was his quarterback. Having already played two-plus NFL seasons, the chances of a breakout aren't great, but they exist.

 I think this trade makes sense for Arizona. The Cardinals didn't have to trade Harrison yet , but he will be worth more to a contending team than he is to them. It's likely his trade value would sink if they waited until the offseason to deal him. And Michael Wilson already had established himself as Arizona's No. 1 receiver.

 Ultimately, I would not have made this trade if I were the Texans because the odds of Harrison breaking out immediately feel too low to justify the compensation. But I at least understand the thought process and desire to maximize a loaded roster's chances of making a real run to make the playoffs and win postseason games. -- Walder 

 
 

 Eagles trade C Jurgens to Ravens 
 Ravens get: C Cam Jurgens , 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

 Ravens grade: D+ 
 Eagles grade: A

 First, Tyler Linderbaum walked in free agency . Then the Ravens lost Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic to injury , suddenly leaving them without a center. Last week, Baltimore moved first-round rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane to center but evidently doesn't see that as a long-term option.

 So Baltimore turned to the trade market and dealt for Jurgens. It's an interesting and unusual move, because Jurgens is no stopgap. He's only 27 years old and is already on a long-term deal after signing an extension with the Eagles in 2025.

 Jurgens moved from center to left guard in Week 2 after the Eagles placed guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve . It has not gone well. Jurgens ranks in the bottom three in both pass block and run block win rate at guard. But the Ravens are trading for Jurgens to have him play center.

 In 2024, Jurgens was a Pro Bowl center who recorded pass block and run block win rates in the 80th and 50th percentiles, respectively. He made the Pro Bowl again in 2025, but his numbers slipped to the 65th and 39th percentile, respectively. He should be a stabilizing force for the Ravens -- perhaps an average to above-average center -- at what has suddenly become a position of need. But the cost is exorbitant.

 

 The Ravens are surrendering a second-round pick (plus a swap of fifth- and seventh-round picks) for the right to pay a non-premium position player market price after this season. Jurgens is due a fully guaranteed $16 million next year. He's due $17 million (non-guaranteed) in 2028 and 2029. Jurgens' $17 million average per year for the duration of his contract makes him the fourth-highest-paid center in the league, behind only Linderbaum, Creed Humphrey and Aaron Brewer , per OverTheCap.com . By comparison,  Connor McGovern , who had better numbers than Jurgens last season, makes a little over $13 million per year.

 One saving grace for Baltimore is that Jurgens' salary is cheap this season . The Eagles have already paid Jurgens' option bonus, so the Ravens should be on the hook for only the remaining portion of his $1.2 million base salary.

 For the Eagles, the loss of Jurgens is the latest blow to an offensive line that is already down Dickerson and recently retired tackle Lane Johnson . Jurgens hadn't played well at guard, but surely they saw him as their long-term center. Drew Kendall , who has played center after Jurgens' shift, has been below average in both pass and run block win rate this season. But the Eagles seemed to believe this was a price too good to pass up.

 I understand that the Ravens rightfully believe they are Super Bowl contenders, probably want Ioane to stay and develop at guard and thought they needed to fill their gap at center. Making a trade before the deadline to fix that issue makes sense. But almost certainly there would have been cheaper options out there than this. And the timing is odd, considering that Jurgens is currently in concussion protocol and not expected to play Sunday.

 So it seems like the Eagles sensed Baltimore's desperation and squeezed an overpay out of the Ravens. -- Walder

title: How Drake Maye has rebounded from bad start despite mounting Patriots injuries
summary: Has Maye found his confidence ... and his deep ball? A dominant Week 5 win over the Raiders suggests he turned things around, even as New England struggles to stay healthy.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. --  Drake Maye is rolling again and his New England Patriots teammates can't help but take notice.

 "It's just fun to see Drake smiling big on the sidelines. That confidence is obviously back," linebacker Robert Spillane said in the aftermath of Sunday's 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders  (3-2).

 Maye's turnaround from the first three games of the season has been dramatic. After throwing only one touchdown with six interceptions in the team's 1-2 start, and being sacked nine times, he has completed 67.6% of his passes with seven touchdowns and one interception over the past two games, while being sacked only twice.

 Maye had a season-high 96.0 Total QBR -- the third best of his career -- against the Raiders while benefitting from strong offensive line play (only two pressures in the first half) that he said allowed him to "eat a ham sandwich" in the pocket on his first scoring pass because of how much time had. Maye became the first player this season with a Total QBR of 90 or better in back-to-back games. His Total QBR over the first three games was 49.

 One thing that worked well Sunday was Maye's deep ball. He finished 6-of-9 for 182 yards and two touchdown passes on throws 15-plus yards downfield, which tied for his second-most such completions in a game in his career. In the Patriots' first four games of the season, he completed only 43.8% of those throws with one total TD.

 

 "That's our leader," receiver  DeMario "Pop" Douglas  said of the 24-year-old Maye. "How he carries himself means a lot. It's by example. I feel like for us, we need to carry ourselves that way too -- ups and downs, you still have to stay straight.

 "From those past games, anybody could have been down on themselves. Not him. He came to work, and he was still like, 'I need you. I got your back.' That's what has been taking us to the next step."

 Maye earned game balls from coach Mike Vrabel each of the past two weeks. When Vrabel presented it to him after a Week 4 road win over the Buffalo Bills , he told him that the time for taking flak from detractors was over, according to video on Patriots.com. Maye and the Patriots (3-2) look to continue the surge Sunday when they host the New York Jets (2-3).

 The shift has come despite a run of injuries ravaging the depth chart, especially at receiver, running back, fullback and along the offensive line. And Maye still sees "juice left to squeeze" with the offense, pointing out the unit has yet to produce a turnover-free game.

 He said Sunday that he took joy in watching 2026 first-round pick Caleb Lomu thrust into a challenging spot at left tackle in place of injured Will Campbell , as well as others such as Douglas (four catches, 65 yards, two TDs) and Kyle Williams (three catches, 91 yards, TD) seizing an expanded receiving role because of injuries to A.J. Brown (ankle) and Mack Hollins (calf).

 Likewise, the Patriots might need to rely more on No. 3 running back Corey Kiner and practice-squad rusher Lan Larison after losing speedy TreVeyon Henderson to an ankle injury Sunday .

 The Patriots also won Sunday despite playing with only three healthy cornerbacks, as veteran Kindle Vildor  -- who was signed to the 53-man roster from the practice squad the day before -- earned a game ball for his competitive coverage and a forced fumble.

 "I'm just proud of the guys for stepping up -- offense, defense, overall as a football team," Maye said. "We talk about 'identity' with Coach Vrabel. That's a Coach Vrabel football team.

 

 "I think one of the best things about my position is being able to spread the wealth and watch guys succeed. It's beautiful to watch."

 Summing up his two-game surge, Maye said his confidence has never wavered.

 "It's really just an example of practice execution showing up in the game," he said. "That's the biggest thing I can maybe hint at."

title: NFL Week 5 trolls: Jets social media jab at Browns leads the way
summary: Teams celebrated their wins by trolling their opponents on social media -- who had the best troll of Week 5?
full_text:
As the NFL season settles into October, trolls will only get (pumpkin) spicier, and such was the case in Week 5.

 

 Through the rain, the New York Jets found a way to bounce the Cleveland Browns with a 17-12 win in front of their home crowd. Jets running back Braelon Allen led the way with 116 rushing yards and a touchdown, followed by wide receiver Garrett Wilson's 104 receiving yards and a touchdown.

 Quarterback Geno Smith finished the game with 182 passing yards and a touchdown.

 After their win, the Jets ran to social media with a clever troll that has Cleveland Brown[s] all over it -- literally. They posted a photo of the character Cleveland Brown, featured on the hit animated television shows "Family Guy" and "The Cleveland Show," but instead of wearing his usual yellow shirt, he wore a green shirt with a Jets cap.

 

 The Jets weren't the only team to get its trolling on after a win. Here are the best trolls from Week 5 in the NFL.

 

 Pittsburgh Steelers 34, Indianapolis Colts 22 

 The Steelers advanced to 3-0 on their home turf after a win that saw quarterback Aaron Rodgers throw for 235 yards and three touchdowns -- two to tight end Pat Freiermuth and one to running back Jaylen Warren . Pittsburgh took the win and ran with it, resulting in a series of trolls. The game's final score graphic was captioned "Hold your horses," while two more posts showed a clip of a horse looking at the final score and a reference to the "Parks and Rec" pony "Little Sebastian."

 

 

 Cincinnati Bengals 31, Miami Dolphins 24 

 Cincinnati extended  Miami 's winless season with a 31-24 home win, led by quarterback Joe Burrow 's four touchdown passes to four different Bengals: Ja'Marr Chase , Tanner Hudson , Samaje Perine  and Mike Gesicki . Cincinnati chose to lean into the lore of the popular video game "Grand Theft Auto." The latest edition of the game, expected to be released next month, takes place in the fictional "Vice City," which is heavily inspired by Miami.

 

 

 Tampa Bay Buccaneers 24, Dallas Cowboys 16 

 Tampa Bay collected its first win of the season on "Thursday Night Football" in the Cowboys ' AT&T Stadium, led by running back Bucky Irving 's 165 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels stepped up in his second start in place of Baker Mayfield , while  Emeka Egbuka also scored a touchdown for the Bucs.

 What's a win over the Cowboys without a troll?

 The Buccaneers leaned on the environment for a proper troll against Dallas, which plays in a climate-controlled dome. Their troll was a thermostat labeled "WIN."

title: Steelers' Warren having strong run while Dowdle is out
summary: Warren had an impressive Week 5 performance against the Colts, marking his third consecutive week of at least 125 all-purpose yards.
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- Even after a 50-yard sprint through the heart of the Indianapolis Colts ' defense, Jaylen Warren exploded for a final burst of energy as he crossed the goal line for the second time Sunday afternoon.  
 
 Warren high-stepped and kicked his feet out in front of him, skip-hopping into the end zone with safety A.J. Haulcy still trailing 5 yards behind him.  
 
 Not only was it a historic moment as Warren became the first player since Herschel Walker in 1986 to record a 50-yard touchdown run and an 80-yard touchdown reception in the same game, but the score and ensuing celebration was also a microcosm of the tough, yet fun-loving demeanor that has led to Warren's long-awaited coming out party over the past three weeks. 
 
 "He's just such a slippery player," quarterback Aaron Rodgers said after the Steelers' 34-22 win . "First guy rarely brings him down. He's good inside the tackles, good outside of tackles, always moving forward, always spinning, slipping out of plays, finishing runs. 
 
 "He's one of the most liked players on the team, and guys want to block for him on the offensive line, and the tight ends and the receivers and just really enjoy his energy from start to finish every day of the week and enjoy what he does for us."  
 
 
 
 And what he did for the Steelers in their Week 5 win was impressive: 15 carries for 101 rushing yards; six receptions on six targets for 87 receiving yards; and, of course, the two touchdowns. All of that amounted to 188 all-purpose yards, marking his third consecutive week of at least 125 all-purpose yards. No Steelers player has had at least 125 scrimmage yards in three straight weeks since James Conner did it four weeks in a row in 2018.  
 
 With the Steelers' defense holding Colts running back Jonathan Taylor , the league's third-highest paid at the position, to 45 yards on 15 carries, Warren was undeniably the best back in the stadium Sunday afternoon. 
 
 "I've always believed in myself wherever they put me, whatever tier they put me in," Warren said. "It's credit to my O-line. [Taylor and I] exchanged a couple words after the game, and it meant a lot coming from someone like him, JT, premier back. 
 
 "So, whatever tier somebody wants to put me in, that's what it is, but I've always believed in myself." 
 
 Since earning a spot on the roster with a standout training camp performance as a rookie UDFA in 2022, Warren has almost always been part of a split backfield. That was coach Mike McCarthy's vision, too, when the team signed free agent Rico Dowdle in the offseason. But with Dowdle still recovering from a twice-dislocated toe in the Week 2 loss to the New England Patriots , Warren was forced into the spotlight. He took it -- and quite literally -- ran with it. Since Week 3, Warren has played at least 85% of the Steelers' offensive snaps. 
 
 "Whenever my name's called, I got to seize the moment," Warren said. "And with Rico being down, obviously it sucks, but knowing he's one day closer to coming back, I feel like I can hold it down until then."  
 
 McCarthy said Sunday that the Steelers hope to have Dowdle back on the field in Week 6 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , but the coach admitted Warren has thrived with a heavier workload. 
 
 "He's the man," McCarthy said of Warren. "He's hauling it right now for us. There's a number you'd like to continue to give him. He's produced, so it's been heavy. It'd be great to get Rico back this week, too. ... Having him as a one-two punch was the vision of this offense, but Jaylen's crushing it right now. He's been awesome for us."  
 
 In his five-year career, Warren has played more than 60% of offensive snaps in only nine of his 69 career regular-season games. Last season, he shared snaps with team MVP Kenneth Gainwell . And in his first three seasons, Warren often split reps -- and often fairly evenly -- with 2021 first-round pick Najee Harris . But that hasn't stopped Warren from constantly preparing as if he's going to shoulder the load. 
 
 "The things he does in practice, he continues to finish, and while everyone stops running, he's taking off 80 yards just to do it," left tackle Troy Fautanu said. "And when he comes out here and does things like that and breaks runs off, I'm not surprised because that's the stuff that he practices every day. He deserves it." 
 
 Before his third-quarter 50-yard score, Warren jump-started the Steelers' offense in the first quarter with an 80-yard catch-and-run score. With the flat wide open, Warren caught the short pass from Rodgers and accelerated to the sideline as wide receiver DK Metcalf paved the way ahead by blocking Colts defensive backs Charvarius Ward and Cam Bynum . 
 
 "His contact balance is just unreal, and he finishes every play," defensive lineman Cameron Heyward said. "That dude does not have a bad day, and we put a lot on his shoulders, but he's able to deliver."  
 
 Because of his rotational role for most of his career, Warren has flown under the radar in conversations about the league's best running backs. Rodgers, though, believes Warren should start getting more respect. 
 
 "I'm not really on the social media checking out what the scuttlebutt is about the great players in the league," Rodgers said. "But yeah, he should."
